51|def _unpack_args(
52|    args: cabc.Sequence[str], nargs_spec: cabc.Sequence[int]
53|) -> tuple[cabc.Sequence[str | cabc.Sequence[str | T_UNSET] | T_UNSET], list[str]]:
54|    """Given an iterable of arguments and an iterable of nargs specifications,
55|    it returns a tuple with all the unpacked arguments at the first index
56|    and all remaining arguments as the second.
57|
58|    The nargs specification is the number of arguments that should be consumed
59|    or `-1` to indicate that this position should eat up all the remainders.
60|
61|    Missing items are filled with ``UNSET``.
62|    """
63|    args = deque(args)
64|    nargs_spec = deque(nargs_spec)
65|    rv: list[str | tuple[str | T_UNSET, ...] | T_UNSET] = []
66|    spos: int | None = None
67|
68|    def _fetch(c: deque[str]) -> str | T_UNSET:
69|        try:
70|            if spos is None:
71|                return c.popleft()
72|            else:
73|                return c.pop()
74|        except IndexError:
75|            return UNSET
76|
77|    while nargs_spec:
78|        if spos is None:
79|            nargs = nargs_spec.popleft()
80|        else:
81|            nargs = nargs_spec.pop()
82|
83|        if nargs == 1:
84|            rv.append(_fetch(args))
85|        elif nargs > 1:
86|            x: list[str | T_UNSET] = [_fetch(args) for _ in range(nargs)]
87|
88|            # If we're reversed, we're pulling in the arguments in reverse,
89|            # so we need to turn them around.
90|            if spos is not None:
91|                x.reverse()
92|
93|            rv.append(tuple(x))
94|        elif nargs < 0:
95|            if spos is not None:
96|                raise TypeError("Cannot have two nargs < 0")
97|
98|            spos = len(rv)
99|            rv.append(UNSET)
100|
101|    # spos is the position of the wildcard (star).  If it's not `None`,
102|    # we fill it with the remainder.
103|    if spos is not None:
104|        rv[spos] = tuple(args)
105|        args = []
106|        rv[spos + 1 :] = reversed(rv[spos + 1 :])
107|
108|    return tuple(rv), list(args)

111|def _split_opt(opt: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
112|    first = opt[:1]
113|    if first.isalnum():
114|        return "", opt
115|    if opt[1:2] == first:
116|        return opt[:2], opt[2:]
117|    return first, opt[1:]

120|def _normalize_opt(opt: str, ctx: Context | None) -> str:
121|    if ctx is None or ctx.token_normalize_func is None:
122|        return opt
123|    prefix, opt = _split_opt(opt)
124|    return f"{prefix}{ctx.token_normalize_func(opt)}"

127|class _Option:
128|    def __init__(
129|        self,
130|        obj: CoreOption,
131|        opts: cabc.Sequence[str],
132|        dest: str | None,
133|        action: str | None = None,
134|        nargs: int = 1,
135|        const: t.Any | None = None,
136|    ):
137|        self._short_opts = []
138|        self._long_opts = []
139|        self.prefixes: set[str] = set()
140|
141|        for opt in opts:
142|            prefix, value = _split_opt(opt)
143|            if not prefix:
144|                raise ValueError(
145|                    _("Invalid start character for option ({option})").format(
146|                        option=opt
147|                    )
148|                )
149|            self.prefixes.add(prefix[0])
150|            if len(prefix) == 1 and len(value) == 1:
151|                self._short_opts.append(opt)
152|            else:
153|                self._long_opts.append(opt)
154|                self.prefixes.add(prefix)
155|
156|        if action is None:
157|            action = "store"
158|
159|        self.dest = dest
160|        self.action = action
161|        self.nargs = nargs
162|        self.const = const
163|        self.obj = obj
164|
165|    @property
166|    def takes_value(self) -> bool:
167|        return self.action in ("store", "append")
168|
169|    def process(self, value: t.Any, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
170|        if self.action == "store":
171|            state.opts[self.dest] = value  # type: ignore
172|        elif self.action == "store_const":
173|            state.opts[self.dest] = self.const  # type: ignore
174|        elif self.action == "append":
175|            state.opts.setdefault(self.dest, []).append(value)  # type: ignore
176|        elif self.action == "append_const":
177|            state.opts.setdefault(self.dest, []).append(self.const)  # type: ignore
178|        elif self.action == "count":
179|            state.opts[self.dest] = state.opts.get(self.dest, 0) + 1  # type: ignore
180|        else:
181|            raise ValueError(f"unknown action '{self.action}'")
182|        state.order.append(self.obj)

185|class _Argument:
186|    def __init__(self, obj: CoreArgument, dest: str | None, nargs: int = 1):
187|        self.dest = dest
188|        self.nargs = nargs
189|        self.obj = obj
190|
191|    def process(
192|        self,
193|        value: str | cabc.Sequence[str | T_UNSET] | T_UNSET,
194|        state: _ParsingState,
195|    ) -> None:
196|        if self.nargs > 1:
197|            assert isinstance(value, cabc.Sequence)
198|            holes = sum(x is UNSET for x in value)
199|            if holes == len(value):
200|                value = UNSET
201|            elif holes != 0:
202|                raise BadArgumentUsage(
203|                    _("Argument {name!r} takes {nargs} values.").format(
204|                        name=self.dest, nargs=self.nargs
205|                    )
206|                )
207|
208|        # We failed to collect any argument value so we consider the argument as unset.
209|        if value == ():
210|            value = UNSET
211|
212|        state.opts[self.dest] = value  # type: ignore
213|        state.order.append(self.obj)

224|class _OptionParser:
225|    """The option parser is an internal class that is ultimately used to
226|    parse options and arguments.  It's modelled after optparse and brings
227|    a similar but vastly simplified API.  It should generally not be used
228|    directly as the high level Click classes wrap it for you.
229|
230|    It's not nearly as extensible as optparse or argparse as it does not
231|    implement features that are implemented on a higher level (such as
232|    types or defaults).
233|
234|    :param ctx: optionally the :class:`~click.Context` where this parser
235|                should go with.
236|
237|    .. deprecated:: 8.2
238|        Will be removed in Click 9.0.
239|    """
240|
241|    def __init__(self, ctx: Context | None = None) -> None:
242|        #: The :class:`~click.Context` for this parser.  This might be
243|        #: `None` for some advanced use cases.
244|        self.ctx = ctx
245|        #: This controls how the parser deals with interspersed arguments.
246|        #: If this is set to `False`, the parser will stop on the first
247|        #: non-option.  Click uses this to implement nested subcommands
248|        #: safely.
249|        self.allow_interspersed_args: bool = True
250|        #: This tells the parser how to deal with unknown options.  By
251|        #: default it will error out (which is sensible), but there is a
252|        #: second mode where it will ignore it and continue processing
253|        #: after shifting all the unknown options into the resulting args.
254|        self.ignore_unknown_options: bool = False
255|
256|        if ctx is not None:
257|            self.allow_interspersed_args = ctx.allow_interspersed_args
258|            self.ignore_unknown_options = ctx.ignore_unknown_options
259|
260|        self._short_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
261|        self._long_opt: dict[str, _Option] = {}
262|        self._opt_prefixes = {"-", "--"}
263|        self._args: list[_Argument] = []
264|
265|    def add_option(
266|        self,
267|        obj: CoreOption,
268|        opts: cabc.Sequence[str],
269|        dest: str | None,
270|        action: str | None = None,
271|        nargs: int = 1,
272|        const: t.Any | None = None,
273|    ) -> None:
274|        """Adds a new option named `dest` to the parser.  The destination
275|        is not inferred (unlike with optparse) and needs to be explicitly
276|        provided.  Action can be any of ``store``, ``store_const``,
277|        ``append``, ``append_const`` or ``count``.
278|
279|        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
280|        that is returned from the parser.
281|        """
282|        opts = [_normalize_opt(opt, self.ctx) for opt in opts]
283|        option = _Option(obj, opts, dest, action=action, nargs=nargs, const=const)
284|        self._opt_prefixes.update(option.prefixes)
285|        for opt in option._short_opts:
286|            self._short_opt[opt] = option
287|        for opt in option._long_opts:
288|            self._long_opt[opt] = option
289|
290|    def add_argument(self, obj: CoreArgument, dest: str | None, nargs: int = 1) -> None:
291|        """Adds a positional argument named `dest` to the parser.
292|
293|        The `obj` can be used to identify the option in the order list
294|        that is returned from the parser.
295|        """
296|        self._args.append(_Argument(obj, dest=dest, nargs=nargs))
297|
298|    def parse_args(
299|        self, args: list[str]
300|    ) -> tuple[dict[str, t.Any], list[str], list[CoreParameter]]:
301|        """Parses positional arguments and returns ``(values, args, order)``
302|        for the parsed options and arguments as well as the leftover
303|        arguments if there are any.  The order is a list of objects as they
304|        appear on the command line.  If arguments appear multiple times they
305|        will be memorized multiple times as well.
306|        """
307|        state = _ParsingState(args)
308|        try:
309|            self._process_args_for_options(state)
310|            self._process_args_for_args(state)
311|        except UsageError:
312|            if self.ctx is None or not self.ctx.resilient_parsing:
313|                raise
314|        return state.opts, state.largs, state.order
315|
316|    def _process_args_for_args(self, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
317|        pargs, args = _unpack_args(
318|            state.largs + state.rargs, [x.nargs for x in self._args]
319|        )
320|
321|        for idx, arg in enumerate(self._args):
322|            arg.process(pargs[idx], state)
323|
324|        state.largs = args
325|        state.rargs = []

327|    def _process_args_for_options(self, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
328|        while state.rargs:
329|            arg = state.rargs.pop(0)
330|            arglen = len(arg)
331|            # Double dashes always handled explicitly regardless of what
332|            # prefixes are valid.
333|            if arg == "--":
334|                return
335|            elif arg[:1] in self._opt_prefixes and arglen > 1:
336|                self._process_opts(arg, state)
337|            elif self.allow_interspersed_args:
338|                state.largs.append(arg)
339|            else:
340|                state.rargs.insert(0, arg)
341|                return
342|
343|        # Say this is the original argument list:
344|        # [arg0, arg1, ..., arg(i-1), arg(i), arg(i+1), ..., arg(N-1)]
345|        #                            ^
346|        # (we are about to process arg(i)).
347|        #
348|        # Then rargs is [arg(i), ..., arg(N-1)] and largs is a *subset* of
349|        # [arg0, ..., arg(i-1)] (any options and their arguments will have
350|        # been removed from largs).
351|        #
352|        # The while loop will usually consume 1 or more arguments per pass.
353|        # If it consumes 1 (eg. arg is an option that takes no arguments),
354|        # then after _process_arg() is done the situation is:
355|        #
356|        #   largs = subset of [arg0, ..., arg(i)]
357|        #   rargs = [arg(i+1), ..., arg(N-1)]
358|        #
359|        # If allow_interspersed_args is false, largs will always be
360|        # *empty* -- still a subset of [arg0, ..., arg(i-1)], but
361|        # not a very interesting subset!
362|
363|    def _match_long_opt(
364|        self, opt: str, explicit_value: str | None, state: _ParsingState
365|    ) -> None:
366|        if opt not in self._long_opt:
367|            raise NoSuchOption(opt, possibilities=self._long_opt, ctx=self.ctx)
368|
369|        option = self._long_opt[opt]
370|        if option.takes_value:
371|            # At this point it's safe to modify rargs by injecting the
372|            # explicit value, because no exception is raised in this
373|            # branch.  This means that the inserted value will be fully
374|            # consumed.
375|            if explicit_value is not None:
376|                state.rargs.insert(0, explicit_value)
377|
378|            value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
379|
380|        elif explicit_value is not None:
381|            raise BadOptionUsage(
382|                opt, _("Option {name!r} does not take a value.").format(name=opt)
383|            )
384|
385|        else:
386|            value = UNSET
387|
388|        option.process(value, state)
389|
390|    def _match_short_opt(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
391|        stop = False
392|        i = 1
393|        prefix = arg[0]
394|        unknown_options = []
395|
396|        for ch in arg[1:]:
397|            opt = _normalize_opt(f"{prefix}{ch}", self.ctx)
398|            option = self._short_opt.get(opt)
399|            i += 1
400|
401|            if not option:
402|                if self.ignore_unknown_options:
403|                    unknown_options.append(ch)
404|                    continue
405|                raise NoSuchOption(opt, ctx=self.ctx)
406|            if option.takes_value:
407|                # Any characters left in arg?  Pretend they're the
408|                # next arg, and stop consuming characters of arg.
409|                if i < len(arg):
410|                    state.rargs.insert(0, arg[i:])
411|                    stop = True
412|
413|                value = self._get_value_from_state(opt, option, state)
414|
415|            else:
416|                value = UNSET
417|
418|            option.process(value, state)
419|
420|            if stop:
421|                break
422|
423|        # If we got any unknown options we recombine the string of the
424|        # remaining options and re-attach the prefix, then report that
425|        # to the state as new large.  This way there is basic combinatorics
426|        # that can be achieved while still ignoring unknown arguments.
427|        if self.ignore_unknown_options and unknown_options:
428|            state.largs.append(f"{prefix}{''.join(unknown_options)}")
429|
430|    def _get_value_from_state(
431|        self, option_name: str, option: _Option, state: _ParsingState
432|    ) -> str | cabc.Sequence[str] | T_UNSET | T_FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE:
433|        nargs = option.nargs
434|
435|        value: str | cabc.Sequence[str] | T_UNSET | T_FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
436|
437|        if len(state.rargs) < nargs:
438|            if option.obj._flag_needs_value:
439|                # Option allows omitting the value.
440|                value = FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
441|            else:
442|                raise BadOptionUsage(
443|                    option_name,
444|                    ngettext(
445|                        "Option {name!r} requires an argument.",
446|                        "Option {name!r} requires {nargs} arguments.",
447|                        nargs,
448|                    ).format(name=option_name, nargs=nargs),
449|                )
450|        elif nargs == 1:
451|            next_rarg = state.rargs[0]
452|
453|            if (
454|                option.obj._flag_needs_value
455|                and isinstance(next_rarg, str)
456|                and next_rarg[:1] in self._opt_prefixes
457|                and len(next_rarg) > 1
458|            ):
459|                # The next arg looks like the start of an option, don't
460|                # use it as the value if omitting the value is allowed.
461|                value = FLAG_NEEDS_VALUE
462|            else:
463|                value = state.rargs.pop(0)
464|        else:
465|            value = tuple(state.rargs[:nargs])
466|            del state.rargs[:nargs]
467|
468|        return value
469|
470|    def _process_opts(self, arg: str, state: _ParsingState) -> None:
471|        explicit_value = None
472|        # Long option handling happens in two parts.  The first part is
473|        # supporting explicitly attached values.  In any case, we will try
474|        # to long match the option first.
475|        if "=" in arg:
476|            long_opt, explicit_value = arg.split("=", 1)
477|        else:
478|            long_opt = arg
479|        norm_long_opt = _normalize_opt(long_opt, self.ctx)
480|
481|        # At this point we will match the (assumed) long option through
482|        # the long option matching code.  Note that this allows options
483|        # like "-foo" to be matched as long options.
484|        try:
485|            self._match_long_opt(norm_long_opt, explicit_value, state)
486|        except NoSuchOption:
487|            # At this point the long option matching failed, and we need
488|            # to try with short options.  However there is a special rule
489|            # which says, that if we have a two character options prefix
490|            # (applies to "--foo" for instance), we do not dispatch to the
491|            # short option code and will instead raise the no option
492|            # error.
493|            if arg[:2] not in self._opt_prefixes:
494|                self._match_short_opt(arg, state)
495|                return
496|
497|            if not self.ignore_unknown_options:
498|                raise
499|
500|            state.largs.append(arg)

31|def wrap_text(
32|    text: str,
33|    width: int = 78,
34|    initial_indent: str = "",
35|    subsequent_indent: str = "",
36|    preserve_paragraphs: bool = False,
37|) -> str:
38|    """A helper function that intelligently wraps text.  By default, it
39|    assumes that it operates on a single paragraph of text but if the
40|    `preserve_paragraphs` parameter is provided it will intelligently
41|    handle paragraphs (defined by two empty lines).
42|
43|    If paragraphs are handled, a paragraph can be prefixed with an empty
44|    line containing the ``\\b`` character (``\\x08``) to indicate that
45|    no rewrapping should happen in that block.
46|
47|    :param text: the text that should be rewrapped.
48|    :param width: the maximum width for the text.
49|    :param initial_indent: the initial indent that should be placed on the
50|                           first line as a string.
51|    :param subsequent_indent: the indent string that should be placed on
52|                              each consecutive line.
53|    :param preserve_paragraphs: if this flag is set then the wrapping will
54|                                intelligently handle paragraphs.
55|
56|    .. versionchanged:: 8.4.0
57|        Width is measured in visible characters. ANSI escape sequences in
58|        ``text``, ``initial_indent``, or ``subsequent_indent`` no longer
59|        count toward the width budget, so styled input wraps based on what
60|        the user sees instead of raw byte length.
61|    """
62|    from ._textwrap import TextWrapper
63|
64|    text = text.expandtabs()
65|    wrapper = TextWrapper(
66|        width,
67|        initial_indent=initial_indent,
68|        subsequent_indent=subsequent_indent,
69|        replace_whitespace=False,
70|    )
71|    if not preserve_paragraphs:
72|        return wrapper.fill(text)
73|
74|    p: list[tuple[int, bool, str]] = []
75|    buf: list[str] = []
76|    indent = None
77|
78|    def _flush_par() -> None:
79|        if not buf:
80|            return
81|        if buf[0].strip() == "\b":
82|            p.append((indent or 0, True, "\n".join(buf[1:])))
83|        else:
84|            p.append((indent or 0, False, " ".join(buf)))
85|        del buf[:]
86|
87|    for line in text.splitlines():
88|        if not line:
89|            _flush_par()
90|            indent = None
91|        else:
92|            if indent is None:
93|                orig_len = term_len(line)
94|                line = line.lstrip()
95|                indent = orig_len - term_len(line)
96|            buf.append(line)
97|    _flush_par()
98|
99|    rv = []
100|    for indent, raw, text in p:
101|        with wrapper.extra_indent(" " * indent):
102|            if raw:
103|                rv.append(wrapper.indent_only(text))
104|            else:
105|                rv.append(wrapper.fill(text))
106|
107|    return "\n\n".join(rv)

110|class HelpFormatter:

113|    exposed so that developers can write their own fancy outputs.
114|

123|    width: int

127|    def __init__(
128|        self,

156|        self.current_indent -= self.indent_increment

158|    def write_usage(self, prog: str, args: str = "", prefix: str | None = None) -> None:
159|        """Writes a usage line into the buffer.

163|        :param prefix: The prefix for the first line. Defaults to
164|            ``"Usage: "``.

166|        if prefix is None:
167|            prefix = "{usage} ".format(usage=_("Usage:"))
168|
169|        usage_prefix = f"{prefix:>{self.current_indent}}{prog} "
170|        text_width = self.width - self.current_indent
171|
172|        if not args:

174|            # call that would normally place args on the line are both
175|            # unnecessary. Emit just the prefix line.
176|            self.write(usage_prefix.rstrip(" "))
177|            self.write("\n")

180|        if text_width >= (term_len(usage_prefix) + 20):
181|            # The arguments will fit to the right of the prefix.
182|            indent = " " * term_len(usage_prefix)

188|                    subsequent_indent=indent,
189|                )
190|            )
191|        else:
192|            # The prefix is too long, put the arguments on the next line.
193|            self.write(usage_prefix)
194|            self.write("\n")

196|            self.write(

304|    way and returns them in the form ``(formatted_string,

383|class _PagerWriter:
384|    """Wrap a pager's output stream to strip ANSI styling when colors are
385|    disabled.
386|
387|    The wrapped stream is owned by the pager strategy that produced it, so this
388|    wrapper never closes it: ``_pipepager`` closes its pipe to signal EOF to the
389|    pager process, ``_tempfilepager`` closes and removes its temporary file, and
390|    ``_nullpager`` leaves an external stream such as ``sys.stdout`` untouched.
391|

393|    is handled here, so it doesn't strip a second time (see
394|    :func:`._compat.should_strip_ansi`).

397|    def __init__(self, stream: t.TextIO, color: bool) -> None:
398|        self._stream = stream
399|        self.color = color

401|    def write(self, text: str) -> int:
402|        if not self.color:
403|            text = strip_ansi(text)

405|        return self._stream.write(text)

407|    def writelines(self, lines: cabc.Iterable[str]) -> None:
408|        for line in lines:

416|        # but never close the underlying stream from here.
417|        self._stream.flush()

419|    def __getattr__(self, name: str) -> t.Any:

427|    :mod:`subprocess` docs recommend on every platform for an unqualified name:
428|    https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#popen-constructor

431|    leaving the caller to pick a fallback.

451|def _pager_contextmanager(
452|    color: bool | None = None,

454|    """Decide what method to use for paging through text."""

458|    # pythonw on Windows.

465|    # Split using POSIX mode (the default) so that quote characters are
466|    # stripped from tokens and quoted Windows paths are preserved.
467|    # Non-POSIX mode retains quotes in tokens, and wrapping tokens
468|    # with shlex.quote re-introduces quoting issues on Windows.
469|    pager_cmd_parts = shlex.split(os.environ.get("PAGER", ""))

520|def _less_uses_raw_mode(less_env: str, cmd_params: list[str]) -> bool:

533|        # splitting rather than failing the pager over it.

539|            if token.casefold() == "--raw-control-chars":
540|                return True
541|        elif token.startswith("-") and len(token) > 1:

548|@contextlib.contextmanager
549|def _pipepager(
550|    cmd_path: Path, cmd_params: list[str], color: bool | None = None
551|) -> t.Iterator[tuple[t.TextIO, bool | None]]:
552|    """Page through text by feeding it to another program.

554|    Invokes the pager via :class:`subprocess.Popen` with an ``argv`` list.
555|

557|    ``less`` and the user hasn't decided on colors, ``LESS=-R`` is set
558|    automatically.

563|    env = dict(os.environ)
564|
565|    # If we're piping to less and the user hasn't decided on colors, we enable
566|    # them: either the invocation already requests raw control characters, or
567|    # ``LESS=-R`` is injected. Match on the stem so a resolved ``less.exe`` is
568|    # recognized like bare ``less``, case-insensitively on Windows since its
569|    # filesystems are. POSIX keeps an exact match.
570|    cmd_name = cmd_path.stem
571|    if WIN:
572|        # ``_pager_contextmanager`` currently routes every Windows invocation
573|        # to ``_tempfilepager``, so this branch is not reachable on Windows
574|        # today: it keeps the detection correct should that routing ever
575|        # change.
576|        cmd_name = cmd_name.casefold()
577|
578|    if color is None and cmd_name == "less":

580|        if _less_uses_raw_mode(less_env, cmd_params):

582|        elif not less_env and not cmd_params:
583|            env["LESS"] = "-R"

586|    c = subprocess.Popen(

588|        shell=False,
589|        stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
590|        env=env,
591|        errors="replace",
592|        text=True,
593|    )
594|    # With ``text=True``, ``c.stdin`` is already a text stream that encodes
595|    # writes for the pager process (honoring ``errors="replace"``).
596|    stdin = t.cast(t.TextIO, c.stdin)

598|        yield stdin, color

601|        pass
602|    except Exception as e:

623|        #

625|        # `LESS='-K'`. It's not our decision to make.

635|@contextlib.contextmanager
636|def _tempfilepager(
637|    cmd_path: Path, cmd_params: list[str], color: bool | None = None
638|) -> t.Iterator[tuple[t.TextIO, bool | None]]:
639|    """Page through text by invoking a program on a temporary file.

642|    ``more`` adds spurious ``\\r\\n``), and as a fallback on other
643|    platforms. The command is invoked with any parameters from ``PAGER``

647|    import tempfile

651|    # while Python still has it open, so we use delete=False and clean up manually
652|    # rather than using a contextmanager here.
653|    f = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(
654|        mode="w", encoding=encoding, errors="replace", delete=False

657|        yield t.cast(t.TextIO, f), color

659|        f.close()
660|        subprocess.call([str(cmd_path), *cmd_params, f.name])
661|    finally:
662|        # An error raised while paging skips the close() above, and Windows
663|        # refuses to unlink a file the process still holds open. Closing here
664|        # keeps that PermissionError from replacing the original exception.
665|        # close() is idempotent, so this is a no-op on the success path.
666|        f.close()
667|        os.unlink(f.name)

11|def _truncate_visible(text: str, n: int) -> str:
12|    """Return the longest prefix of ``text`` containing at most ``n`` visible
13|    characters.
14|
15|    ANSI escape sequences inside the prefix are kept intact and do not count
16|    toward the visible width. A cut is never placed inside an escape sequence.
17|    """
18|    if n <= 0:
19|        return ""
20|
21|    visible = 0
22|    i = 0
23|    cut = 0
24|    end = len(text)
25|    while i < end:
26|        m = _ansi_re.match(text, i)
27|        if m is not None:
28|            i = m.end()
29|            continue
30|        visible += 1
31|        i += 1
32|        cut = i
33|        if visible >= n:
34|            break
35|    return text[:cut]

38|class TextWrapper(textwrap.TextWrapper):
39|    """``textwrap.TextWrapper`` variant that measures widths by visible
40|    character count.
41|
42|    ANSI escape sequences embedded in chunks, indents, or the placeholder are
43|    excluded from the width budget. Without this, styled help text (a styled
44|    ``Usage:`` prefix, a colorized option name, ...) would be wrapped earlier
45|    than its visible length warrants and tokens would split mid-word.
46|    """
47|
48|    def _handle_long_word(
49|        self,
50|        reversed_chunks: list[str],
51|        cur_line: list[str],
52|        cur_len: int,
53|        width: int,
54|    ) -> None:
55|        space_left = max(width - cur_len, 1)
56|
57|        if self.break_long_words:
58|            last = reversed_chunks[-1]
59|            cut = _truncate_visible(last, space_left)
60|            res = last[len(cut) :]
61|            cur_line.append(cut)
62|            reversed_chunks[-1] = res
63|        elif not cur_line:
64|            cur_line.append(reversed_chunks.pop())
65|
66|    def _wrap_chunks(self, chunks: list[str]) -> list[str]:
67|        """Wrap chunks counting widths in visible characters.
68|
69|        Mirrors the algorithm of :meth:`textwrap.TextWrapper._wrap_chunks`
70|        with every width measurement routed through
71|        :func:`click._compat.term_len` instead of :func:`len`, so ANSI escape
72|        bytes in chunks, indents, or the placeholder do not inflate the count.
73|
74|        .. seealso::
75|            :class:`textwrap.TextWrapper` in the Python standard library documentation:
76|            https://docs.python.org/3/library/textwrap.html#textwrap.TextWrapper
77|
78|            Reference implementation in CPython:
79|            https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/textwrap.py
80|        """
81|        lines: list[str] = []
82|        if self.width <= 0:
83|            raise ValueError(f"invalid width {self.width!r} (must be > 0)")
84|        if self.max_lines is not None:
85|            if self.max_lines > 1:
86|                indent = self.subsequent_indent
87|            else:
88|                indent = self.initial_indent
89|            if term_len(indent) + term_len(self.placeholder.lstrip()) > self.width:
90|                raise ValueError("placeholder too large for max width")
91|
92|        chunks.reverse()
93|
94|        while chunks:
95|            cur_line: list[str] = []
96|            cur_len = 0
97|
98|            if lines:
99|                indent = self.subsequent_indent
100|            else:
101|                indent = self.initial_indent
102|
103|            width = self.width - term_len(indent)
104|
105|            if self.drop_whitespace and chunks[-1].strip() == "" and lines:
106|                del chunks[-1]
107|
108|            while chunks:
109|                n = term_len(chunks[-1])
110|
111|                if cur_len + n <= width:
112|                    cur_line.append(chunks.pop())
113|                    cur_len += n
114|
115|                else:
116|                    break
117|
118|            if chunks and term_len(chunks[-1]) > width:
119|                self._handle_long_word(chunks, cur_line, cur_len, width)
120|                cur_len = sum(map(term_len, cur_line))
121|
122|            if self.drop_whitespace and cur_line and cur_line[-1].strip() == "":
123|                cur_len -= term_len(cur_line[-1])
124|                del cur_line[-1]
125|
126|            if cur_line:
127|                if (
128|                    self.max_lines is None
129|                    or len(lines) + 1 < self.max_lines
130|                    or (
131|                        not chunks
132|                        or self.drop_whitespace
133|                        and len(chunks) == 1
134|                        and not chunks[0].strip()
135|                    )
136|                    and cur_len <= width

138|                    lines.append(indent + "".join(cur_line))

783|        cwd = os.getcwd()
784|        dt = tempfile.mkdtemp(dir=temp_dir)
785|        os.chdir(dt)
786|
787|        try:
788|            yield dt
789|        finally:
790|            os.chdir(cwd)
791|
792|            if temp_dir is None:
793|                import shutil
794|
795|                try:
796|                    shutil.rmtree(dt)
797|                except OSError:

2|
3|# Options
4|
5|```{eval-rst}
6|.. currentmodule:: click
7|```
8|
9|Adding options to commands can be accomplished with the {func}`option`
10|decorator. At runtime the decorator invokes the {class}`Option` class. Options
11|in Click are distinct from {ref}`positional arguments <arguments>`.
12|
13|Useful and often used kwargs are:
14|
15|- `default`: Passes a default.
16|- `help`: Sets help message.
17|- `nargs`: Sets the number of arguments.
18|- `required`: Makes option required.
19|- `type`: Sets {ref}`parameter type <parameter-types>`
20|
21|```{contents}
22|:depth: 2
23|:local: true
24|```
25|
26|## Option Decorator
27|
28|The {func}`option()` decorator is usually passed two positional arguments: the
29|option name and the decorated function argument name.
30|
31|```{eval-rst}
32|.. click:example::
33|
34|    @click.command()
35|    @click.option('--string-to-echo', 'string_to_echo')
36|    def echo(string_to_echo):
37|        click.echo(string_to_echo)
38|
39|
40|.. click:run::
41|
42|    invoke(echo, args=['--help'])
43|```
44|
45|However, if the decorated function argument name is not passed in, then Click
46|will try to infer it. A simple way to name the option so that Click will infer
47|it correctly is by taking the function argument, adding two dashes to the front
48|and converting underscores to dashes.
49|
50|```{eval-rst}
51|.. click:example::
52|
53|    @click.command()
54|    @click.option('--string-to-echo')
55|    def echo(string_to_echo):
56|        click.echo(string_to_echo)
57|
58|.. click:run::
59|
60|    invoke(echo, args=['--string-to-echo', 'Hi!'])
61|```
62|
63|More formally, Click will try to infer the decorated function argument name as
64|follows:
65|
66|1. If a positional argument is a valid [Python identifier](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#identifiers) (and thus does not have dashes), it is chosen.
67|2. If multiple positional arguments are prefixed with `--`, the first one
68|  declared is chosen.
69|3. Otherwise, the first positional argument prefixed with `-` is chosen.
70|
71|To get the argument name, the chosen positional argument is converted to lower
72|case, a leading `-` or `--` is removed if found, and any remaining `-`
73|characters are replaced with `_`.
74|
75|```{eval-rst}
76|.. list-table:: Examples
77|    :widths: 15 15
78|    :header-rows: 1
79|
80|    * - Decorator Arguments
81|      - Inferred Argument Name
82|    * - ``"-f", "--foo-bar"``
83|      - foo_bar
84|    * - ``"-x"``
85|      - x
86|    * - ``"-f", "--filename", "dest"``
87|      - dest
88|    * - ``"--CamelCase"``
89|      - camelcase
90|    * - ``"-f", "-fb"``
91|      - f
92|    * - ``"--f", "--foo-bar"``
93|      - f
94|    * - ``"---f"``
95|      - _f
96|```
97|
98|## Basic Example
99|
100|A simple {class}`click.Option` takes one option name. By default, it's assumed
101|that the decorated function argument is not required and the expected type is
102|`str`. If the decorated function takes a positional argument but the option is
103|not passed with the command, then `None` is passed.
104|
105|```{eval-rst}
106|.. click:example::
107|
108|    @click.command()
109|    @click.option('--text')
110|    def print_this(text):
111|        click.echo(text)
112|
113|
114|.. click:run::
115|
116|    invoke(print_this, args=['--text=this'])
117|
118|    invoke(print_this, args=[])
119|
120|
121|.. click:run::
122|
123|    invoke(print_this, args=['--help'])
124|
125|```
126|
127|## Setting a Default
128|
129|Instead of setting the `type`, you may set a default and Click will try to infer
130|the type.
131|
132|```{eval-rst}
133|.. click:example::
134|
135|    @click.command()
136|    @click.option('--n', default=1)
137|    def dots(n):
138|        click.echo('.' * n)
139|
140|.. click:run::
141|
142|    invoke(dots, args=['--help'])
143|```
144|
145|## Multi Value Options
146|
147|To make an option take multiple values, pass in `nargs`. Note you may pass in
148|any positive integer, but not -1. The values are passed to the decorated
149|function as a tuple.
150|
151|```{eval-rst}
152|.. click:example::
153|
154|    @click.command()
155|    @click.option('--pos', nargs=2, type=float)
156|    def findme(pos):
157|        a, b = pos
158|        click.echo(f"{a} / {b}")
159|
160|.. click:run::
161|
162|    invoke(findme, args=['--pos', '2.0', '3.0'])
163|
164|```
165|
166|(tuple-type)=
167|
168|## Multi Value Options as Tuples
169|
170|```{versionadded} 4.0
171|```
172|
173|By setting `nargs` to a specific number, each item in
174|the resulting tuple is of the same type. Alternatively, you might want to use
175|different types for different indexes in
176|the tuple. For this you can directly specify a tuple as `type`:
177|
178|```{eval-rst}
179|.. click:example::
180|
181|    @click.command()
182|    @click.option('--item', type=(str, int))
183|    def putitem(item):
184|        name, id = item
185|        click.echo(f"name={name} id={id}")
186|
187|
188|And on the command line:
189|
190|.. click:run::
191|
192|    invoke(putitem, args=['--item', 'peter', '1338'])
193|```
194|
195|By using a tuple literal as the `type`, `nargs` gets automatically set to the
196|length of the tuple and the {class}`click.Tuple` type is automatically
197|used. The above example is thus equivalent to this:
198|
199|```{eval-rst}
200|.. click:example::
201|
202|    @click.command()
203|    @click.option('--item', nargs=2, type=click.Tuple([str, int]))
204|    def putitem(item):
205|        name, id = item
206|        click.echo(f"name={name} id={id}")
207|```
208|
209|(multiple-options)=
210|
211|## Multiple Options
212|
213|The multiple options format allows options to take an arbitrary number of
214|arguments (which is called variadic). The arguments are passed to the decorated
215|function as a tuple. If set, `default` must be a list or tuple. Setting a string
216|as `default` will be interpreted as a list of characters.
217|
218|```{eval-rst}
219|.. click:example::
220|
221|    @click.command()
222|    @click.option('--message', '-m', multiple=True)
223|    def commit(message):
224|        click.echo(message)
225|        for m in message:
226|            click.echo(m)
227|
228|.. click:run::
229|
230|    invoke(commit, args=['-m', 'foo', '-m', 'bar', '-m', 'here'])
231|```
232|
233|## Combining short options
234|
235|Short options made of a single character can be combined into one argument: `-abc` is equivalent to `-a -b -c`. This is the standard POSIX behavior for short option stacking, and it is the reason a repeated flag like `-vvv` works with the [Counting](#counting) feature.
236|
237|```{eval-rst}
238|.. click:example::
239|
240|    @click.command()
241|    @click.option('-a', is_flag=True)
242|    @click.option('-b', is_flag=True)
243|    @click.option('-c', is_flag=True)
244|    def cli(a, b, c):
245|        click.echo(f"a={a} b={b} c={c}")
246|
247|.. click:run::
248|
249|    invoke(cli, args=['-a', '-b', '-c'])
250|    invoke(cli, args=['-abc'])
251|```
252|
253|If the last option in the combination takes a value, the value can either follow as the next argument or be attached directly:
254|
255|```{eval-rst}
256|.. click:example::
257|
258|    @click.command()
259|    @click.option('-v', is_flag=True)
260|    @click.option('-n', type=int)
261|    def cli(v, n):
262|        click.echo(f"v={v} n={n}")
263|
264|.. click:run::
265|
266|    invoke(cli, args=['-v', '-n', '5'])
267|    invoke(cli, args=['-vn', '5'])
268|    invoke(cli, args=['-vn5'])
269|```
270|
271|```{note}
272|Multi-character short option names are not supported. An argument like `-dbg` is interpreted as the combination of `-d`, `-b`, and `-g`, so Click reports `No such option: -d` if `-d` is not declared. For longer option names, use a long option with the `--` prefix (like `--debug`).
273|```
274|
275|## Counting
276|
277|To count the occurrence of an option, set `count=True`. If the option is not
278|passed on the command line, then the count is 0. Counting is commonly used for
279|verbosity.
280|
281|```{eval-rst}
282|.. click:example::
283|
284|    @click.command()
285|    @click.option('-v', '--verbose', count=True)
286|    def log(verbose):
287|        click.echo(f"Verbosity: {verbose}")
288|
289|.. click:run::
290|
291|    invoke(log, args=[])
292|    invoke(log, args=['-vvv'])
293|```
294|
295|(option-boolean-flag)=
296|
297|## Boolean
298|
299|Boolean options (boolean flags) take the values `True` or `False`. The simplest
300|case sets the default value to `False` if the flag is not passed, and `True` if
301|it is.
302|
303|```{eval-rst}
304|.. click:example::
305|
306|    import sys
307|
308|    @click.command()
309|    @click.option('--shout', is_flag=True)
310|    def info(shout):
311|        rv = sys.platform
312|        if shout:
313|            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
314|        click.echo(rv)
315|
316|
317|.. click:run::
318|
319|    invoke(info)
320|    invoke(info, args=['--shout'])
321|
322|```
323|
324|To implement this more explicitly, declare `--{on-option}/--{off-option}`. Click
325|will automatically set `is_flag=True`.
326|
327|```{eval-rst}
328|.. click:example::
329|
330|    import sys
331|
332|    @click.command()
333|    @click.option('--shout/--no-shout', default=False)
334|    def info(shout):
335|        rv = sys.platform
336|        if shout:
337|            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
338|        click.echo(rv)
339|
340|.. click:run::
341|
342|    invoke(info)
343|    invoke(info, args=['--shout'])
344|    invoke(info, args=['--no-shout'])
345|```
346|
347|Use cases for this more explicit pattern include:
348|
349|* The default can be dynamic so the user can explicitly specify the option with
350|  either on or off option, or pass in no option to use the dynamic default.
351|* Shell scripts sometimes want to be explicit even when it's the default
352|* Shell aliases can set a flag, then an invocation can add a negation of the
353|  flag
354|
355|If a forward slash (`/`) is contained in your option name already, you can split
356|the parameters using `;`. In Windows `/` is commonly used as the prefix
357|character.
358|
359|```{eval-rst}
360|.. click:example::
361|
362|    @click.command()
363|    @click.option('/debug;/no-debug')
364|    def log(debug):
365|        click.echo(f"debug={debug}")
366|```
367|
368|```{versionchanged} 6.0
369|```
370|
371|If you want to define an alias for the second option only, then you will need to
372|use leading whitespace to disambiguate the format string.
373|
374|```{eval-rst}
375|.. click:example::
376|
377|    import sys
378|
379|    @click.command()
380|    @click.option('--shout/--no-shout', ' /-N', default=False)
381|    def info(shout):
382|        rv = sys.platform
383|        if shout:
384|            rv = rv.upper() + '!!!!111'
385|        click.echo(rv)
386|
387|.. click:run::
388|
389|    invoke(info, args=['--help'])
390|```
391|
392|## Flag Value
393|
394|To have a flag pass a value to the decorated function set `flag_value`. This
395|automatically sets `is_flag=True`. To mark the flag as default, set
396|`default=True`. Setting flag values can be used to create patterns like this:
397|
398|```{eval-rst}
399|.. click:example::
400|
401|    import sys
402|
403|    @click.command()
404|    @click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)
405|    @click.option('--lower', 'transformation', flag_value='lower')
406|    def info(transformation):
407|        click.echo(getattr(sys.platform, transformation)())
408|
409|.. click:run::
410|
411|    invoke(info, args=['--help'])
412|    invoke(info, args=['--upper'])
413|    invoke(info, args=['--lower'])
414|    invoke(info)
415|```
416|
417|### How `default` and `flag_value` interact
418|
419|The `default` value is given to the underlying function
420|as-is. So if you set `default=None`, the function receives
421|`None`. Same for any other type.
422|
423|But there is a special case for **non-boolean** flags: if a
424|flag has a non-boolean `flag_value` (like a string or a
425|class), then `default=True` is interpreted as *the flag
426|should be activated by default*. The function receives the
427|`flag_value`, not the Python `True`.
428|
429|Which means, in the example above, this option:
430|
431|```python
432|@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default=True)
433|```
434|
435|is equivalent to:
436|
437|```python
438|@click.option('--upper', 'transformation', flag_value='upper', default='upper')
439|```
440|
441|Because the two are equivalent, it is recommended to always
442|use the second form and set `default` to the actual value
443|you want. This makes code more explicit and predictable.
444|
445|This special case does **not** apply to boolean flags (where
446|`flag_value` is `True` or `False`). For boolean flags,
447|`default=True` is the literal Python value `True`.
448|
449|The tables below show the value received by the function for
450|each combination of `default`, `flag_value`, and whether
451|the flag was passed on the command line.
452|
453|#### Boolean flags (`is_flag=True`, boolean `flag_value`)
454|
455|These are flags where `flag_value` is `True` or `False`.
456|The `default` value is always passed through literally
457|without any special substitution.
458|
459|| `default` | `flag_value` | Not passed | `--flag` passed |
460||-----------|--------------|------------|-----------------|
461|| *(unset)* | *(unset)*    | `False`    | `True`          |
462|| `True`    | *(unset)*    | `True`     | `True`          |
463|| `False`   | *(unset)*    | `False`    | `True`          |
464|| `None`    | *(unset)*    | `None`     | `True`          |
465|| `True`    | `True`       | `True`     | `True`          |
466|| `True`    | `False`      | `True`     | `False`         |
467|| `False`   | `True`       | `False`    | `True`          |
468|| `False`   | `False`      | `False`    | `False`         |
469|| `None`    | `True`       | `None`     | `True`          |
470|| `None`    | `False`      | `None`     | `False`         |
471|
472|````{tip}
473|For a negative flag that defaults to off, prefer the
474|explicit pair form `--with-xyz/--without-xyz` over the
475|single-flag `flag_value=False, default=True`:
476|
477|```python
478|@click.option('--with-xyz/--without-xyz', 'enable_xyz', default=True)
479|```
480|````
481|
482|#### Boolean flag pairs (`--flag/--no-flag`)
483|
484|These use secondary option names to provide both an on and
485|off switch. The `default` value is always literal.
486|
487|| `default` | Not passed | `--flag` | `--no-flag` |
488||-----------|------------|----------|-------------|
489|| *(unset)* | `False`    | `True`   | `False`     |
490|| `True`    | `True`     | `True`   | `False`     |
491|| `False`   | `False`    | `True`   | `False`     |
492|| `None`    | `None`     | `True`   | `False`     |
493|
494|#### Non-boolean feature switches (`flag_value` is a string, class, etc.)
495|
496|For these flags, `default=True` is a **special case**: it
497|means "activate this flag by default" and resolves to the
498|`flag_value`. All other `default` values are passed through
499|literally.
500|
501|| `default`  | `flag_value` | Not passed  | `--flag` passed |
502||------------|--------------|-------------|-----------------|
503|| *(unset)*  | `"upper"`    | `None`      | `"upper"`       |
504|| `True`     | `"upper"`    | `"upper"`¹  | `"upper"`       |
505|| `"lower"`  | `"upper"`    | `"lower"`   | `"upper"`       |
506|| `None`     | `"upper"`    | `None`      | `"upper"`       |
507|
508|```{hint}
509|¹: `default=True` is substituted with `flag_value`.
510|```
511|
512|#### Feature switch groups (multiple flags sharing one variable)
513|
514|Several `flag_value` options can target the same parameter name to form a
515|feature switch group. The user picks one flag on the command line, and the
516|function receives the corresponding `flag_value`. When the user picks none,
517|Click falls back to whichever option claims the slot under the arbitration
518|rules described below.
519|
520|##### Non-boolean groups
521|
522|For non-boolean `flag_value` (strings, enum members, classes, ...), place
523|`default=True` on the option that should win when no flag is passed. The
524|substitution rule above resolves it to that option's `flag_value`. Any other
525|explicit `default` is passed through literally.
526|
527|| Definition                                             | Not passed | `--upper` | `--lower` |
528||--------------------------------------------------------|------------|-----------|-----------|
529|| `--upper` with `flag_value='upper'`, `default=True`    | `"upper"`  | `"upper"` | `"lower"` |
530|| `--upper` with `flag_value='upper'`, `default='upper'` | `"upper"`  | `"upper"` | `"lower"` |
531|| `--upper` with `flag_value='upper'`, `default=None`    | `None`     | `"upper"` | `"lower"` |
532|| Neither option carries a `default`                     | `None`     | `"upper"` | `"lower"` |
533|
534|The third row is the three-state pattern: the function receives `None` when no
535|flag is passed, distinguishable from either explicit choice.
536|
537|##### Boolean groups
538|
539|When `flag_value` is `True` or `False`, the substitution rule does not apply:
540|`default=True` is the literal Python `True`. To make one flag in an
541|enable/disable pair the default, set its `default=True` explicitly:
542|
543|```python
544|@click.option("--without-xyz", "enable_xyz", flag_value=False)
545|@click.option("--with-xyz", "enable_xyz", flag_value=True, default=True)
546|```
547|
548|| Definition                                              | Not passed | `--with-xyz` | `--without-xyz` |
549||---------------------------------------------------------|------------|--------------|-----------------|
550|| `--with-xyz` with `flag_value=True`, `default=True`     | `True`     | `True`       | `False`         |
551|| `--without-xyz` with `flag_value=False`, `default=False`| `False`    | `True`       | `False`         |
552|| `--with-xyz` with `flag_value=True`, `default=None`     | `None`     | `True`       | `False`         |
553|| Neither option carries a `default`                      | `False`    | `True`       | `False`         |
554|
555|```{tip}
556|For most enable/disable cases, the pair form `--with-xyz/--without-xyz` is
557|shorter and equivalent. The multi-flag group form is useful when the on and off
558|flags need distinct names without a shared stem, or when each flag needs its
559|own help text.
560|```
561|
562|##### Arbitration rules
563|
564|When several options in a group resolve their values simultaneously, only one
565|wins the parameter slot. The full arbitration policy (source precedence,
566|explicit-beats-auto tie-break, last-declared fallback) is enumerated under
567|[Option value resolution](#option-value-resolution).
568|
569|## Option value resolution
570|
571|This section enumerates the rules Click applies when computing the value
572|delivered to the decorated function for every option. Rules are listed in the
573|order they fire during the parsing pipeline.
574|
575|### Type inference
576|
577|Without an explicit `type=`, Click infers the parameter type at construction:
578|
579|1. If `flag_value` is `True` or `False`, the type is {class}`BoolParamType`.
580|2. If `flag_value` is an `int`, `float`, or `str`, the type is the matching
581|   basic type.
582|3. If `flag_value` is any other Python object (a class, an enum member, a
583|   `frozenset`, ...), the type is {data}`UNPROCESSED` so the value passes
584|   through unchanged.
585|4. Otherwise, the type is inferred from `default` if set, falling back to
586|   {class}`StringParamType` when neither hint is available.
587|
588|### `default` interpretation
589|
590|The literal value passed as `default=` is interpreted differently depending on
591|whether the option is a flag and what `flag_value` it carries:
592|
593|1. `default=UNSET` (the absence sentinel) is treated as if `default` was not
594|   passed at all. It does not count as "the user picked nothing", and it does
595|   not count as an explicit default for arbitration purposes.
596|2. For a bare boolean flag (no `flag_value`, or `flag_value` of `True` or
597|   `False`), an unset `default` auto-derives to `False`.
598|3. For a non-boolean flag with a `flag_value`, `default=True` is substituted
599|   with `flag_value`. This is the "activate this flag by default" shorthand.
600|   Any non-`True` `default` is passed through literally.
601|4. For a boolean flag with `flag_value` set, `default=True` is the literal
602|   Python `True`. The substitution from rule 3 does not apply.
603|5. `default=None` is always a real explicit value, distinct from `UNSET`
604|   absence.
605|6. Any other `default` is delivered to the function unchanged after conversion
606|   through the parameter's type.
607|
608|### Value sources
609|
610|Click resolves the value of every option from the following
611|sources, in order of decreasing precedence:
612|
613|1. **command line input** ({attr}`ParameterSource.COMMANDLINE`),
614|2. **environment variable** named in `envvar=` or derived from `auto_envvar_prefix`
615|   ({attr}`ParameterSource.ENVIRONMENT`),
616|3. **`default_map` entry** matching the parameter name on the active {class}`Context`
617|   ({attr}`ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP`),
618|4. **parameter default** ({attr}`ParameterSource.DEFAULT`).
619|
620|The first source that produces a value wins. Environment variables and
621|`default_map` entries set to `Sentinel.UNSET` are skipped, so they fall through
622|to the next source rather than supplying `UNSET` to the function.
623|
624|If after the four sources above no explicit value was found (or only a
625|`default_map`/`default` value was) and the option declares `prompt=`, Click
626|prompts the user for one. The resulting value is recorded as
627|{attr}`ParameterSource.PROMPT`, which ranks above every source listed above
628|for arbitration purposes (see [Slot arbitration](#slot-arbitration)).
629|
630|### Slot arbitration
631|
632|Several options can target the same `name` to form a feature switch group. When
633|they do, only one option's value reaches the function. Arbitration applies
634|these rules, in order:
635|
636|1. **By source.** Whichever option resolved its value from the most explicit
637|   source wins, regardless of decorator order. Any command-line input beats any
638|   default, an environment variable beats a `default_map` entry, and so on.
639|2. **Within the default tier, explicit beats auto-derived.** An option that
640|   received an explicit `default=` keyword wins over one whose default came
641|   from `default` interpretation.
642|3. **Otherwise, last declared wins.** When all options in the group resolved
643|   from the same source and tier (all auto-derived defaults, or all explicit
644|   defaults), the option declared last in the source code keeps the slot.
645|
646|## Values from Environment Variables
647|
648|To pass in a value from a specific environment variable use `envvar`.
649|
650|```{eval-rst}
651|.. click:example::
652|
653|    @click.command()
654|    @click.option('--username', envvar='USERNAME')
655|    def greet(username):
656|       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")
657|
658|.. click:run::
659|
660|    invoke(greet, env={'USERNAME': 'john'})
661|```
662|
663|If a list is passed to `envvar`, the first environment variable found is picked.
664|
665|```{eval-rst}
666|.. click:example::
667|
668|    @click.command()
669|    @click.option('--username', envvar=['ALT_USERNAME', 'USERNAME'])
670|    def greet(username):
671|       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")
672|
673|.. click:run::
674|
675|    invoke(greet, env={'ALT_USERNAME': 'Bill', 'USERNAME': 'john'})
676|
677|```
678|
679|Variable names are:
680| - [Case-insensitive on Windows but not on other platforms](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/aa9eb5f757ceff461e6e996f12c89e5d9b583b01/Lib/os.py#L777-L789).
681| - Not stripped of whitespace and should match the exact name provided to the
682|   `envvar` argument.
683|
684|For flag options, there are two concepts to consider: the activation of the flag
685|driven by the environment variable, and the value of the flag if it is
686|activated.
687|
688|The values read from environment variables are always strings and will require
689|extra processing. We need to transform these strings into boolean values that
690|will determine if the flag is activated or not.
691|
692|Here are the rules used to parse environment variable values for flag options:
693|   - `true`, `1`, `yes`, `on`, `t`, `y` are interpreted as activating the flag
694|   - `false`, `0`, `no`, `off`, `f`, `n` are interpreted as deactivating the
695|     flag
696|   - The presence of the environment variable without value is interpreted as
697|     deactivating the flag
698|   - Empty strings are interpreted as deactivating the flag
699|   - Values are case-insensitive, so the `True`, `TRUE`, `tRuE` strings are all
700|     interpreted as activating the flag
701|   - Values are stripped of leading and trailing whitespace before being
702|     interpreted, so the `" True "` string is transformed to `"true"` and thus
703|     activates the flag
704|   - If the flag option has a `flag_value` argument, passing that value in the
705|     environment variable will activate the flag, in addition to all the cases
706|     described above
707|   - Any other value is interpreted as deactivating the flag
708|
709|```{caution}
710|For boolean flags with a pair of values, the only recognized environment variable is the one provided to the `envvar` argument.
711|
712|So an option defined as `--flag/--no-flag`, with an `envvar="FLAG"` parameter, there is no magical `NO_FLAG=<anything>` variable that is recognized. Only the `FLAG=<anything>` environment variable is recognized.
713|```
714|
715|If the flag is activated, its value is set to `flag_value`. Otherwise, the value
716|defaults to `None`.
717|
718|## Multiple Options from Environment Values
719|
720|As options can accept multiple values, pulling in such values from
721|environment variables (which are strings) is a bit more complex. Click handles
722|this by deferring customization of the behavior to the `type`. For both
723|`multiple` and `nargs` with values other than
724|`1`, Click will invoke the {meth}`ParamType.split_envvar_value` method to
725|perform the splitting.
726|
727|The default implementation for all types is to split on whitespace. The
728|exceptions to this rule are the {class}`File` and {class}`Path` types
729|which both split according to the operating system's path splitting rules.
730|On Unix systems like Linux and OS X, the splitting happens on
731|every colon (`:`), and for Windows, splitting on every semicolon (`;`).
732|
733|```{eval-rst}
734|.. click:example::
735|
736|    @click.command()
737|    @click.option('paths', '--path', envvar='PATHS', multiple=True,
738|                  type=click.Path())
739|    def perform(paths):
740|        for path in paths:
741|            click.echo(path)
742|
743|    if __name__ == '__main__':
744|        perform()
745|
746|.. click:run::
747|
748|    import os
749|    invoke(perform, env={"PATHS": f"./foo/bar{os.path.pathsep}./test"})
750|```
751|
752|## Other Prefix Characters
753|
754|Click can deal with prefix characters besides `-` for options, including `/` and
755|`+`, as well as others. Note that alternative prefix characters are generally
756|used very sparingly if at all within POSIX.
757|
758|```{eval-rst}
759|.. click:example::
760|
761|    @click.command()
762|    @click.option('+w/-w')
763|    def chmod(w):
764|        click.echo(f"writable={w}")
765|
766|.. click:run::
767|
768|    invoke(chmod, args=['+w'])
769|    invoke(chmod, args=['-w'])
770|```
771|
772|There are special considerations for using `/` as prefix character. See
773|{ref}`option-boolean-flag` for more.
774|
775|(optional-value)=
776|
777|## Optional Value
778|
779|Providing the value to an option can be made optional, in which case
780|providing only the option's flag without a value will either show a
781|prompt or use its `flag_value`.
782|
783|Setting `is_flag=False, flag_value=value` tells Click that the option
784|can still be passed a value, but if only the flag is given, the
785|value will be `flag_value`.
786|
787|```{eval-rst}
788|.. click:example::
789|
790|    @click.command()
791|    @click.option("--name", is_flag=False, flag_value="Flag", default="Default")
792|    def hello(name):
793|        click.echo(f"Hello, {name}!")
794|
795|.. click:run::
796|
797|    invoke(hello, args=[])
798|    invoke(hello, args=["--name", "Value"])
799|    invoke(hello, args=["--name"])
800|```

1|# Advanced Groups and Context
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|In addition to the capabilities covered in the previous section, Groups have
7|more advanced capabilities that leverage the Context.
8|
9|```{contents}
10|---
11|depth: 1
12|local: true
13|---
14|```
15|
16|## Callback Invocation
17|
18|For a regular command, the callback is executed whenever the command runs.
19|If the script is the only command, it will always fire (unless a parameter
20|callback prevents it.  This for instance happens if someone passes
21|`--help` to the script).
22|
23|For groups, the situation looks different. In this case, the callback fires
24|whenever a subcommand fires.  What this means in practice is that an outer
25|command runs when an inner command runs:
26|
27|```{eval-rst}
28|.. click:example::
29|
30|    @click.group()
31|    @click.option('--debug/--no-debug', default=False)
32|    def cli(debug):
33|        click.echo(f"Debug mode is {'on' if debug else 'off'}")
34|
35|    @cli.command()  # @cli, not @click!
36|    def sync():
37|        click.echo('Syncing')
38|
39|Here is what this looks like:
40|
41|.. click:run::
42|
43|    invoke(cli, prog_name='tool.py')
44|    println()
45|    invoke(cli, prog_name='tool.py', args=['--debug', 'sync'])
46|```
47|
48|## Nested Handling and Contexts
49|
50|As you can see from the earlier example, the basic command group accepts a
51|debug argument which is passed to its callback, but not to the sync
52|command itself.  The sync command only accepts its own arguments.
53|
54|This allows tools to act completely independent of each other, but how
55|does one command talk to a nested one?  The answer to this is the
56|{class}`Context`.
57|
58|Each time a command is invoked, a new context is created and linked with the
59|parent context.  Normally, you can't see these contexts, but they are
60|there.  Contexts are passed to parameter callbacks together with the
61|value automatically.  Commands can also ask for the context to be passed
62|by marking themselves with the {func}`pass_context` decorator.  In that
63|case, the context is passed as first argument.
64|
65|The context can also carry a program specified object that can be
66|used for the program's purposes.  What this means is that you can build a
67|script like this:
68|
69|```{eval-rst}
70|.. click:example::
71|
72|    @click.group()
73|    @click.option('--debug/--no-debug', default=False)
74|    @click.pass_context
75|    def cli(ctx, debug):
76|        # ensure that ctx.obj exists and is a dict (in case `cli()` is called
77|        # by means other than the `if` block below)
78|        ctx.ensure_object(dict)
79|
80|        ctx.obj['DEBUG'] = debug
81|
82|    @cli.command()
83|    @click.pass_context
84|    def sync(ctx):
85|        click.echo(f"Debug is {'on' if ctx.obj['DEBUG'] else 'off'}")
86|
87|    if __name__ == '__main__':
88|        cli(obj={})
89|```
90|
91|If the object is provided, each context will pass the object onwards to
92|its children, but at any level a context's object can be overridden.  To
93|reach to a parent, `context.parent` can be used.
94|
95|In addition to that, instead of passing an object down, nothing stops the
96|application from modifying global state.  For instance, you could just flip
97|a global `DEBUG` variable and be done with it.
98|
99|## Decorating Commands
100|
101|As you have seen in the earlier example, a decorator can change how a
102|command is invoked.  What actually happens behind the scenes is that
103|callbacks are always invoked through the {meth}`Context.invoke` method
104|which automatically invokes a command correctly (by either passing the
105|context or not).
106|
107|This is very useful when you want to write custom decorators.  For
108|instance, a common pattern would be to configure an object representing
109|state and then storing it on the context and then to use a custom
110|decorator to find the most recent object of this sort and pass it as first
111|argument.
112|
113|For instance, the {func}`pass_obj` decorator can be implemented like this:
114|
115|```{eval-rst}
116|.. click:example::
117|
118|    from functools import update_wrapper
119|
120|    def pass_obj(f):
121|        @click.pass_context
122|        def new_func(ctx, *args, **kwargs):
123|            return ctx.invoke(f, ctx.obj, *args, **kwargs)
124|        return update_wrapper(new_func, f)
125|```
126|
127|The {meth}`Context.invoke` command will automatically invoke the function
128|in the correct way, so the function will either be called with`f(ctx,
129|obj)` or `f(obj)` depending on whether or not it itself is decorated with
130|{func}`pass_context`.
131|
132|This is a very powerful concept that can be used to build very complex
133|nested applications; see {ref}`complex-guide` for more information.
134|
135|(command-chaining)=
136|
137|## Command Chaining
138|
139|It is useful to invoke more than one subcommand in one call. For example,
140|`my-app validate build upload` would invoke `validate`, then `build`, then
141|`upload`. To implement this, pass `chain=True` when creating a group.
142|
143|```{eval-rst}
144|.. click:example::
145|
146|    @click.group(chain=True)
147|    def cli():
148|        pass
149|
150|    @cli.command('validate')
151|    def validate():
152|        click.echo('validate')
153|
154|    @cli.command('build')
155|    def build():
156|        click.echo('build')
157|
158|You can invoke it like this:
159|
160|.. click:run::
161|
162|    invoke(cli, prog_name='my-app', args=['validate', 'build'])
163|```
164|
165|When using chaining, there are a few restrictions:
166|
167|- Only the last command may use `nargs=-1` on an argument, otherwise the
168|  parser will not be able to find further commands.
169|- It is not possible to nest groups below a chain group.
170|- On the command line, options must be specified before arguments for each
171|  command in the chain.
172|- The {attr}`Context.invoked_subcommand` attribute will be `'*'` because the
173|  parser doesn't know the full list of commands that will run yet.
174|
175|(command-pipelines)=
176|
177|## Command Pipelines
178|
179|When using chaining, a common pattern is to have each command process the
180|result of the previous command.
181|
182|A straightforward way to do this is to use {func}`make_pass_decorator` to pass
183|a context object to each command, and store and read the data on that object.
184|
185|```{eval-rst}
186|.. click:example::
187|
188|    pass_ns = click.make_pass_decorator(dict, ensure=True)
189|
190|    @click.group(chain=True)
191|    @click.argument("name")
192|    @pass_ns
193|    def cli(ns, name):
194|        ns["name"] = name
195|
196|    @cli.command
197|    @pass_ns
198|    def lower(ns):
199|        ns["name"] = ns["name"].lower()
200|
201|    @cli.command
202|    @pass_ns
203|    def show(ns):
204|        click.echo(ns["name"])
205|
206|.. click:run::
207|
208|    invoke(cli, prog_name="process", args=["Click", "show", "lower", "show"])
209|```
210|
211|Another way to do this is to collect data returned by each command, then process
212|it at the end of the chain. Use the group's {meth}`~Group.result_callback`
213|decorator to register a function that is called after the chain is finished. It
214|is passed the list of return values as well as any parameters registered on the
215|group.
216|
217|A command can return anything, including a function. Here's an example of that,
218|where each subcommand creates a function that processes the input, then the
219|result callback calls each function. The command takes a file, processes each
220|line, then outputs it. If no subcommands are given, it outputs the contents
221|of the file unchanged.
222|
223|```python
224|@click.group(chain=True, invoke_without_command=True)
225|@click.argument("fin", type=click.File("r"))
226|def cli(fin):
227|    pass
228|
229|@cli.result_callback()
230|def process_pipeline(processors, fin):
231|    iterator = (x.rstrip("\r\n") for x in input)
232|
233|    for processor in processors:
234|        iterator = processor(iterator)
235|
236|    for item in iterator:
237|        click.echo(item)
238|
239|@cli.command("upper")
240|def make_uppercase():
241|    def processor(iterator):
242|        for line in iterator:
243|            yield line.upper()
244|    return processor
245|
246|@cli.command("lower")
247|def make_lowercase():
248|    def processor(iterator):
249|        for line in iterator:
250|            yield line.lower()
251|    return processor
252|
253|@cli.command("strip")
254|def make_strip():
255|    def processor(iterator):
256|        for line in iterator:
257|            yield line.strip()
258|    return processor
259|```
260|
261|That's a lot in one go, so let's go through it step by step.
262|
263|1. The first thing is to make a {func}`group` that is chainable.  In
264|   addition to that we also instruct Click to invoke even if no
265|   subcommand is defined.  If this would not be done, then invoking an
266|   empty pipeline would produce the help page instead of running the
267|   result callbacks.
268|2. The next thing we do is to register a result callback on our group.
269|   This callback will be invoked with an argument which is the list of
270|   all return values of all subcommands and then the same keyword
271|   parameters as our group itself.  This means we can access the input
272|   file easily there without having to use the context object.
273|3. In this result callback we create an iterator of all the lines in the
274|   input file and then pass this iterator through all the returned
275|   callbacks from all subcommands and finally we print all lines to
276|   stdout.
277|
278|After that point we can register as many subcommands as we want and each
279|subcommand can return a processor function to modify the stream of lines.
280|
281|One important thing of note is that Click shuts down the context after
282|each callback has been run.  This means that for instance file types
283|cannot be accessed in the `processor` functions as the files will already
284|be closed there.  This limitation is unlikely to change because it would
285|make resource handling much more complicated.  For such it's recommended
286|to not use the file type and manually open the file through
287|{func}`open_file`.
288|
289|For a more complex example that also improves upon handling of the pipelines,
290|see the [imagepipe example](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/imagepipe)
291|in the Click repository. It implements a pipeline based image editing tool
292|that has a nice internal structure.
293|
294|## Overriding Defaults
295|
296|By default, the default value for a parameter is pulled from the
297|`default` flag that is provided when it's defined, but that's not the
298|only place defaults can be loaded from.  The other place is the
299|{attr}`Context.default_map` (a dictionary) on the context.  This allows
300|defaults to be loaded from a configuration file to override the regular
301|defaults.
302|
303|This is useful if you plug in some commands from another package but
304|you're not satisfied with the defaults.
305|
306|The default map can be nested arbitrarily for each subcommand:
307|
308|```python
309|
310|    default_map = {
311|        "debug": True,  # default for a top level option
312|        "runserver": {"port": 5000}  # default for a subcommand
313|    }
314|```
315|
316|The default map can be provided when the script is invoked, or
317|overridden at any point by commands. For instance, a top-level command
318|could load the defaults from a configuration file.
319|
320|Example usage:
321|
322|```{eval-rst}
323|.. click:example::
324|
325|    import click
326|
327|    @click.group()
328|    def cli():
329|        pass
330|
331|    @cli.command()
332|    @click.option('--port', default=8000)
333|    def runserver(port):
334|        click.echo(f"Serving on http://127.0.0.1:{port}/")
335|
336|    if __name__ == '__main__':
337|        cli(default_map={
338|            'runserver': {
339|                'port': 5000
340|            }
341|        })
342|
343|And in action:
344|
345|.. click:run::
346|
347|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['runserver'], default_map={
348|        'runserver': {
349|            'port': 5000
350|        }
351|    })
352|```
353|
354|### Multi-value parameters
355|
356|When a `default_map` value is a string for a parameter with `nargs > 1` or a
357|{class}`Tuple` type, the string is split automatically, the same way an
358|environment variable would be. By default, values are split on whitespace. See
359|[Multiple Options from Environment
360|Values](options.md#multiple-options-from-environment-values) for details on
361|splitting behavior.
362|
363|```python
364|default_map = {
365|    "draw": {
366|        "point": "3 4",  # split into ("3", "4") for nargs=2
367|        "color": "red",  # passed as-is for nargs=1
368|    }
369|}
370|```
371|
372|You can also pass an already-structured tuple or list, which will be used as-is
373|without splitting:
374|
375|```python
376|default_map = {
377|    "draw": {
378|        "point": (3, 4),  # used directly
379|    }
380|}
381|```
382|
383|## Context Defaults
384|
385|```{versionadded} 2.0
386|```
387|
388|Starting with Click 2.0 you can override defaults for contexts not just
389|when calling your script, but also in the decorator that declares a
390|command.  For instance given the previous example which defines a custom
391|`default_map` this can also be accomplished in the decorator now.
392|
393|This example does the same as the previous example:
394|
395|```{eval-rst}
396|.. click:example::
397|
398|    import click
399|
400|    CONTEXT_SETTINGS = dict(
401|        default_map={'runserver': {'port': 5000}}
402|    )
403|
404|    @click.group(context_settings=CONTEXT_SETTINGS)
405|    def cli():
406|        pass
407|
408|    @cli.command()
409|    @click.option('--port', default=8000)
410|    def runserver(port):
411|        click.echo(f"Serving on http://127.0.0.1:{port}/")
412|
413|    if __name__ == '__main__':
414|        cli()
415|
416|And again the example in action:
417|
418|.. click:run::
419|
420|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['runserver'])
421|```
422|
423|## Command Return Values
424|
425|```{versionadded} 3.0
426|```
427|
428|One of the new introductions in Click 3.0 is the full support for return
429|values from command callbacks.  This enables a whole range of features
430|that were previously hard to implement.
431|
432|In essence any command callback can now return a value.  This return value
433|is bubbled to certain receivers.  One usecase for this has already been
434|show in the example of {ref}`command-chaining` where it has been
435|demonstrated that chained groups can have callbacks that process
436|all return values.
437|
438|When working with command return values in Click, this is what you need to
439|know:
440|
441|- The return value of a command callback is generally returned from the
442|  {meth}`Command.invoke` method.  The exception to this rule has to
443|  do with {class}`Group`s:
444|
445|  - In a group the return value is generally the return value of the
446|    subcommand invoked.  The only exception to this rule is that the
447|    return value is the return value of the group callback if it's
448|    invoked without arguments and `invoke_without_command` is enabled.
449|  - If a group is set up for chaining then the return value is a list
450|    of all subcommands' results.
451|  - Return values of groups can be processed through a
452|    {attr}`Group.result_callback`.  This is invoked with the
453|    list of all return values in chain mode, or the single return
454|    value in case of non chained commands.
455|
456|- The return value is bubbled through from the {meth}`Context.invoke`
457|  and {meth}`Context.forward` methods.  This is useful in situations
458|  where you internally want to call into another command.
459|
460|- Click does not have any hard requirements for the return values and
461|  does not use them itself.  This allows return values to be used for
462|  custom decorators or workflows (like in the command chaining
463|  example).
464|
465|- When a Click script is invoked as command line application (through
466|  {meth}`Command.main`) the return value is ignored unless the
467|  `standalone_mode` is disabled in which case it's bubbled through.
