1|# Advanced Patterns
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|In addition to common functionality, Click offers some advanced features.
7|
8|```{contents}
9|:depth: 1
10|:local: true
11|```
12|
13|## Callbacks and Eager Options
14|
15|Sometimes, you want a parameter to completely change the execution flow.
16|For instance, this is the case when you want to have a `--version`
17|parameter that prints out the version and then exits the application.
18|
19|Note: an actual implementation of a `--version` parameter that is
20|reusable is available in Click as {func}`click.version_option`. The code
21|here is merely an example of how to implement such a flag.
22|
23|In such cases, you need two concepts: eager parameters and a callback. An
24|eager parameter is a parameter handled before others, and a
25|callback is what executes after the parameter is handled. The eagerness
26|is necessary so that an earlier required parameter does not produce an
27|error message. For instance, if `--version` was not eager and a
28|parameter `--foo` was required and defined before, you would need to
29|specify it for `--version` to work. For more information, see
30|{ref}`callback-evaluation-order`.
31|
32|A callback is a function invoked with three parameters: the
33|current {class}`Context`, the current {class}`Parameter`, and the value.
34|The context provides some useful features such as quitting the
35|application and gives access to other already processed parameters.
36|
37|Here's an example for a `--version` flag:
38|
39|```{eval-rst}
40|.. click:example::
41|
42|    def print_version(ctx, param, value):
43|        if not value or ctx.resilient_parsing:
44|            return
45|        click.echo('Version 1.0')
46|        ctx.exit()
47|
48|    @click.command()
49|    @click.option('--version', is_flag=True, callback=print_version,
50|                  expose_value=False, is_eager=True)
51|    def hello():
52|        click.echo('Hello World!')
53|
54|
55|What it looks like:
56|
57|
58|.. click:run::
59|
60|    invoke(hello)
61|    invoke(hello, args=['--version'])
62|```
63|The `expose_value` parameter prevents the pretty pointless `version`
64|parameter from being passed to the callback. If that was not specified, a
65|boolean would be passed to the `hello` script. The `resilient_parsing`
66|flag is applied to the context if Click wants to parse the command line
67|without any destructive behavior that would change the execution flow. In
68|this case, because we would exit the program, we instead do nothing.
69|
70|## Callbacks for Validation
71|
72|```{versionchanged} 2.0
73|```
74|
75|If you want to apply custom validation logic, you can do this in the
76|parameter callbacks. These callbacks can both modify values and
77|raise errors if the validation does not work. The callback runs after
78|type conversion. It is called for all sources, including prompts.
79|
80|In Click 1.0, you can only raise the {exc}`UsageError` but starting with
81|Click 2.0, you can also raise the {exc}`BadParameter` error, which has the
82|added advantage that it will automatically format the error message to
83|also contain the parameter name.
84|
85|```{eval-rst}
86|.. click:example::
87|
88|    def validate_rolls(ctx, param, value):
89|        if isinstance(value, tuple):
90|            return value
91|
92|        try:
93|            rolls, _, dice = value.partition("d")
94|            return int(dice), int(rolls)
95|        except ValueError:
96|            raise click.BadParameter("format must be 'NdM'")
97|
98|    @click.command()
99|    @click.option(
100|        "--rolls", type=click.UNPROCESSED, callback=validate_rolls,
101|        default="1d6", prompt=True,
102|    )
103|    def roll(rolls):
104|        sides, times = rolls
105|        click.echo(f"Rolling a {sides}-sided dice {times} time(s)")
106|
107|.. click:run::
108|
109|    invoke(roll, args=["--rolls=42"])
110|    println()
111|    invoke(roll, args=["--rolls=2d12"])
112|    println()
113|    invoke(roll, input=["42", "2d12"])
114|```
115|
116|## Parameter Modifications
117|
118|Parameters (options and arguments) are forwarded to the command callbacks,
119|as you have seen. One common way to prevent a parameter from being passed
120|to the callback is the `expose_value` argument to a parameter which hides
121|the parameter entirely. The way this works is that the {class}`Context`
122|object has a {attr}`~Context.params` attribute which is a dictionary of
123|all parameters. Whatever is in that dictionary is being passed to the
124|callbacks.
125|
126|This can be used to make up additional parameters. Generally, this pattern
127|is not recommended, but in some cases it can be useful. At the very least,
128|it's good to know that the system works this way.
129|
130|```{eval-rst}
131|.. click:example::
132|
133|    import urllib.request
134|
135|    def open_url(ctx, param, value):
136|        if value is not None:
137|            ctx.params['fp'] = urllib.request.urlopen(value)
138|            return value
139|
140|    @click.command()
141|    @click.option('--url', callback=open_url)
142|    def cli(url, fp=None):
143|        if fp is not None:
144|            click.echo(f"{url}: {fp.code}")
145|
146|In this case the callback returns the URL unchanged but also passes a
147|second `fp` value to the callback.
148|
149|.. caution::
150|
151|   Writing to :attr:`~click.Context.params` directly bypasses Click's
152|   per-parameter pipeline: :meth:`~click.Context.get_parameter_source` returns
153|   ``None`` for it, the value is never run through any :class:`~click.ParamType`
154|   conversion. And if the key collides with a declared parameter, then the
155|   shared-name arbitration loses information about where the value came from.
156|   Prefer the wrapper pattern below when any of those semantics matter.
157|
158|What's more recommended is to pass the information in a wrapper, however:
159|
160|.. click:example::
161|
162|    import urllib.request
163|
164|    class URL:
165|        def __init__(self, url, fp):
166|            self.url = url
167|            self.fp = fp
168|
169|    def open_url(ctx, param, value):
170|        if value is not None:
171|            return URL(value, urllib.request.urlopen(value))
172|
173|    @click.command()
174|    @click.option('--url', callback=open_url)
175|    def cli(url):
176|        if url is not None:
177|            click.echo(f"{url.url}: {url.fp.code}")
178|
179|```
180|
181|## Token Normalization
182|
183|```{versionadded} 2.0
184|```
185|
186|Starting with Click 2.0, it's possible to provide a function used
187|for normalizing tokens. Tokens are option names, choice values, or command
188|values. This can be used to implement case-insensitive options, for
189|instance.
190|
191|To use this feature, the context needs to be passed a function that
192|performs the normalization of the token. Such as a function that converts the
193|token to lowercase:
194|
195|```{eval-rst}
196|.. click:example::
197|
198|    CONTEXT_SETTINGS = {'token_normalize_func': lambda x: x.lower()}
199|
200|    @click.command(context_settings=CONTEXT_SETTINGS)
201|    @click.option('--name', default='Pete')
202|    def cli(name):
203|        click.echo(f"Name: {name}")
204|
205|# And how it works on the command line:
206|
207|.. click:run::
208|
209|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['--NAME=Pete'])
210|```
211|
212|## Invoking Other Commands
213|
214|Sometimes, it might be interesting to invoke one command from another
215|command. This is a pattern generally discouraged with Click, but
216|possible nonetheless. For this, you can use the {func}`Context.invoke`
217|or {func}`Context.forward` methods.
218|
219|They work similarly, but the difference is that {func}`Context.invoke` merely
220|invokes another command with the arguments you provide as a caller,
221|whereas {func}`Context.forward` fills in the arguments from the current
222|command. Both accept the command as the first argument, and everything else
223|is passed onwards as you would expect.
224|
225|Example:
226|
227|```{eval-rst}
228|.. click:example::
229|
230|    cli = click.Group()
231|
232|    @cli.command()
233|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
234|    def test(count):
235|        click.echo(f'Count: {count}')
236|
237|    @cli.command()
238|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
239|    @click.pass_context
240|    def dist(ctx, count):
241|        ctx.forward(test)
242|        ctx.invoke(test, count=42)
243|
244|And what it looks like:
245|
246|.. click:run::
247|
248|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['dist'])
249|```
250|
251|(forwarding-unknown-options)=
252|
253|## Forwarding Unknown Options
254|
255|In some situations, it is interesting to be able to accept all unknown
256|options for further manual processing. Click can generally do that as of
257|Click 4.0, but it has some limitations that lie in the nature of the
258|problem. The support for this is provided through a parser flag called
259|`ignore_unknown_options` which will instruct the parser to collect all
260|unknown options and to put them to the leftover argument instead of
261|triggering a parsing error.
262|
263|This can generally be activated in two different ways:
264|
265|1. It can be enabled on custom {class}`Command` subclasses by changing
266|   the {attr}`~Command.ignore_unknown_options` attribute.
267|2. It can be enabled by changing the attribute of the same name on the
268|   context class ({attr}`Context.ignore_unknown_options`). This is best
269|   changed through the `context_settings` dictionary on the command.
270|
271|For most situations, the easiest solution is the second. Once the behavior
272|is changed, something needs to pick up those leftover options (which at
273|this point are considered arguments). For this again, you have two
274|options:
275|
276|1. You can use {func}`pass_context` to get the context passed. This will
277|   only work if in addition to {attr}`~Context.ignore_unknown_options`
278|   you also set {attr}`~Context.allow_extra_args` as otherwise the
279|   command will abort with an error that there are leftover arguments.
280|   If you go with this solution, the extra arguments will be collected in
281|   {attr}`Context.args`.
282|2. You can attach an {func}`argument` with `nargs` set to `-1` which
283|   will eat up all leftover arguments. In this case it's recommended to
284|   set the `type` to {data}`UNPROCESSED` to avoid any string processing
285|   on those arguments as otherwise they are forced into Unicode strings
286|   automatically which is often not what you want.
287|
288|In the end, the result looks something like this:
289|
290|```{eval-rst}
291|.. click:example::
292|
293|    from subprocess import call
294|
295|    @click.command(context_settings={'ignore_unknown_options': True})
296|    @click.option('-v', '--verbose', is_flag=True, help='Enables verbose mode')
297|    @click.argument('timeit_args', nargs=-1, type=click.UNPROCESSED)
298|    def cli(verbose, timeit_args):
299|        """A fake wrapper around Python's timeit."""
300|        cmdline = ['echo', 'python', '-mtimeit', *timeit_args]
301|        if verbose:
302|            click.echo(f"Invoking: {' '.join(cmdline)}")
303|        call(cmdline)
304|
305|
306|And the final output resembles the following:
307|
308|.. click:run::
309|
310|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['--help'])
311|    println()
312|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['-n', '100', 'a = 1; b = 2; a * b'])
313|    println()
314|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['-v', 'a = 1; b = 2; a * b'])
315|```
316|
317|As you can see, Click handles the verbosity flag and everything else
318|ends up in the `timeit_args` variable for further processing, which then
319|for instance, allows invoking a subprocess. There are a few things that
320|are important to know about how this ignoring of unhandled flag happens:
321|
322|- Unknown long options are generally ignored and not processed at all.
323|  So for instance if `--foo=bar` or `--foo bar` are passed they
324|  generally end up like that. Note that because the parser cannot know
325|  if an option will accept an argument or not, the `bar` part might be
326|  handled as an argument.
327|- Unknown short options might be partially handled and reassembled if
328|  necessary. For instance in the above example there is an option
329|  called `-v` which enables verbose mode. If the command would be
330|  invoked with `-va` then the `-v` part would be handled by Click
331|  (as it is known) and `-a` would end up in the leftover parameters
332|  for further processing.
333|- Depending on what you plan on doing you might have some success by
334|  disabling interspersed arguments
335|  ({attr}`~Context.allow_interspersed_args`) which instructs the parser
336|  to not allow arguments and options to be mixed. Depending on your
337|   situation, this might improve your results.
338|
339|Generally, combining the handling of options and arguments from your own
340|commands with those from another application is discouraged, and you
341|should avoid it if possible. It's a much better idea to have
342|everything below a subcommand be forwarded to another application than to
343|handle some arguments yourself.
344|
345|## Managing Resources
346|
347|It can be useful to open a resource in a group, to be made available to
348|subcommands. Many types of resources need to be closed or otherwise
349|cleaned up after use. The standard way to do this in Python is by using
350|a context manager with the `with` statement.
351|
352|For example, the `Repo` class from {doc}`complex` might actually be
353|defined as a context manager:
354|
355|```python
356|class Repo:
357|    def __init__(self, home=None):
358|        self.home = os.path.abspath(home or ".")
359|        self.db = None
360|
361|    def __enter__(self):
362|        path = os.path.join(self.home, "repo.db")
363|        self.db = open_database(path)
364|        return self
365|
366|    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, tb):
367|        self.db.close()
368|```
369|
370|Ordinarily, it would be used with the `with` statement:
371|
372|```python
373|with Repo() as repo:
374|    repo.db.query(...)
375|```
376|
377|However, a `with` block in a group would exit and close the database
378|before it could be used by a subcommand.
379|
380|Instead, use the context's {meth}`~click.Context.with_resource` method
381|to enter the context manager and return the resource. When the group and
382|any subcommands finish, the context's resources are cleaned up.
383|
384|```python
385|@click.group()
386|@click.option("--repo-home", default=".repo")
387|@click.pass_context
388|def cli(ctx, repo_home):
389|    ctx.obj = ctx.with_resource(Repo(repo_home))
390|
391|@cli.command()
392|@click.pass_obj
393|def log(obj):
394|    # obj is the repo opened in the cli group
395|    for entry in obj.db.query(...):
396|        click.echo(entry)
397|```
398|
399|If the resource isn't a context manager, usually it can be wrapped in
400|one using something from {mod}`contextlib`. If that's not possible, use
401|the context's {meth}`~click.Context.call_on_close` method to register a
402|cleanup function.
403|
404|```python
405|@click.group()
406|@click.option("--name", default="repo.db")
407|@click.pass_context
408|def cli(ctx, name):
409|    ctx.obj = db = open_db(name)
410|
411|    @ctx.call_on_close
412|    def close_db():
413|        db.record_use()
414|        db.save()
415|        db.close()
416|```
417|
418|```{versionchanged} 8.2
419|`Context.call_on_close` and context managers registered via `Context.with_resource`
420|will be closed when the CLI exits. These were previously not called on exit.
421|```

1|(complex-guide)=
2|
3|# Complex Applications
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click
6|```
7|
8|Click is designed to assist with the creation of complex and simple CLI tools
9|alike.  However, the power of its design is the ability to arbitrarily nest
10|systems together.  For instance, if you have ever used Django, you will
11|have realized that it provides a command line utility, but so does Celery.
12|When using Celery with Django, there are two tools that need to interact with
13|each other and be cross-configured.
14|
15|In a theoretical world of two separate Click command line utilities, they
16|could solve this problem by nesting one inside the other.  For instance, the
17|web framework could also load the commands for the message queue framework.
18|
19|```{contents}
20|---
21|depth: 1
22|local: true
23|---
24|```
25|
26|## Basic Concepts
27|
28|To understand how this works, you need to understand two concepts: contexts
29|and the calling convention.
30|
31|### Contexts
32|
33|Whenever a Click command is executed, a {class}`Context` object is created
34|which holds state for this particular invocation.  It remembers parsed
35|parameters, what command created it, which resources need to be cleaned up
36|at the end of the function, and so forth.  It can also optionally hold an
37|application-defined object.
38|
39|Context objects build a linked list until they hit the top one.  Each context
40|is linked to a parent context.  This allows a command to work below
41|another command and store its own information there without having to be
42|afraid of altering up the state of the parent command.
43|
44|Because the parent data is available, however, it is possible to navigate to
45|it if needed.
46|
47|Most of the time, you do not see the context object, but when writing more
48|complex applications it comes in handy.  This brings us to the next point.
49|
50|### Calling Convention
51|
52|When a Click command callback is executed, it's passed all the non-hidden
53|parameters as keyword arguments.  Notably absent is the context.  However,
54|a callback can opt into being passed to the context object by marking itself
55|with {func}`pass_context`.
56|
57|So how do you invoke a command callback if you don't know if it should
58|receive the context or not?  The answer is that the context itself
59|provides a helper function ({meth}`Context.invoke`) which can do this for
60|you.  It accepts the callback as first argument and then invokes the
61|function correctly.
62|
63|## Building a Git Clone
64|
65|In this example, we want to build a command line tool that resembles a
66|version control system.  Systems like Git usually provide one
67|over-arching command that already accepts some parameters and
68|configuration, and then have extra subcommands that do other things.
69|
70|### The Root Command
71|
72|At the top level, we need a group that can hold all our commands.  In this
73|case, we use the basic {func}`click.group` which allows us to register
74|other Click commands below it.
75|
76|For this command, we also want to accept some parameters that configure the
77|state of our tool:
78|
79|```{eval-rst}
80|.. click:example::
81|
82|    import os
83|    import click
84|
85|
86|    class Repo(object):
87|        def __init__(self, home=None, debug=False):
88|            self.home = os.path.abspath(home or '.')
89|            self.debug = debug
90|
91|
92|    @click.group()
93|    @click.option('--repo-home', envvar='REPO_HOME', default='.repo')
94|    @click.option('--debug/--no-debug', default=False,
95|                  envvar='REPO_DEBUG')
96|    @click.pass_context
97|    def cli(ctx, repo_home, debug):
98|        ctx.obj = Repo(repo_home, debug)
99|```
100|
101|Let's understand what this does.  We create a group command which can
102|have subcommands.  When it is invoked, it will create an instance of a
103|`Repo` class.  This holds the state for our command line tool.  In this
104|case, it just remembers some parameters, but at this point it could also
105|start loading configuration files and so on.
106|
107|This state object is then remembered by the context as {attr}`~Context.obj`.
108|This is a special attribute where commands are supposed to remember what
109|they need to pass on to their children.
110|
111|In order for this to work, we need to mark our function with
112|{func}`pass_context`, because otherwise, the context object would be
113|entirely hidden from us.
114|
115|### The First Child Command
116|
117|Let's add our first child command to it, the clone command:
118|
119|```python
120|@cli.command()
121|@click.argument('src')
122|@click.argument('dest', required=False)
123|def clone(src, dest):
124|    pass
125|```
126|
127|So now we have a clone command, but how do we get access to the repo?  As
128|you can imagine, one way is to use the {func}`pass_context` function which
129|again will make our callback also get the context passed on which we
130|memorized the repo.  However, there is a second version of this decorator
131|called {func}`pass_obj` which will just pass the stored object, (in our case
132|the repo):
133|
134|```python
135|@cli.command()
136|@click.argument('src')
137|@click.argument('dest', required=False)
138|@click.pass_obj
139|def clone(repo, src, dest):
140|    pass
141|```
142|
143|### Interleaved Commands
144|
145|While not relevant for the particular program we want to build, there is
146|also quite good support for interleaving systems.  Imagine for instance that
147|there was a super cool plugin for our version control system that needed a
148|lot of configuration and wanted to store its own configuration as
149|{attr}`~Context.obj`.  If we would then attach another command below that,
150|we would all of a sudden get the plugin configuration instead of our repo
151|object.
152|
153|One obvious way to remedy this is to store a reference to the repo in the
154|plugin, but then a command needs to be aware that it's attached below such a
155|plugin.
156|
157|There is a much better system that can be built by taking advantage of the
158|linked nature of contexts.  We know that the plugin context is linked to the
159|context that created our repo.  Because of that, we can start a search for
160|the last level where the object stored by the context was a repo.
161|
162|Built-in support for this is provided by the {func}`make_pass_decorator`
163|factory, which will create decorators for us that find objects (it
164|internally calls into {meth}`Context.find_object`).  In our case, we
165|know that we want to find the closest `Repo` object, so let's make a
166|decorator for this:
167|
168|```python
169|pass_repo = click.make_pass_decorator(Repo)
170|```
171|
172|If we now use `pass_repo` instead of `pass_obj`, we will always get a
173|repo instead of something else:
174|
175|```python
176|@cli.command()
177|@click.argument('src')
178|@click.argument('dest', required=False)
179|@pass_repo
180|def clone(repo, src, dest):
181|    pass
182|```
183|
184|### Ensuring Object Creation
185|
186|The above example only works if there was an outer command that created a
187|`Repo` object and stored it in the context.  For some more advanced use
188|cases, this might become a problem.  The default behavior of
189|{func}`make_pass_decorator` is to call {meth}`Context.find_object`
190|which will find the object.  If it can't find the object,
191|{meth}`make_pass_decorator` will raise an error.
192|The alternative behavior is to use {meth}`Context.ensure_object`
193|which will find the object, and if it cannot find it, will create one and
194|store it in the innermost context.  This behavior can also be enabled for
195|{func}`make_pass_decorator` by passing `ensure=True`:
196|
197|```python
198|pass_repo = click.make_pass_decorator(Repo, ensure=True)
199|```
200|
201|In this case, the innermost context gets an object created if it is
202|missing.  This might replace objects being placed there earlier.  In this
203|case, the command stays executable, even if the outer command does not run.
204|For this to work, the object type needs to have a constructor that accepts
205|no arguments.
206|
207|As such it runs standalone:
208|
209|```python
210|@click.command()
211|@pass_repo
212|def cp(repo):
213|    click.echo(isinstance(repo, Repo))
214|```
215|As you can see:
216|
217|```console
218|$ cp
219|True
220|```
221|
222|## Lazily Loading Subcommands
223|
224|Large CLIs and CLIs with slow imports may benefit from deferring the loading of
225|subcommands. The interfaces which support this mode of use are
226|{meth}`Group.list_commands` and {meth}`Group.get_command`. A custom
227|{class}`Group` subclass can implement a lazy loader by storing extra data such
228|that {meth}`Group.get_command` is responsible for running imports.
229|
230|Since the primary case for this is a {class}`Group` which loads its subcommands lazily,
231|the following example shows a lazy-group implementation.
232|
233|```{warning}
234|Lazy loading of python code can result in hard to track down bugs, circular imports
235|in order-dependent codebases, and other surprising behaviors. It is recommended that
236|this technique only be used in concert with testing which will at least run the
237|`--help` on each subcommand. That will guarantee that each subcommand can be loaded
238|successfully.
239|```
240|
241|### Defining the Lazy Group
242|
243|The following {class}`Group` subclass adds an attribute, `lazy_subcommands`, which
244|stores a mapping from subcommand names to the information for importing them.
245|
246|
247|```python
248|# in lazy_group.py
249|import importlib
250|import click
251|
252|class LazyGroup(click.Group):
253|    def __init__(self, *args, lazy_subcommands=None, **kwargs):
254|        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
255|        # lazy_subcommands is a map of the form:
256|        #
257|        #   {command-name} -> {module-name}.{command-object-name}
258|        #
259|        self.lazy_subcommands = lazy_subcommands or {}
260|
261|    def list_commands(self, ctx):
262|        base = super().list_commands(ctx)
263|        lazy = sorted(self.lazy_subcommands.keys())
264|        return base + lazy
265|
266|    def get_command(self, ctx, cmd_name):
267|        if cmd_name in self.lazy_subcommands:
268|            return self._lazy_load(cmd_name)
269|        return super().get_command(ctx, cmd_name)
270|
271|    def _lazy_load(self, cmd_name):
272|        # lazily loading a command, first get the module name and attribute name
273|        import_path = self.lazy_subcommands[cmd_name]
274|        modname, cmd_object_name = import_path.rsplit(".", 1)
275|        # do the import
276|        mod = importlib.import_module(modname)
277|        # get the Command object from that module
278|        cmd_object = getattr(mod, cmd_object_name)
279|        # check the result to make debugging easier
280|        if not isinstance(cmd_object, click.Command):
281|            raise ValueError(
282|                f"Lazy loading of {import_path} failed by returning "
283|                "a non-command object"
284|            )
285|        return cmd_object
286|```
287|
288|### Using LazyGroup To Define a CLI
289|
290|With `LazyGroup` defined, it's now possible to write a group which lazily loads its
291|subcommands like so:
292|
293|```python
294|# in main.py
295|import click
296|from lazy_group import LazyGroup
297|
298|@click.group(
299|    cls=LazyGroup,
300|    lazy_subcommands={"foo": "foo.cli", "bar": "bar.cli"},
301|    help="main CLI command for lazy example",
302|)
303|def cli():
304|    pass
305|```
306|
307|```python
308|# in foo.py
309|import click
310|
311|@click.group(help="foo command for lazy example")
312|def cli():
313|    pass
314|```
315|
316|```python
317|# in bar.py
318|import click
319|from lazy_group import LazyGroup
320|
321|@click.group(
322|    cls=LazyGroup,
323|    lazy_subcommands={"baz": "baz.cli"},
324|    help="bar command for lazy example",
325|)
326|def cli():
327|    pass
328|```
329|
330|```python
331|# in baz.py
332|import click
333|
334|@click.group(help="baz command for lazy example")
335|def cli():
336|    pass
337|```
338|
339|### What triggers Lazy Loading?
340|
341|There are several events which may trigger lazy loading by running the
342|{meth}`Group.get_command` function.
343|Some are intuititve, and some are less so.
344|
345|All cases are described with respect to the above example, assuming the main program
346|name is `cli`.
347|
348|1. Command resolution. If a user runs `cli bar baz`, this must first resolve `bar`,
349|   and then resolve `baz`. Each subcommand resolution step does a lazy load.
350|2. Helptext rendering. In order to get the short help description of subcommands,
351|   `cli --help` will load `foo` and `bar`. Note that it will still not load
352|   `baz`.
353|3. Shell completion. In order to get the subcommands of a lazy command, completing
354|   `cli` with {kbd}`Tab` will need to resolve the subcommands of `cli`. This process
355|   will trigger the lazy loads.
356|
357|### Further Deferring Imports
358|
359|It is possible to make the process even lazier, but it is generally more difficult the
360|more you want to defer work.
361|
362|For example, subcommands could be represented as a custom {class}`Command` subclass
363|which defers importing the command until it is invoked, but which provides
364|{meth}`Command.get_short_help_str` in order to support completions and helptext.
365|More simply, commands can be constructed whose callback functions defer any actual work
366|until after an import.
367|
368|This command definition provides `foo`, but any of the work associated with importing
369|the "real" callback function is deferred until invocation time:
370|
371|```{eval-rst}
372|.. click:example::
373|
374|    @click.command()
375|    @click.option("-n", type=int)
376|    @click.option("-w", type=str)
377|    def foo(n, w):
378|        from mylibrary import foo_concrete
379|
380|        foo_concrete(n, w)
381|```
382|
383|Because Click builds helptext and usage info from options, arguments, and command
384|attributes, it has no awareness that the underlying function is in any way handling a
385|deferred import. Therefore, all Click-provided utilities and functionality will work
386|as normal on such a command.

1|# Utilities
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|Besides the functionality that Click provides to interface with argument parsing and handling, it also provides a bunch
7|of addon functionality that is useful for writing command line utilities.
8|
9|## Printing to Stdout
10|
11|The most obvious helper is the {func}`echo` function, which in many ways works like the Python `print` statement or
12|function. The main difference is that it works the same in many different terminal environments.
13|
14|Example:
15|
16|```python
17|import click
18|
19|click.echo('Hello World!')
20|```
21|
22|It can output both text and binary data. It will emit a trailing newline by default, which needs to be suppressed by
23|passing `nl=False`:
24|
25|```python
26|click.echo(b'\xe2\x98\x83', nl=False)
27|```
28|
29|Last but not least {func}`echo` uses click's intelligent internal output streams to stdout and stderr which support
30|unicode output on the Windows console. This means for as long as you are using `click.echo` you can output unicode
31|characters (there are some limitations on the default font with regards to which characters can be displayed).
32|
33|```{versionadded} 6.0
34|```
35|
36|Click emulates output streams on Windows to support unicode to the Windows console through separate APIs. For more
37|information see {doc}`wincmd`.
38|
39|```{versionadded} 3.0
40|```
41|
42|You can also easily print to standard error by passing `err=True`:
43|
44|```python
45|click.echo('Hello World!', err=True)
46|```
47|
48|(ansi-colors)=
49|
50|## ANSI Colors
51|
52|```{versionadded} 2.0
53|```
54|
55|The {func}`echo` function supports ANSI colors and styles. It will
56|automatically strip ANSI color codes if the stream is not connected to a
57|terminal.
58|
59|```{admonition} Older Windows Support
60|:class: note
61|
62|Recent versions of Windows 11 support ANSI styling by default, in both
63|Windows Terminal and cmd.exe. If you need to support color output on older
64|versions of Windows, install
65|[colorama](https://pypi.org/project/colorama/) and call `colorama.init()`.
66|```
67|
68|For styling a string, the {func}`style` function can be used:
69|
70|```python
71|import click
72|
73|click.echo(click.style('Hello World!', fg='green'))
74|click.echo(click.style('Some more text', bg='blue', fg='white'))
75|click.echo(click.style('ATTENTION', blink=True, bold=True))
76|```
77|
78|The combination of {func}`echo` and {func}`style` is also available in a single function called {func}`secho`:
79|
80|```python
81|click.secho('Hello World!', fg='green')
82|click.secho('Some more text', bg='blue', fg='white')
83|click.secho('ATTENTION', blink=True, bold=True)
84|```
85|
86|## Pager Support
87|
88|In some situations, you might want to show long texts on the terminal and let a user scroll through it. This can be
89|achieved by using the {func}`echo_via_pager` function which works similarly to the {func}`echo` function, but always
90|writes to stdout and, if possible, through a pager.
91|
92|Example:
93|
94|```{eval-rst}
95|.. click:example::
96|    @click.command()
97|    def less():
98|        click.echo_via_pager("\n".join(f"Line {idx}" for idx in range(200)))
99|```
100|
101|If you want to use the pager for a lot of text, especially if generating everything in advance would take a lot of time,
102|you can pass a generator (or generator function) instead of a string:
103|
104|```{eval-rst}
105|.. click:example::
106|    def _generate_output():
107|        for idx in range(50000):
108|            yield f"Line {idx}\n"
109|
110|    @click.command()
111|    def less():
112|        click.echo_via_pager(_generate_output())
113|```
114|
115|For more complex programs, which can't easily use a simple generator, you
116|can get access to a writable file-like object for the pager, and write to
117|that instead:
118|
119|```{eval-rst}
120|.. click:example::
121|    @click.command()
122|    def less():
123|        with click.get_pager_file() as pager:
124|            for idx in range(50000):
125|                print(idx, file=pager)
126|```
127|
128|```{admonition} Why print() instead of echo()?
129|:class: hint
130|
131|The pager object deals with ANSI color and style codes itself: they are kept or
132|stripped depending on what the pager supports, exactly as {func}`echo` would do.
133|Any code that writes to a file, including plain {func}`print`, can therefore be
134|used with it.
135|```
136|
137|## Screen Clearing
138|
139|```{versionadded} 2.0
140|```
141|
142|To clear the terminal screen, you can use the {func}`clear` function that is provided starting with Click 2.0. It does
143|what the name suggests: it clears the entire visible screen in a platform-agnostic way:
144|
145|```python
146|import click
147|click.clear()
148|```
149|
150|## Getting Characters from Terminal
151|
152|```{versionadded} 2.0
153|```
154|
155|Normally, when reading input from the terminal, you would read from standard input. However, this is buffered input and
156|will not show up until the line has been terminated. In certain circumstances, you might not want to do that and instead
157|read individual characters as they are being written.
158|
159|For this, Click provides the {func}`getchar` function which reads a single character from the terminal buffer and
160|returns it as a Unicode character.
161|
162|Note that this function will always read from the terminal, even if stdin is instead a pipe.
163|
164|Example:
165|
166|```python
167|import click
168|
169|click.echo('Continue? [yn] ', nl=False)
170|c = click.getchar()
171|click.echo()
172|if c == 'y':
173|    click.echo('We will go on')
174|elif c == 'n':
175|    click.echo('Abort!')
176|else:
177|    click.echo('Invalid input :(')
178|```
179|
180|Note that this reads raw input, which means that things like arrow keys will show up in the platform's native escape
181|format. The only characters translated are the ones produced by {kbd}`Ctrl+C` and {kbd}`Ctrl+D`, or {kbd}`Ctrl+Z` on
182|Windows, which are converted into keyboard interrupts and end of file exceptions respectively. This is done because
183|otherwise, it's too easy to forget about that and to create scripts that cannot be properly exited.
184|
185|## Waiting for Key Press
186|
187|```{versionadded} 2.0
188|```
189|
190|Sometimes, it's useful to pause until the user presses any key on the keyboard. This is especially useful on Windows
191|where `cmd.exe` will close the window at the end of the command execution by default, instead of waiting.
192|
193|In click, this can be accomplished with the {func}`pause` function. This function will print a quick message to the
194|terminal (which can be customized) and wait for the user to press a key. In addition to that, it will also become a NOP
195|(no operation instruction) if the script is not run interactively.
196|
197|Example:
198|
199|```python
200|import click
201|click.pause()
202|```
203|
204|## Launching Editors
205|
206|```{versionadded} 2.0
207|```
208|
209|Click supports launching editors automatically through {func}`edit`. This is very useful for asking users for multi-line
210|input. It will automatically open the user's defined editor or fall back to a sensible default. If the user closes the
211|editor without saving, the return value will be `None`, otherwise the entered text.
212|
213|Example usage:
214|
215|```python
216|import click
217|
218|def get_commit_message():
219|    MARKER = '# Everything below is ignored\n'
220|    message = click.edit('\n\n' + MARKER)
221|    if message is not None:
222|        return message.split(MARKER, 1)[0].rstrip('\n')
223|```
224|
225|Alternatively, the function can also be used to launch editors for files by a specific filename. In this case, the
226|return value is always `None`.
227|
228|Example usage:
229|
230|```python
231|import click
232|click.edit(filename='/etc/passwd')
233|```
234|
235|## Launching Applications
236|
237|```{versionadded} 2.0
238|```
239|
240|Click supports launching applications through {func}`launch`. This can be used to open the default application
241|associated with a URL or filetype. This can be used to launch web browsers or picture viewers, for instance. In addition
242|to this, it can also launch the file manager and automatically select the provided file.
243|
244|Example usage:
245|
246|```python
247|click.launch("https://click.palletsprojects.com/")
248|click.launch("/my/downloaded/file.txt", locate=True)
249|```
250|
251|## Printing Filenames
252|
253|Because filenames might not be Unicode, formatting them can be a bit tricky.
254|
255|The way this works with click is through the {func}`format_filename` function. It does a best-effort conversion of the
256|filename to Unicode and will never fail. This makes it possible to use these filenames in the context of a full Unicode
257|string.
258|
259|Example:
260|
261|```python
262|click.echo(f"Path: {click.format_filename(b'foo.txt')}")
263|```
264|
265|## Intelligent File Opening
266|
267|```{versionadded} 3.0
268|```
269|
270|Starting with Click 3.0 the logic for opening files from the {func}`File` type is exposed through the {func}`open_file`
271|function. It can intelligently open stdin/stdout as well as any other file.
272|
273|Example:
274|
275|```python
276|import click
277|
278|stdout = click.open_file('-', 'w')
279|test_file = click.open_file('test.txt', 'w')
280|```
281|
282|If stdin or stdout are returned, the return value is wrapped in a special file where the context manager will prevent
283|the closing of the file. This makes the handling of standard streams transparent and you can always use it like this:
284|
285|```python
286|with click.open_file(filename, 'w') as f:
287|    f.write('Hello World!\n')
288|```
289|
290|## Finding Application Folders
291|
292|```{versionadded} 2.0
293|```
294|
295|Very often, you want to open a configuration file that belongs to your application. However, different operating systems
296|store these configuration files in different locations depending on their standards. Click provides a
297|{func}`get_app_dir` function which returns the most appropriate location for per-user config files for your application
298|depending on the OS.
299|
300|Example usage:
301|
302|```python
303|import os
304|import click
305|import ConfigParser
306|
307|APP_NAME = 'My Application'
308|def read_config():
309|cfg = os.path.join(click.get_app_dir(APP_NAME), 'config.ini')
310|parser = ConfigParser.RawConfigParser()
311|parser.read([cfg])
312|rv = {}
313|for section in parser.sections():
314|    for key, value in parser.items(section):
315|        rv[f"{section}.{key}"] = value
316|return rv
317|```
318|
319|## Showing Progress Bars
320|
321|Sometimes, you have command line scripts that need to process a lot of data, but you want to quickly show the user some
322|progress about how long that will take. Click supports simple progress bar rendering for that through the
323|{func}`progressbar` function.
324|
325|```{note} If you find that you have requirements beyond what Click's progress bar supports, try using [tqdm](https://tqdm.github.io/).
326|```
327|
328|The basic usage is very simple: the idea is that you have an iterable that you want to operate on. For each item in the
329|iterable it might take some time to do processing. So say you have a loop like this:
330|
331|```python
332|for user in all_the_users_to_process:
333|    modify_the_user(user)
334|```
335|
336|To hook this up with an automatically updating progress bar, all you need to do is to change the code to this:
337|
338|```python
339|import click
340|
341|with click.progressbar(all_the_users_to_process) as bar:
342|    for user in bar:
343|        modify_the_user(user)
344|```
345|
346|Click will then automatically print a progress bar to the terminal and calculate the remaining time for you. The
347|calculation of remaining time requires that the iterable has a length. If it does not have a length but you know the
348|length, you can explicitly provide it:
349|
350|```python
351|with click.progressbar(all_the_users_to_process,
352|                       length=number_of_users) as bar:
353|    for user in bar:
354|        modify_the_user(user)
355|```
356|
357|Note that {func}`progressbar` updates the bar *after* each iteration of the loop. So code like this will render
358|correctly:
359|
360|```python
361|import time
362|
363|with click.progressbar([1, 2, 3]) as bar:
364|    for x in bar:
365|        click.echo(f"sleep({x})...")
366|        time.sleep(x)
367|```
368|
369|Another useful feature is to associate a label with the progress bar which will be shown preceding the progress bar:
370|
371|```python
372|with click.progressbar(all_the_users_to_process,
373|                       label='Modifying user accounts',
374|                       length=number_of_users) as bar:
375|    for user in bar:
376|        modify_the_user(user)
377|```
378|
379|Sometimes, one may need to iterate over an external iterator, and advance the progress bar irregularly. To do so, you
380|need to specify the length (and no iterable), and use the update method on the context return value instead of iterating
381|directly over it:
382|
383|```python
384|with click.progressbar(length=total_size,
385|                       label='Unzipping archive') as bar:
386|    for archive in zip_file:
387|        archive.extract()
388|        bar.update(archive.size)
389|```

1|# Basic Commands, Groups, Context
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|Commands and Groups are the building blocks for Click applications.
7|{class}`Command` wraps a function to make it into a cli command. {class}`Group`
8|wraps Commands and Groups to make them into applications. {class}`Context` is
9|how groups and commands communicate.
10|
11|```{contents}
12|---
13|depth: 2
14|local: true
15|---
16|```
17|
18|## Commands
19|
20|### Basic Command Example
21|
22|A simple command decorator takes no arguments.
23|
24|```{eval-rst}
25|.. click:example::
26|
27|    @click.command()
28|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
29|    def hello(count):
30|        for x in range(count):
31|            click.echo("Hello!")
32|
33|.. click:run::
34|    invoke(hello, args=['--count', '2',])
35|```
36|
37|### Renaming Commands
38|
39|By default the command is the function name with underscores replaced by dashes.
40|To change this pass the  desired name into the first positional argument.
41|
42|```{eval-rst}
43|.. click:example::
44|
45|    @click.command('say-hello')
46|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
47|    def hello(count):
48|        for x in range(count):
49|            click.echo("Hello!")
50|
51|.. click:run::
52|    invoke(hello, args=['--count', '2',])
53|```
54|
55|### Deprecating Commands
56|
57|To mark a command as deprecated pass in `deprecated=True`
58|
59|```{eval-rst}
60|.. click:example::
61|
62|    @click.command('say-hello', deprecated=True)
63|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
64|    def hello(count):
65|        for x in range(count):
66|            click.echo("Hello!")
67|
68|.. click:run::
69|    invoke(hello, args=['--count', '2',])
70|```
71|
72|## Groups
73|
74|### Basic Group Example
75|
76|A group wraps one or more commands. After being wrapped, the commands are nested
77|under that group. You can see that on the help pages and in the execution. By
78|default, invoking the group with no command shows the help page.
79|
80|```{eval-rst}
81|.. click:example::
82|
83|    @click.group()
84|    def greeting():
85|        click.echo('Starting greeting ...')
86|
87|    @greeting.command('say-hello')
88|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
89|    def hello(count):
90|        for x in range(count):
91|            click.echo("Hello!")
92|
93|At the top level:
94|
95|.. click:run::
96|
97|    invoke(greeting)
98|
99|At the command level:
100|
101|.. click:run::
102|
103|    invoke(greeting, args=['say-hello'])
104|    invoke(greeting, args=['say-hello', '--help'])
105|```
106|
107|As you can see from the above example, the function wrapped by the group
108|decorator executes unless it is interrupted (for example by calling the help).
109|
110|### Renaming Groups
111|
112|To have a name other than the decorated function name as the group name, pass it
113|in as the first positional argument.
114|
115|```{eval-rst}
116|.. click:example::
117|
118|    @click.group('greet-someone')
119|    def greeting():
120|        click.echo('Starting greeting ...')
121|
122|    @greeting.command('say-hello')
123|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
124|    def hello(count):
125|        for x in range(count):
126|            click.echo("Hello!")
127|
128|.. click:run::
129|
130|    invoke(greeting, args=['say-hello'])
131|```
132|
133|### Group Invocation Without Command
134|
135|By default, if a group is passed without a command, the group is not invoked and
136|a command automatically passes `--help`. To change this, pass
137|`invoke_without_command=True` to the group. The context object also includes
138|information about whether or not the group invocation would go to a command
139|nested under it.
140|
141|```{eval-rst}
142|.. click:example::
143|
144|    @click.group(invoke_without_command=True)
145|    @click.pass_context
146|    def cli(ctx):
147|        if ctx.invoked_subcommand is None:
148|            click.echo('I was invoked without subcommand')
149|        else:
150|            click.echo(f"I am about to invoke {ctx.invoked_subcommand}")
151|
152|    @cli.command()
153|    def sync():
154|        click.echo('The subcommand')
155|
156|.. click:run::
157|
158|    invoke(cli, prog_name='tool', args=[])
159|    invoke(cli, prog_name='tool', args=['sync'])
160|```
161|
162|### Group Separation
163|
164|Command {ref}`parameters` attached to a command belong only to that command.
165|
166|```{eval-rst}
167|.. click:example::
168|
169|    @click.group()
170|    def greeting():
171|        pass
172|
173|    @greeting.command()
174|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
175|    def hello(count):
176|        for x in range(count):
177|            click.echo("Hello!")
178|
179|    @greeting.command()
180|    @click.option('--count', default=1)
181|    def goodbye(count):
182|        for x in range(count):
183|            click.echo("Goodbye!")
184|
185|.. click:run::
186|
187|    invoke(greeting, args=['hello', '--count', '2'])
188|    invoke(greeting, args=['goodbye', '--count', '2'])
189|    invoke(greeting)
190|```
191|
192|Additionally parameters for a given group belong only to that group and not to
193|the commands under it. What this means is that options and arguments for a
194|specific command have to be specified *after* the command name itself, but
195|*before* any other command names.
196|
197|This behavior is observable with the `--help` option. Suppose we have a group
198|called `tool` containing a command called `sub`.
199|
200|- `tool --help` returns the help for the whole program (listing subcommands).
201|- `tool sub --help` returns the help for the `sub` subcommand.
202|- But `tool --help sub` treats `--help` as an argument for the main program.
203|  Click then invokes the callback for `--help`, which prints the help and aborts
204|  the program before click can process the subcommand.
205|
206|### Arbitrary Nesting
207|
208|{class}`Commands <Command>` are attached to a {class}`Group`. Multiple groups can be attached to another group. Groups containing multiple groups can be attached to a group, and so on. To invoke a command nested under multiple groups, all the groups under which it is nested must be invoked.
209|
210|```{eval-rst}
211|.. click:example::
212|
213|    @click.group()
214|    def cli():
215|        pass
216|
217|    # Not @click so that the group is registered now.
218|    @cli.group()
219|    def session():
220|        click.echo('Starting session')
221|
222|    @session.command()
223|    def initdb():
224|        click.echo('Initialized the database')
225|
226|    @session.command()
227|    def dropdb():
228|        click.echo('Dropped the database')
229|
230|.. click:run::
231|
232|    invoke(cli, args=['session', 'initdb'])
233|```
234|
235|### Lazily Attaching Commands
236|
237|Most examples so far have attached the commands to a group immediately, but
238|commands may be registered later. This could be used to split commands into
239|multiple Python modules. Regardless of how they are attached, the commands are
240|invoked identically.
241|
242|```{eval-rst}
243|.. click:example::
244|
245|    @click.group()
246|    def cli():
247|        pass
248|
249|    @cli.command()
250|    def initdb():
251|        click.echo('Initialized the database')
252|
253|    @click.command()
254|    def dropdb():
255|        click.echo('Dropped the database')
256|
257|    cli.add_command(dropdb)
258|
259|.. click:run::
260|
261|    invoke(cli, args=['initdb'])
262|    invoke(cli, args=['dropdb'])
263|```
264|
265|## Context Object
266|The {class}`Context` object is how commands and groups communicate.
267|
268|### Auto Envvar Prefix
269|
270|Automatically built environment variables are supported for options only. To
271|enable this feature, the `auto_envvar_prefix` parameter needs to be passed to
272|the script that is invoked.  Each command and parameter is then added as an
273|uppercase underscore-separated variable.  If you have a subcommand
274|called `run` taking an option called `reload` and the prefix is `WEB`, then the
275|variable is `WEB_RUN_RELOAD`.
276|
277|Example usage:
278|
279|```{eval-rst}
280|.. click:example::
281|
282|    @click.command()
283|    @click.option('--username')
284|    def greet(username):
285|        click.echo(f'Hello {username}!')
286|
287|    if __name__ == '__main__':
288|        greet(auto_envvar_prefix='GREETER')
289|
290|And from the command line:
291|
292|.. click:run::
293|
294|    invoke(greet, env={'GREETER_USERNAME': 'john'},
295|           auto_envvar_prefix='GREETER')
296|```
297|
298|When using `auto_envvar_prefix` with command groups, the command name
299|needs to be included in the environment variable, between the prefix and
300|the parameter name, *i.e.* `PREFIX_COMMAND_VARIABLE`. If you have a
301|subcommand called `run-server` taking an option called `host` and
302|the prefix is `WEB`, then the variable is `WEB_RUN_SERVER_HOST`.
303|
304|```{eval-rst}
305|.. click:example::
306|
307|   @click.group()
308|   @click.option('--debug/--no-debug')
309|   def cli(debug):
310|       click.echo(f"Debug mode is {'on' if debug else 'off'}")
311|
312|   @cli.command()
313|   @click.option('--username')
314|   def greet(username):
315|       click.echo(f"Hello {username}!")
316|
317|   if __name__ == '__main__':
318|       cli(auto_envvar_prefix='GREETER')
319|
320|.. click:run::
321|
322|   invoke(cli, args=['greet',],
323|          env={'GREETER_GREET_USERNAME': 'John', 'GREETER_DEBUG': 'false'},
324|          auto_envvar_prefix='GREETER')
325|```
326|
327|### Global Context Access
328|
329|```{versionadded} 5.0
330|```
331|
332|Starting with Click 5.0 it is possible to access the current context from
333|anywhere within the same thread through the use of the
334|{func}`get_current_context` function which returns it.  This is primarily
335|useful for accessing the context bound object as well as some flags that
336|are stored on it to customize the runtime behavior.  For instance the
337|{func}`echo` function does this to infer the default value of the `color`
338|flag.
339|
340|Example usage:
341|
342|```python
343|    def get_current_command_name():
344|        return click.get_current_context().info_name
345|```
346|
347|It should be noted that this only works within the current thread.  If you
348|spawn additional threads then those threads will not have the ability to
349|refer to the current context.  If you want to give another thread the
350|ability to refer to this context you need to use the context within the
351|thread as a context manager:
352|
353|```python
354|    def spawn_thread(ctx, func):
355|        def wrapper():
356|            with ctx:
357|                func()
358|        t = threading.Thread(target=wrapper)
359|        t.start()
360|        return t
361|```
362|
363|Now the thread function can access the context like the main thread would
364|do.  However if you do use this for threading you need to be very careful
365|as the vast majority of the context is not thread safe!  You are only
366|allowed to read from the context, but not to perform any modifications on
367|it.
368|
369|
370|### Parameter Source Priority
371|
372|When a parameter's value is resolved, Click checks several sources
373|in the following order of precedence:
374|
375|1.  **Prompt** (`PROMPT`): interactively provided by the user at a prompt.
376|2.  **Command line** (`COMMANDLINE`): provided as a CLI argument or option.
377|3.  **Environment variable** (`ENVIRONMENT`): read from an environment variable.
378|4.  **Default map** (`DEFAULT_MAP`): looked up from {attr}`Context.default_map`.
379|5.  **Default** (`DEFAULT`): the default value defined on the parameter.
380|
381|{class}`~click.core.ParameterSource` members are ordered from most
382|explicit to least explicit. Because it is an {class}`~enum.IntEnum`,
383|you can use comparison operators to check how explicitly a value was
384|provided:
385|
386|```python
387|source = ctx.get_parameter_source("port")
388|
389|# True if the value was explicitly set (command line, prompt, or env var).
390|if source < click.ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP:
391|    ...
392|
393|# True if the value came from any kind of default.
394|if source >= click.ParameterSource.DEFAULT_MAP:
395|    ...
396|```
397|
398|
399|### Detecting the Source of a Parameter
400|
401|In some situations it's helpful to understand whether or not an option
402|or parameter came from the command line, the environment, the default
403|value, or {attr}`Context.default_map`. The
404|{meth}`Context.get_parameter_source` method can be used to find this
405|out. It will return a member of the {class}`~click.core.ParameterSource`
406|enum.
407|
408|```{eval-rst}
409|.. click:example::
410|
411|    @click.command()
412|    @click.argument('port', nargs=1, default=8080, envvar="PORT")
413|    @click.pass_context
414|    def cli(ctx, port):
415|        source = ctx.get_parameter_source("port")
416|        click.echo(f"Port came from {source.name}")
417|
418|.. click:run::
419|
420|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=['8080'])
421|    println()
422|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=[], env={"PORT": "8080"})
423|    println()
424|    invoke(cli, prog_name='cli', args=[])
425|    println()
426|```

8|## General
9|
10|### Calling a command as a regular function
11|
12|I decorated a function with `@click.command()` to make it a CLI. When I import that name and call it from Python, it does not run my function. It parses arguments, prints a usage error and exits the process:
13|
14|```pytb
15|>>> nasa_date_to_iso("2017-090")
16|Usage: cli [OPTIONS] DATESTR
17|Try 'cli --help' for help.
18|
19|Error: Got unexpected extra arguments (0 1 7 - 0 9 0)
20|SystemExit: 2
21|```
22|
23|#### Answer
24|
25|This is not a bug in Click. The decorator replaced the function with a {class}`Command` object. Calling that object runs the Click pipeline, and its argument is the list of command line arguments to parse, not the function's parameters.
26|
27|The recommended pattern is to keep a plain function and wrap it with a thin command:
28|
29|```python
30|def nasa_date_to_iso(datestr): ...
31|
32|
33|@click.command("nasa_date_to_iso")
34|@click.argument("datestr")
35|def nasa_date_to_iso_command(datestr):
36|    click.echo(nasa_date_to_iso(datestr))
37|```
38|
39|The function stays available as a Python API, and the command adds the CLI on top. Extracting behavior into a shared function used by several entry points is a common refactor.
40|
41|If you still want to run the command itself from Python, call it with a list of arguments and `standalone_mode=False` so it returns the result instead of exiting. This runs the Click pipeline, including parsing, validation and callbacks:
42|
43|```python
44|nasa_date_to_iso_command(["2017-090"], standalone_mode=False)
45|```
46|
47|An alternative form is:
48|
49|```python
50|nasa_date_to_iso_command.main(["2017-090"], standalone_mode=False)
51|```
52|
53|### Shell Variable Expansion On Windows
54|
55|I have a simple Click app :
56|
57|```
58|import click
59|
60|@click.command()
61|@click.argument('message')
62|def main(message: str):
63|    click.echo(message)
64|
65|if __name__ == '__main__':
66|    main()
67|
68|```
69|
70|When you pass an environment variable in the argument, it expands it:
71|
72|```{code-block} powershell
73|> Desktop python foo.py '$M0/.viola/2025-01-25-17-20-23-307878'
74|> M:/home/ramrachum/.viola/2025-01-25-17-20-23-307878
75|>
76|```
77|Note that I used single quotes above, so my shell is not expanding the environment variable, Click does. How do I get Click to not expand it?
78|
79|#### Answer
80|
81|If you don't want Click to emulate (as best it can) unix expansion on Windows, pass windows_expand_args=False when calling the CLI.
82|Windows command line doesn't do any *, ~, or $ENV expansion. It also doesn't distinguish between double quotes and single quotes (where the later means "don't expand here"). Click emulates the expansion so that the app behaves similarly on both platforms, but doesn't receive information about what quotes were used.
83|
84|### `UnicodeEncodeError` on Windows
85|
86|A Click CLI that uses Unicode characters in its help text or `echo` output can raise `UnicodeEncodeError`:
87|
88|```pytb
89|UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u2023' in position 62: character maps to <undefined>
90|```
91|
92|This is not a bug in Click. When `<stdout>` is a console, Click relies on the Windows console API, which supports full Unicode rendering. But when `<stdout>` is redirected, it cannot use that API, so Python falls back to encoding the stream with the system's code page (often `cp1252`) and `errors="strict"`. That codec cannot represent every Unicode character, so the write fails.
93|
94|#### Answer
95|
96|Run Python in [UTF-8 mode](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#utf8-mode) so that redirected streams use UTF-8 instead of the code page.
97|
98|You can enforce that by:
99|- Setting the `PYTHONUTF8=1` environment variable, or
100|- Passing `-X utf8` to the `python` executable, or
101|- Setting `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf8`, which configures only the standard streams, or
102|- From your code, call `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")` and `sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")` before producing output.
103|
104|This is not a bug for Click to fix, but a system configuration. It will naturally go away with UTF-8 mode becoming the default in Python 3.15 (see [PEP 686](https://peps.python.org/pep-0686/)).
105|
106|#### For library authors
107|
108|Click intentionally does not fix this in code: it has no way to know what the caller expects. Reconfiguring the stream itself would mix encodings within one process: `echo` could write UTF-8 to a redirected file while a bare `print()` still writes the code page. A loud `UnicodeEncodeError` is easier to diagnose than silently interleaved encodings.
109|
110|But if your own CLI knows the environment it runs under, it can choose to degrade its output:
111|
112|```python
113|import sys
114|
115|encoding = getattr(sys.stdout, "encoding", "") or ""
116|ascii_only = not encoding.lower().startswith("utf")
117|```
118|
119|Note that the check we recommend here is against `sys.stdout.encoding`, not `sys.flags.utf8_mode`: only the former reports UTF-8 for all three options listed below.
120|
121|| Invocation                              | `sys.flags.utf8_mode` | `sys.stdout.encoding` |
122|| :-------------------------------------- | :-------------------: | :-------------------: |
123|| `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf8`                 |          `0`          |        `utf-8`        |
124|| `python -X utf8`                        |          `1`          |        `utf-8`        |
125|| `sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding=…)`    |          `0`          |        `utf-8`        |
126|
127|Do not rely on `sys.getfilesystemencoding()` on Windows either: [PEP 529](https://peps.python.org/pep-0529/) makes it `utf-8` regardless of the actual stream encoding.
128|
129|(edit-wait)=
130|### The `edit` utility fails to open Visual Studio Code
131|
132|Let's say our default editor is Visual Studio Code. A Click CLI calling `edit()` is supposed to open a new VSCode window on a temporary file then wait for us to edit that file before returning back the CLI execution.
133|
134|But VSCode (and some other editors) returns immediately: the file is deleted before you had a chance to edit it. With `require_save=True` (the default), the function also returns `None` instead of the edited content.
135|
136|This is not a bug in Click. In that particular case, the `code` command (VSCode's executable) is a launcher: it starts the real editor in the background, then exits. Click waits on that process and reads its exit as the end of the editing session. The same happens on any platform with any editor whose command returns before its window closes.
137|
138|#### Answer
139|
140|Setup your editor to make its launcher block until the window is closed, so Click keeps waiting on it.
141|
142|You can set the `EDITOR` in your environment with its appropriate flags:
143|
144|| Editor | Flags |
145||---|---|
146|| Visual Studio Code | `EDITOR="code --wait"` |
147|| Sublime Text | `EDITOR="subl -w"` |
148|
149|For an editor with no such flag, a workaround is to point `EDITOR` at a small wrapper script that opens the editor and blocks until it exits.
150|
151|### Tab completion during interactive prompts
152|
153|A command asks for a file path while it runs:
154|
155|```python
156|import click
157|
158|
159|@click.command()
160|def convert():
161|    source = click.prompt("File to convert", type=click.Path(exists=True))
162|    click.echo(f"Converting {source}")
163|```
164|
165|Pressing {kbd}`Tab` while typing the answer inserts a tab character instead of completing the path:
166|
167|```console
168|$ convert
169|File to convert: Doc<TAB>
170|Error: Path 'Doc\t' does not exist.
171|```
172|
173|This is not a bug in Click. Tab completion of the command line belongs to the shell: the shell asks the program for candidates through Click's completion mode, before any command code runs. A prompt works the other way around. The program already runs and reads the line itself, so Click never sees the {kbd}`Tab` key.
174|
175|{func}`~click.prompt` reads that line with the built-in {func}`input`, and Click passes the whole prompt text to it as-is. This is where Python's {mod}`readline` module takes over, but nothing binds {kbd}`Tab` to completion by default.
176|
177|#### Answer
178|
179|Bind {kbd}`Tab` in `readline` and the prompt completes paths with no other change:
180|
181|```python
182|import readline
183|
184|if "libedit" in (readline.__doc__ or ""):
185|    readline.parse_and_bind("bind ^I rl_complete")
186|else:
187|    readline.parse_and_bind("tab: complete")
188|```
189|
190|See the {mod}`readline` documentation for the binding syntax, for the two libraries it can be built on, and for writing a completer of your own. The module is Unix-only, so the import fails on Windows.
191|
192|Readline completes file names. It knows nothing about the parameter, so it cannot complete other values, such as the choices of a {class}`~click.Choice` parameter. Click embeds no line editor of its own: for completion of such values at a prompt, use one of the [interactive input libraries](contrib.md#interactive-input-libraries).
193|
194|When the value does not have to be asked while the command runs, another option is to take it out of the prompt and put it on the command line, as an argument or an option:
195|
196|```python
197|@click.command()
198|@click.argument("source", type=click.Path(exists=True))
199|def convert(source):
200|    click.echo(f"Converting {source}")
201|```
202|
203|The shell completes paths there natively and Click's completion mode takes part in it (as described in [Shell Completion](shell-completion.md)).
204|
205|(custom-completions-show-the-full-value)=
206|### Custom completions show the full value
207|
208|`Path` and `File` parameters complete differently from a parameter with a custom completer. Take a command with one of each:
209|
210|```python
211|def complete_dirs(ctx, param, incomplete):
212|    return [
213|        CompletionItem(incomplete + name)
214|        for name in ("Documents", "Downloads", "Pictures")
215|    ]
216|
217|
218|@click.command()
219|@click.option("--src", type=click.Path())
220|@click.option("--dest", shell_complete=complete_dirs)
221|def copy(src, dest):
222|    click.echo(f"Copy from {src} to {dest}")
223|```
224|
225|Completing `--src` shows only the last component of each candidate, and omits the leading path:
226|
227|```console
228|$ copy --src /home/user/<TAB><TAB>
229|Documents  Downloads  Pictures
230|```
231|
232|Completing `--dest` shows each value in full, exactly as the completer returned it:
233|
234|```console
235|$ copy --dest /home/user/<TAB><TAB>
236|/home/user/Documents  /home/user/Downloads  /home/user/Pictures
237|```
238|
239|This is not a bug in Click. The two parameters are completed by different sides.
240|
241|`Path.shell_complete` and `File.shell_complete` never enumerate the directory: each returns a single item that is the incomplete value itself, tagged `file` (or `dir` for a `Path` restricted to directories). Then the shell takes over to propose completions, and each shell does so in its own way.
242|
243|A custom completer sends no such marker. Its `CompletionItem` carries the value, a `type` marker, and an optional `help` string. The value a completer returns is both what the shell displays and what it inserts into the command line.
244|
245|#### Answer
246|
247|To change how suggestions are displayed, work on the shell side:
248|
249|- Check whether your shell's completion system has an option that changes how candidates are displayed.
250|- Write a `ShellComplete` subclass and register it with `add_completion_class`, as described in [Adding Support for a Shell](shell-completion.md#adding-support-for-a-shell).
251|- Or return the shortened form directly from your completer, but make the parameter accept and interpret that shortened form into the full value.

1|(shell-completion)=
2|
3|# Shell Completion
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click.shell_completion
6|```
7|
8|Click provides tab completion support for Bash (version 4.4 and up), Zsh, Fish, and PowerShell. It is possible to add
9|support for other shells too, and suggestions can be customized at multiple levels.
10|
11|Shell completion suggests command names, option names, and values for choice, file, and path parameter types. Options
12|are only listed if at least a dash has been entered. Hidden commands and options are not shown.
13|
14|```console
15|$ repo <TAB><TAB>
16|clone  commit  copy  delete  setuser
17|$ repo clone -<TAB><TAB>
18|--deep  --help  --rev  --shallow  -r
19|```
20|
21|## Enabling Completion
22|
23|Completion is only available if a script is installed and invoked through an entry point, not through the `python`
24|command. See {doc}`entry-points`. Once the executable is installed, calling it with a special environment variable will
25|put Click in completion mode.
26|
27|To enable shell completion, the user needs to register a special function with their shell. The exact script varies
28|depending on the shell you are using. Click will output it when called with `_{FOO_BAR}_COMPLETE` set to
29|`{shell}_source`. `{FOO_BAR}` is the executable name in uppercase with dashes replaced by underscores. It is
30|conventional but not strictly required for environment variable names to be in upper case. This convention helps
31|distinguish environment variables from regular shell variables and commands, making scripts and configuration files more
32|readable and easier to maintain. The built-in shells are `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, and `powershell`.
33|
34|Provide your users with the following instructions customized to your program name. This uses `foo-bar` as an example.
35|
36|```{eval-rst}
37|.. tabs::
38|
39|    .. group-tab:: Bash
40|
41|        Add this to ``~/.bashrc``:
42|
43|        .. code-block:: bash
44|
45|            eval "$(_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=bash_source foo-bar)"
46|
47|    .. group-tab:: Zsh
48|
49|        Add this to ``~/.zshrc``:
50|
51|        .. code-block:: zsh
52|
53|            eval "$(_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=zsh_source foo-bar)"
54|
55|    .. group-tab:: Fish
56|
57|        Add this to ``~/.config/fish/completions/foo-bar.fish``:
58|
59|        .. code-block:: fish
60|
61|            _FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=fish_source foo-bar | source
62|
63|        This is the same file used for the activation script method
64|        below. For Fish it's probably always easier to use that method.
65|
66|    .. group-tab:: PowerShell
67|
68|        Add this to your PowerShell profile (the path of ``$PROFILE``):
69|
70|        .. code-block:: powershell
71|
72|            $env:_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE = 'powershell_source'
73|            foo-bar | Out-String | Invoke-Expression
74|            Remove-Item Env:_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE
75|```
76|
77|Using `eval` means that the command is invoked and evaluated every time a shell is started, which can delay shell
78|responsiveness. To speed it up, write the generated script to a file, then source that. You can generate the files ahead
79|of time and distribute them with your program to save your users a step.
80|
81|```{eval-rst}
82|.. tabs::
83|
84|    .. group-tab:: Bash
85|
86|        Save the script somewhere.
87|
88|        .. code-block:: bash
89|
90|            _FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=bash_source foo-bar > ~/.foo-bar-complete.bash
91|
92|        Source the file in ``~/.bashrc``.
93|
94|        .. code-block:: bash
95|
96|            . ~/.foo-bar-complete.bash
97|
98|    .. group-tab:: Zsh
99|
100|        Save the script somewhere.
101|
102|        .. code-block:: bash
103|
104|            _FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=zsh_source foo-bar > ~/.foo-bar-complete.zsh
105|
106|        Source the file in ``~/.zshrc``.
107|
108|        .. code-block:: bash
109|
110|            . ~/.foo-bar-complete.zsh
111|
112|    .. group-tab:: Fish
113|
114|        Save the script to ``~/.config/fish/completions/foo-bar.fish``:
115|
116|        .. code-block:: fish
117|
118|            _FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=fish_source foo-bar > ~/.config/fish/completions/foo-bar.fish
119|
120|    .. group-tab:: PowerShell
121|
122|        Save the script somewhere.
123|
124|        .. code-block:: powershell
125|
126|            $env:_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE = 'powershell_source'
127|            foo-bar | Out-File -Encoding utf8 ~/.foo-bar-complete.ps1
128|            Remove-Item Env:_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE
129|
130|        Source the file in your PowerShell profile (the path of ``$PROFILE``):
131|
132|        .. code-block:: powershell
133|
134|            . ~/.foo-bar-complete.ps1
135|```
136|
137|After modifying the shell config, you need to start a new shell in order for the changes to be loaded.
138|
139|## Custom Type Completion
140|
141|When creating a custom {class}`~click.ParamType`, override its {meth}`~click.ParamType.shell_complete` method to provide
142|shell completion for parameters with the type. The method must return a list of {class}`~CompletionItem` objects.
143|Besides the value, these objects hold metadata that shell support might use. The built-in implementations use `type` to
144|indicate special handling for paths, and `help` for shells that support showing a help string next to a suggestion.
145|
146|In this example, the type will suggest environment variables that start with the incomplete value.
147|
148|```python
149|class EnvVarType(ParamType[str]):
150|    name = "envvar"
151|
152|    def shell_complete(self, ctx, param, incomplete):
153|        return [
154|            CompletionItem(name)
155|            for name in os.environ if name.startswith(incomplete)
156|        ]
157|
158|@click.command()
159|@click.option("--ev", type=EnvVarType())
160|def cli(ev):
161|    click.echo(os.environ[ev])
162|```
163|
164|See {ref}`custom-completions-show-the-full-value` in the FAQ for why these values are displayed in full, while `Path` completions show only the last component of the path.
165|
166|## Overriding Value Completion
167|
168|Value completions for a parameter can be customized without a custom type by providing a `shell_complete` function. The
169|function is used instead of any completion provided by the type. It is passed 3 positional arguments:
170|
171|- `ctx` - The current command context.
172|- `param` - The current parameter requesting completion.
173|- `incomplete` - The partial word that is being completed. May be an empty string if no characters have been entered
174|  yet.
175|
176|It must return a list of {class}`CompletionItem` objects, or as a shortcut it can return a list of strings.
177|
178|In this example, the command will suggest environment variables that start with the incomplete value.
179|
180|```python
181|def complete_env_vars(ctx, param, incomplete):
182|    return [k for k in os.environ if k.startswith(incomplete)]
183|
184|@click.command()
185|@click.argument("name", shell_complete=complete_env_vars)
186|def cli(name):
187|    click.echo(f"Name: {name}")
188|    click.echo(f"Value: {os.environ[name]}")
189|```
190|
191|## Adding Support for a Shell
192|
193|Support can be added for shells that do not come built in. Be sure to check PyPI to see if there's already a package
194|that adds support for your shell. This topic is very technical, you'll want to look at Click's source to study the
195|built-in implementations.
196|
197|Shell support is provided by subclasses of {class}`ShellComplete` registered with {func}`add_completion_class`. When
198|Click is invoked in completion mode, it calls {meth}`~ShellComplete.source` to output the completion script, or
199|{meth}`~ShellComplete.complete` to output completions. The base class provides default implementations that require
200|implementing some smaller parts.
201|
202|First, you'll need to figure out how your shell's completion system works and write a script to integrate it with Click.
203|It must invoke your program with the environment variable `_{FOO_BAR}_COMPLETE` set to `{shell}_complete` and pass the
204|complete args and incomplete value. How it passes those values, and the format of the completion response from Click is
205|up to you.
206|
207|In your subclass, set {attr}`ShellComplete.source_template` to the completion script. The default implementation will
208|perform `%` formatting with the following variables:
209|
210|- `complete_func` - A safe name for the completion function defined in the script.
211|- `complete_var` - The environment variable name for passing the `{shell}_complete` instruction.
212|- `foo_bar` - The name of the executable being completed.
213|
214|The example code is for a made up shell "My Shell" or "mysh" for short.
215|
216|```python
217|from click.shell_completion import add_completion_class
218|from click.shell_completion import ShellComplete
219|
220|_mysh_source = """\
221|%(complete_func)s {
222|    response=$(%(complete_var)s=mysh_complete %(foo_bar)s)
223|    # parse response and set completions somehow
224|}
225|call-on-complete %(foo_bar)s %(complete_func)s
226|"""
227|
228|@add_completion_class
229|class MyshComplete(ShellComplete):
230|    name = "mysh"
231|    source_template = _mysh_source
232|```
233|
234|Next, implement {meth}`~ShellComplete.get_completion_args`. This must get, parse, and return the complete args and
235|incomplete value from the completion script. For example, for the Bash implementation the `COMP_WORDS` env var contains
236|the command line args as a string, and the `COMP_CWORD` env var contains the index of the incomplete arg. The method
237|must return a `(args, incomplete)` tuple.
238|
239|```python
240|import os
241|from click.parser import split_arg_string
242|
243|class MyshComplete(ShellComplete):
244|    ...
245|
246|    def get_completion_args(self):
247|        args = split_arg_string(os.environ["COMP_WORDS"])
248|
249|        if os.environ["COMP_PARTIAL"] == "1":
250|            incomplete = args.pop()
251|            return args, incomplete
252|
253|        return args, ""
254|```
255|
256|Finally, implement {meth}`~ShellComplete.format_completion`. This is called to format each {class}`CompletionItem` into a string. For example, the Bash implementation returns `f"{item.type},{item.value}` (it doesn't support help strings), and the Zsh implementation returns each part separated by a newline, replacing empty help with a `_` placeholder. This format is entirely up to what you parse with your completion script.
257|
258|The `type` value is usually `plain`, but it can be another value that the completion script can switch on. For example,
259|`file` or `dir` can tell the shell to handle path completion, since the shell is better at that than Click.
260|
261|```python
262|class MyshComplete(ShellComplete):
263|    ...
264|
265|    def format_completion(self, item):
266|        return f"{item.type}\t{item.value}"
267|```
268|
269|With those three things implemented, the new shell support is ready. In case those weren't sufficient, there are more
270|parts that can be overridden, but that probably isn't necessary.
271|
272|The activation instructions will again depend on how your shell works. Use the following to generate the completion
273|script, then load it into the shell somehow.
274|
275|```console
276|_FOO_BAR_COMPLETE=mysh_source foo-bar
277|```
