1|# Help Pages
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|Click makes it very easy to document your command line tools. For most things Click automatically generates help pages for you. By design the text is customizable, but the layout is not.
7|
8|## Help Texts
9|
10|Commands and options accept help arguments. For commands, the docstring of the function is automatically used if provided.
11|
12|Simple example:
13|
14|```{eval-rst}
15|.. click:example::
16|
17|    @click.command()
18|    @click.argument('name', help='The name to print.')
19|    @click.option('--count', default=1, help='number of greetings')
20|    def hello(name: str, count: int):
21|        """This script prints hello and a name one or more times."""
22|        for x in range(count):
23|            if name:
24|                click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
25|            else:
26|                click.echo("Hello!")
27|
28|.. click:run::
29|    invoke(hello, args=['--help'])
30|```
31|
32|## Command Short Help
33|
34|For subcommands, a short help snippet is generated. By default, it's the first sentence of the docstring. If too long, then it will ellipsize what cannot be fit on a single line with `...`. The short help snippet can also be overridden with `short_help`:
35|
36|```{eval-rst}
37|.. click:example::
38|
39|    import click
40|
41|    @click.group()
42|    def cli():
43|        """A simple command line tool."""
44|
45|    @cli.command('init', short_help='init the repo')
46|    def init():
47|        """Initializes the repository."""
48|
49|.. click:run::
50|    invoke(cli, args=['--help'])
51|```
52|
53|## Group Help Page
54|
55|The group help prints sub commands, options, epilog help, and arguments, and prints them together.
56|
57|```{eval-rst}
58|.. click:example::
59|
60|    import click
61|
62|    @click.group(
63|        help="Example Click app with subcommands, options, and positional arguments.",
64|        epilog=("Examples:\n\n\b\n  python hello.py greet Alice --count 2\n"),
65|    )
66|    def cli() -> None:
67|        """Run the example CLI."""
68|
69|    @cli.command()
70|    @click.argument("name")
71|    @click.option(
72|        "--count",
73|        default=1,
74|        show_default=True,
75|        type=click.IntRange(1, None),
76|        help="Number of greetings to print.",
77|    )
78|    @click.option(
79|        "--greeting",
80|        default="Hello",
81|        show_default=True,
82|        help="Greeting prefix to use.",
83|    )
84|    def greet(name: str, count: int, greeting: str) -> None:
85|        """Greet NAME one or more times."""
86|        for _ in range(count):
87|            click.echo(f"{greeting} {name}!")
88|
89|.. click:run::
90|    invoke(cli, args=['--help'])
91|```
92|
93|## Command Epilog Help
94|
95|The help epilog is printed at the end of the help and is useful for showing example command usages or referencing additional help resources.
96|
97|```{eval-rst}
98|.. click:example::
99|
100|    import click
101|
102|    @click.command(
103|        epilog='See https://example.com for more details',
104|        )
105|    def init():
106|        """Initializes the repository."""
107|
108|.. click:run::
109|    invoke(init, args=['--help'])
110|```
111|
112|(documenting-arguments)=
113|
114|## Documenting Arguments
115|
116|{class}`click.argument` accepts an optional `help` parameter that is shown in
117|the `Positional arguments` section of the help page. You can still document
118|arguments in the command docstring, especially when you want to describe them
119|in the main help text by name.
120|
121|The section shows up as soon as one argument of the command has a `help`. It
122|then lists every argument, so it always matches the usage line. Arguments with
123|no `help` are listed with an empty description.
124|
125|A brief example:
126|
127|```{eval-rst}
128|.. click:example::
129|
130|    @click.command()
131|    @click.argument('filename', help='The file to print.')
132|    def touch(filename):
133|        """Print FILENAME."""
134|        click.echo(filename)
135|
136|.. click:run::
137|    invoke(touch, args=['--help'])
138|```
139|
140|Or more explicitly in the docstring:
141|
142|```{eval-rst}
143|.. click:example::
144|
145|    @click.command()
146|    @click.argument('filename')
147|    def touch(filename):
148|        """Print FILENAME.
149|
150|        FILENAME is the name of the file to check.
151|        """
152|        click.echo(filename)
153|
154|.. click:run::
155|    invoke(touch, args=['--help'])
156|```
157|
158|## Showing Defaults
159|
160|To control the appearance of defaults pass `show_default`.
161|
162|```{eval-rst}
163|.. click:example::
164|
165|    @click.command()
166|    @click.option('--n', default=1, show_default=False, help='number of dots')
167|    def dots(n):
168|        click.echo('.' * n)
169|
170|.. click:run::
171|    invoke(dots, args=['--help'])
172|```
173|
174|For single option boolean flags, the default remains hidden if the default value is False, even if show default is set to true.
175|
176|```{eval-rst}
177|.. click:example::
178|
179|    @click.command()
180|    @click.option('--n', default=1, show_default=True)
181|    @click.option("--gr", is_flag=True, show_default=True, default=False, help="Greet the world.")
182|    @click.option("--br", is_flag=True, show_default=True, default=True, help="Add a thematic break")
183|    def dots(n, gr, br):
184|        if gr:
185|            click.echo('Hello world!')
186|        click.echo('.' * n)
187|        if br:
188|            click.echo('-' * n)
189|
190|.. click:run::
191|   invoke(dots, args=['--help'])
192|```
193|
194|## Showing Environment Variables
195|
196|To control the appearance of environment variables pass `show_envvar`.
197|
198|```{eval-rst}
199|.. click:example::
200|
201|    @click.command()
202|    @click.option('--username', envvar='USERNAME', show_envvar=True)
203|    def greet(username):
204|        click.echo(f'Hello {username}!')
205|
206|.. click:run::
207|    invoke(greet, args=['--help'])
208|```
209|
210|## Click's Wrapping Behavior
211|
212|Click's default wrapping ignores single new lines and rewraps the text based on the width of the terminal to a maximum of 80 characters by default, but this can be modified with {attr}`~Context.max_content_width`. In the example notice how the second grouping of three lines is rewrapped into a single paragraph.
213|
214|```{eval-rst}
215|.. click:example::
216|
217|    import click
218|
219|    @click.command()
220|    def cli():
221|        """
222|        This is a very long paragraph and as you
223|        can see wrapped very early in the source text
224|        but will be rewrapped to the terminal width in
225|        the final output.
226|
227|        This is
228|        a paragraph
229|        that is compacted.
230|        """
231|
232|.. click:run::
233|    invoke(cli, args=['--help'])
234|```
235|
236|## Escaping Click's Wrapping
237|
238|Sometimes Click's wrapping can be a problem, such as when showing code examples where new lines are significant. This behavior can be escaped on a per-paragraph basis by adding a line with only `\b` . The `\b` is removed from the rendered help text.
239|
240|Example:
241|
242|```{eval-rst}
243|.. click:example::
244|
245|    import click
246|
247|    @click.command()
248|    def cli():
249|        """First paragraph.
250|
251|        \b
252|        This is
253|        a paragraph
254|        without rewrapping.
255|
256|        And this is a paragraph
257|        that will be rewrapped again.
258|        """
259|
260|.. click:run::
261|    invoke(cli, args=['--help'])
262|```
263|
264|To change the rendering maximum width, pass `max_content_width` when calling the command.
265|
266|```bash
267|cli(max_content_width=120)
268|```
269|
270|## Truncating Help Texts
271|
272|Click gets {class}`Command` help text from the docstring. If you do not want to include part of the docstring, add the `\f` escape marker to have Click truncate the help text after the marker.
273|
274|Example:
275|
276|```{eval-rst}
277|.. click:example::
278|
279|    import click
280|
281|    @click.command()
282|    def cli():
283|        """First paragraph.
284|        \f
285|
286|        Words to not be included.
287|        """
288|
289|.. click:run::
290|    invoke(cli, args=['--help'])
291|```
292|
293|(doc-meta-variables)=
294|
295|## Placeholder / Meta Variable
296|
297|The default placeholder variable ([meta variable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metasyntactic_variable#IETF_Requests_for_Comments)) in the help pages is the parameter name in uppercase with underscores. This can be changed for Commands and Parameters with the `options_metavar` and `metavar` kwargs.
298|
299|```{eval-rst}
300|.. click:example::
301|
302|    # This controls entry on the usage line.
303|    @click.command(options_metavar='[[options]]')
304|    @click.option('--count', default=1, help='number of greetings',
305|                  metavar='<int>')
306|    @click.argument('name', metavar='<name>')
307|    def hello(name: str, count: int) -> None:
308|        """This script prints 'hello <name>' a total of <count> times."""
309|        for x in range(count):
310|            click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
311|
312|# Example usage:
313|
314|.. click:run::
315|    invoke(hello, args=['--help'])
316|
317|```
318|
319|```{admonition} Optional elements are bracketed
320|:class: note
321|
322|   The usage line follows a consistent convention: an element is optional when it is enclosed in square brackets and required when it appears outside them. A required argument appears as `FOO` and an optional one as `[FOO]`, with a variadic argument adding a trailing `...` (so `[FOO]...`). A single pair of brackets can group several tokens, so a chained group renders an extra command and its arguments as one optional, repeatable unit: `[COMMAND2 [ARGS]...]...`. A {class}`Group` that can run without naming a subcommand (`invoke_without_command=True`) also brackets the leading command, showing `[COMMAND]` instead of `COMMAND`. The `[OPTIONS]` placeholder is always bracketed, since adding options is itself optional.
323|
324|   This mirrors the conventional utility-argument syntax for optional arguments and operands ([POSIX §12.1](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap12.html), [`man-pages(7)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/man-pages.7.html)), where a bracketed expression followed by `...` denotes zero or more occurrences. A subcommand name is a positional operand, so Click brackets it under the same rule.
325|```
326|
327|## Help Parameter Customization
328|
329|Help parameters are automatically added by Click for any command. The default is `--help` but can be overridden by the context setting {attr}`~Context.help_option_names`. Click resolves conflicts automatically: an option reusing one of the help option names takes it over, and the default help parameter is dropped once all its names are taken. A parameter merely named `help`, like `click.argument("help")`, does not disable it: both keep working independently.
330|
331|This example changes the default parameters to `-h` and `--help`
332|instead of just `--help`:
333|
334|```{eval-rst}
335|.. click:example::
336|
337|    import click
338|
339|    CONTEXT_SETTINGS = dict(help_option_names=['-h', '--help'])
340|
341|    @click.command(context_settings=CONTEXT_SETTINGS)
342|    def cli():
343|        pass
344|
345|.. click:run::
346|    invoke(cli, ['-h'])
347|```

1|(parameter-types)=
2|
3|# Parameter Types
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click
6|```
7|
8|When the parameter type is set using `type`, Click will leverage the type to make your life easier, for example adding
9|data to your help pages. Most examples are done with options, but types are available to options and arguments.
10|
11|```{contents}
12|---
13|depth: 2
14|local: true
15|---
16|```
17|
18|## Built-in Types Examples
19|
20|(choice-opts)=
21|
22|### Choice
23|
24|Sometimes, you want to have a parameter be a choice of a list of values. In that case you can use {class}`Choice` type.
25|It can be instantiated with a list of valid values. The originally passed choice will be returned, not the str passed on
26|the command line. Token normalization functions and `case_sensitive=False` can cause the two to be different but still
27|match. {meth}`Choice.normalize_choice` for more info.
28|
29|
30|Example:
31|
32|```{eval-rst}
33|.. click:example::
34|
35|    import enum
36|
37|    class HashType(enum.Enum):
38|        MD5 = enum.auto()
39|        SHA1 = enum.auto()
40|
41|    @click.command()
42|    @click.option('--hash-type',
43|                  type=click.Choice(HashType, case_sensitive=False))
44|    def digest(hash_type: HashType):
45|        click.echo(hash_type)
46|
47|What it looks like:
48|
49|.. click:run::
50|
51|    invoke(digest, args=['--hash-type=MD5'])
52|    println()
53|    invoke(digest, args=['--hash-type=md5'])
54|    println()
55|    invoke(digest, args=['--hash-type=foo'])
56|    println()
57|    invoke(digest, args=['--help'])
58|```
59|
60|Any iterable may be passed to {class}`Choice`. If an `Enum` is passed, the names of the enum members will be used as
61|valid choices.
62|
63|Choices work with options that have `multiple=True`. If a `default` value is given with `multiple=True`, it should be a
64|list or tuple of valid choices.
65|
66|Choices should be unique after normalization, see {meth}`Choice.normalize_choice` for more info.
67|
68|```{versionchanged} 7.1
69|The resulting value from an option will always be one of the originally passed choices
70|regardless of `case_sensitive`.
71|```
72|
73|```{versionchanged} 8.4.0
74|{class}`Choice` is now generic. Parameterize it with the choice value type
75|({class}`!Choice[HashType]` for an enum, {class}`!Choice[str]` for plain
76|strings) to enable type-checked consumers.
77|```
78|
79|(ranges)=
80|
81|### Int and Float Ranges
82|
83|The {class}`IntRange` type extends the {data}`INT` type to ensure the value is contained in the given range. The
84|{class}`FloatRange` type does the same for {data}`FLOAT`.
85|
86|If `min` or `max` is omitted, that side is *unbounded*. Any value in that direction is accepted. By default, both bounds
87|are *closed*, which means the boundary value is included in the accepted range. `min_open` and `max_open` can be used to
88|exclude that boundary from the range.
89|
90|If `clamp` mode is enabled, a value that is outside the range is set to the boundary instead of failing. For example,
91|the range `0, 5` would return `5` for the value `10`, or `0` for the value `-1`. When using {class}`FloatRange`, `clamp`
92|can only be enabled if both bounds are *closed* (the default).
93|
94|```{eval-rst}
95|.. click:example::
96|
97|    @click.command()
98|    @click.option("--count", type=click.IntRange(0, 20, clamp=True))
99|    @click.option("--digit", type=click.IntRange(0, 9))
100|    def repeat(count, digit):
101|        click.echo(str(digit) * count)
102|
103|.. click:run::
104|
105|    invoke(repeat, args=['--count=100', '--digit=5'])
106|    invoke(repeat, args=['--count=6', '--digit=12'])
107|```
108|
109|## Built-in Types Listing
110|
111|The supported parameter {ref}`click-api-types` are
112|
113|- `str` / {data}`click.STRING`: The default parameter type which indicates unicode strings.
114|
115|- `int` / {data}`click.INT`: A parameter that only accepts integers.
116|
117|- `float` / {data}`click.FLOAT`: A parameter that only accepts floating point values.
118|
119|- `bool` / {data}`click.BOOL`: A parameter that accepts boolean values. This is automatically used for boolean flags.
120|  The string values "1", "true", "t", "yes", "y", and "on" convert to `True`. "0", "false", "f", "no", "n", and "off"
121|  convert to `False`.
122|
123|- {data}`click.UUID`: A parameter that accepts UUID values. This is not automatically guessed but represented as
124|  {class}`uuid.UUID`.

156|(type-inference)=
157|
158|## How Click Infers a Type
159|
160|When `type` is not given, Click infers it from `default`. Only the defaults listed below
161|are recognized. Every other default gives {data}`STRING`.
162|
163|| `default`                                        | Inferred type                                   |
164|| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
165|| not given, or `None`                             | {data}`STRING`                                  |
166|| `"git"`                                          | {data}`STRING`                                  |
167|| `5`                                              | {data}`INT`                                     |
168|| `1.5`                                            | {data}`FLOAT`                                   |
169|| `True`                                           | {data}`BOOL`                                    |
170|| `[]` or `()`                                     | {data}`STRING`                                  |
171|| `[1, 2]` or `(1, 2)`                             | {data}`INT`                                     |
172|| `[1.5, 2.5]`                                     | {data}`FLOAT`                                   |
173|| `[1, "git"]`                                     | {data}`INT`                                     |
174|| `[(1, "git")]`                                   | {class}`Tuple` of ({data}`INT`, {data}`STRING`) |
175|| `{1, 2}` or `frozenset({1, 2})`                  | {data}`STRING`                                  |
176|| `{"a": 1}`                                       | {data}`STRING`                                  |
177|| {class}`uuid.UUID` or {class}`datetime.datetime` | {data}`STRING`                                  |
178|| `b"git"`, or any other object                    | {data}`STRING`                                  |
179|
180|A `list` or `tuple` gives the type of its **first item only**, so `[1, "git"]` gives
181|{data}`INT` and the second item is converted with it. A first item that is itself a
182|`list` or `tuple` gives a {class}`Tuple`, which also sets `nargs`.
183|
184|A `set`, a `frozenset`, a `dict`, and a type Click ships but does not guess, such as
185|{class}`uuid.UUID`, all land in the last group. Their default is converted with
186|{data}`STRING`, so the command receives the `str()` form of the value.
187|
188|```{eval-rst}
189|.. click:example::
190|
191|    @click.command()
192|    @click.option('--count', default=5)
193|    @click.option('--tag', default={'git'})
194|    def show(count, tag):
195|        click.echo(f"count is {type(count).__name__}, tag is {type(tag).__name__}")
196|
197|.. click:run::
198|
199|    invoke(show, args=[])
200|```
201|
202|When `type` is given a callable Click does not recognize, that callable is called on the
203|string coming from the command line, and a `ValueError` it raises is reported as a bad
204|parameter. A container is rarely useful there, because calling it on a string splits the
205|string: `set` turns `"git"` into `{"g", "i", "t"}`. Pass a {class}`ParamType` instead,
206|as described in [](#how-to-implement-custom-types).
207|
208|## How to Implement Custom Types
209|
210|To implement a custom type, you need to subclass the {class}`ParamType` class. For simple cases, passing a Python
211|function that fails with a `ValueError` is also supported, though discouraged. Override the {meth}`~ParamType.convert`
212|method to convert the value from a string to the correct type.
213|
214|{class}`ParamType` is generic in the converted value type: parameterize it with
215|the type returned by `convert` so that consumers (and type checkers) can rely
216|on the narrowed return type.
217|
218|The following code implements an integer type that accepts hex and octal numbers in addition to normal integers, and
219|converts them into regular integers.
220|
221|```python
222|import click
223|
224|
225|class BasedIntParamType(click.ParamType[int]):
226|    name = "integer"
227|
228|    def convert(self, value, param, ctx) -> int:
229|        if isinstance(value, int):
230|            return value
231|
232|        try:
233|            if value[:2].lower() == "0x":
234|                return int(value[2:], 16)
235|            elif value[:1] == "0":
236|                return int(value, 8)
237|            return int(value, 10)
238|        except ValueError:
239|            self.fail(f"{value!r} is not a valid integer", param, ctx)
240|
241|
242|BASED_INT = BasedIntParamType()
243|```
244|
245|The {attr}`~ParamType.name` attribute is optional and is used for documentation. Call {meth}`~ParamType.fail` if
246|conversion fails. The `param` and `ctx` arguments may be `None` in some cases such as prompts.
247|
248|Values from user input or the command line will be strings, but default values and Python arguments may already be the
249|correct type. The custom type should check at the top if the value is already valid and pass it through to support those
250|cases.
251|
252|```{versionchanged} 8.4.0
253|{class}`ParamType` is now a generic abstract base class. Parameterize it with
254|the converted value type ({class}`!ParamType[int]` for an integer-returning
255|type) so that {meth}`~ParamType.convert` and downstream consumers carry the
256|narrowed type.
257|```

1|# Testing Click Applications
2|
3|```{eval-rst}
4|.. currentmodule:: click.testing
5|```
6|
7|Click provides the {ref}`click.testing <testing>` module to help you invoke
8|command line applications and check their behavior.
9|
10|```{warning}
11|These tools should only be used for testing since they change the entire
12|interpreter state for simplicity. They are not thread-safe: see
13|[Running tests in parallel](#running-tests-in-parallel) for the supported
14|way to run CLI tests concurrently.
15|```
16|
17|The examples use [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/) style tests.
18|
19|```{contents}
20|:depth: 1
21|:local: true
22|```
23|
24|## Basic Example
25|
26|The key pieces are:
27|  - {class}`CliRunner` - used to invoke commands as command line scripts.
28|  - {class}`Result` - returned from {meth}`CliRunner.invoke`. Captures output
29|    data, exit code, optional exception, and captures the output as bytes and
30|    binary data.
31|
32|```{code-block} python
33|:caption: hello.py
34|
35|import click
36|
37|@click.command()
38|@click.argument('name')
39|def hello(name):
40|   click.echo(f'Hello {name}!')
41|```
42|
43|```{code-block} python
44|:caption: test_hello.py
45|
46|from click.testing import CliRunner
47|from hello import hello
48|
49|def test_hello_world():
50|  runner = CliRunner()
51|  result = runner.invoke(hello, ['Peter'])
52|  assert result.exit_code == 0
53|  assert result.output == 'Hello Peter!\n'
54|```
55|
56|## Subcommands
57|
58|A subcommand name must be specified in the `args` parameter
59|{meth}`CliRunner.invoke`:
60|
61|```{code-block} python
62|:caption: sync.py
63|
64|import click
65|
66|@click.group()
67|@click.option('--debug/--no-debug', default=False)
68|def cli(debug):
69|   click.echo(f"Debug mode is {'on' if debug else 'off'}")
70|
71|@cli.command()
72|def sync():
73|   click.echo('Syncing')
74|```
75|
76|```{code-block} python
77|:caption: test_sync.py
78|
79|from click.testing import CliRunner
80|from sync import cli
81|
82|def test_sync():
83|  runner = CliRunner()
84|  result = runner.invoke(cli, ['--debug', 'sync'])
85|  assert result.exit_code == 0
86|  assert 'Debug mode is on' in result.output
87|  assert 'Syncing' in result.output
88|```
89|
90|## Context Settings
91|
92|Additional keyword arguments passed to {meth}`CliRunner.invoke` will be used to
93|construct the initial {class}`Context object <click.Context>`.
94|For example, setting a fixed terminal width equal to 60:
95|
96|```{code-block} python
97|:caption: sync.py
98|
99|import click
100|
101|@click.group()
102|def cli():
103|   pass
104|
105|@cli.command()
106|def sync():
107|   click.echo('Syncing')
108|```
109|
110|```{code-block} python
111|:caption: test_sync.py
112|
113|from click.testing import CliRunner
114|from sync import cli
115|
116|def test_sync():
117|  runner = CliRunner()
118|  result = runner.invoke(cli, ['sync'], terminal_width=60)
119|  assert result.exit_code == 0
120|  assert 'Debug mode is on' in result.output
121|  assert 'Syncing' in result.output
122|```
123|
124|## File System Isolation
125|
126|To test a command that reads or writes files, give each test its own
127|directory and pass absolute paths to the command. Pytest's
128|[`tmp_path`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/tmp_path.html) fixture
129|provides a fresh directory per test; {class}`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory`
130|works without pytest.
131|
132|```{code-block} python
133|:caption: cat.py
134|
135|import click
136|
137|@click.command()
138|@click.argument('f', type=click.File())
139|def cat(f):
140|   click.echo(f.read())
141|```
142|
143|```{code-block} python
144|:caption: test_cat.py
145|
146|from click.testing import CliRunner
147|from cat import cat
148|
149|def test_cat(tmp_path):
150|   hello = tmp_path / 'hello.txt'
151|   hello.write_text('Hello World!')
152|
153|   runner = CliRunner()
154|   result = runner.invoke(cat, [str(hello)])
155|   assert result.exit_code == 0
156|   assert result.output == 'Hello World!\n'
157|```
158|
159|Because the directory is unique to the test and the command receives an
160|absolute path, nothing leaks between tests and the working directory is never
161|changed.
162|
163|### Running tests in parallel
164|
165|Isolating the file system with pytest is thread-safe: each test, or each thread,
166|works in its own directory through absolute paths, with no shared state.
167|
168|{meth}`CliRunner.invoke` is different. While a command runs it swaps several
169|pieces of process-global state into place (like `sys.stdout`, `sys.stderr`,
170|`sys.stdin`, etc). Two invocations active at the same time in one interpreter
171|overwrite each other's state, so the runner cannot be driven from several
172|threads at once.
173|
174|```{warning}
175|Do not parallelize CLI tests with threads. Use process-based isolation
176|instead, where each worker has its own interpreter and its own copy of those
177|globals. [pytest-xdist](https://pytest-xdist.readthedocs.io/) does this with
178|`pytest --numprocesses=auto`.
179|```
180|
181|Click's own test suite uses exactly this setup: the `tests-random` dependency
182|group and the `random` tox environment in
183|[`pyproject.toml`](https://github.com/pallets/click/blob/main/pyproject.toml)
184|run the suite under `pytest-randomly` and `pytest-xdist` to surface ordering
185|bugs and races.
186|
187|```{deprecated} 8.5.0
188|{meth}`CliRunner.isolated_filesystem` is deprecated and will be removed in
189|Click 9.0. Use a temporary directory with absolute paths, as shown above.
190|```
191|
192|## Input Streams
193|
194|The test wrapper can provide input data for the input stream (stdin). This is
195|very useful for testing prompts.
196|
197|```{code-block} python
198|:caption: prompt.py
199|
200|import click
201|
202|@click.command()
203|@click.option('--foo', prompt=True)
204|def prompt(foo):
205|   click.echo(f"foo={foo}")
206|```
207|
208|```{code-block} python
209|:caption: test_prompt.py
210|
211|from click.testing import CliRunner
212|from prompt import prompt
213|
214|def test_prompts():
215|   runner = CliRunner()
216|   result = runner.invoke(prompt, input='wau wau\n')
217|   assert not result.exception
218|   assert result.output == 'Foo: wau wau\nfoo=wau wau\n'
219|```
220|
221|Prompts will be emulated so they write the input data to
222|the output stream as well. If hidden input is expected then this
223|does not happen.
224|
225|## Capture modes
226|
227|{class}`CliRunner` captures output by replacing `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr`
228|with in-memory wrappers. The `capture` parameter controls which strategy is
229|used.
230|
231|### `capture="sys"` (default)
232|
233|Captures Python-level writes (`print()`, `click.echo()`, `sys.stdout.write()`).
234|It is fast and sufficient for most Click applications.
235|
236|Code that holds a reference to the original `sys.stdout` (like a library that
237|does `from sys import stdout` at import time) bypasses the capture and its
238|output is lost.
239|
240|In this mode `sys.stdout.fileno()` and `sys.stderr.fileno()` raise
241|{exc}`io.UnsupportedOperation`, matching the pre-`8.3.3` behavior. C-level
242|consumers ({mod}`faulthandler`, {mod}`subprocess`, C extensions) that expect a
243|real file descriptor must opt into the `capture="fd"` mode.
244|
245|### `capture="fd"`
246|
247|Redirects OS file descriptors `1` and `2` to a temporary file via
248|{func}`os.dup2`, inspired by [Pytest's
249|`capfd`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/how-to/capture-stdout-stderr.html).
250|This catches output that bypasses `sys.stdout`, including:
251|
252|- Stale references to the original `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr`.
253|- Logging frameworks that cache the original stream (like `structlog` or the
254|  stdlib's `logging` module).
255|- C extensions and subprocesses that write directly to `fd 1` or `fd 2`.
256|
257|```python
258|from click.testing import CliRunner
259|from myapp import cli
260|
261|
262|def test_captures_everything():
263|    runner = CliRunner(capture="fd")
264|    result = runner.invoke(cli)
265|    # result.stdout contains both Python-level and fd-level output
266|    assert "expected output" in result.stdout
267|```
268|
269|In this mode `sys.stdout.fileno()` returns the saved (pre-redirection) `fd`, so
270|{mod}`faulthandler` and similar consumers keep working. Writes to `fd 1` and
271|`fd 2` land in the capture tmpfile, so `os.dup2()` calls inside the CLI no
272|longer leak into the host runner's stdout.
273|
274|```{note}
275|`capture="fd"` is not available on Windows.
276|```
277|
278|```{versionchanged} 8.4.0
279|Added the `capture` parameter. The default `sys` mode no longer exposes the
280|original `fd` through `fileno()`, reverting the change introduced in `8.3.3`
281|that broke Pytest's `fd`-level capture teardown. Use `capture="fd"` to restore
282|that behavior with proper isolation.
283|```

1|# Why Click?
2|
3|There are so many libraries out there for writing command line utilities; why does Click exist?
4|
5|This question is easy to answer: because there is not a single command line utility for Python out there which ticks the
6|following boxes:
7|
8|- Is lazily composable without restrictions.
9|- Supports implementation of Unix/POSIX command line conventions.
10|- Supports loading values from environment variables out of the box.
11|- Support for prompting of custom values.
12|- Is fully nestable and composable.
13|- Supports file handling out of the box.
14|- Comes with useful common helpers (getting terminal dimensions, ANSI colors, fetching direct keyboard input, screen
15|  clearing, finding config paths, launching apps and editors, etc.).
16|
17|There are many alternatives to Click; the obvious ones are `optparse` and `argparse` from the standard library. Have a
18|look to see if something else resonates with you.
19|
20|Click actually implements its own parsing of arguments and does not use `optparse` or `argparse` following the
21|`optparse` parsing behavior. The reason it's not based on `argparse` is that `argparse` does not allow proper nesting of
22|commands by design and has some deficiencies when it comes to POSIX compliant argument handling.
23|
24|Click is designed to be fun and customizable but not overly flexible. For instance, the customizability of help pages is
25|constrained. This constraint is intentional because Click promises multiple Click instances will continue to function as
26|intended when strung together.
27|
28|Too much customizability would break this promise.
29|
30|Click was written to support the [Flask](https://palletsprojects.com/p/flask/) microframework ecosystem because no tool
31|could provide it with the functionality it needed.
32|
33|To get an understanding of what Click is all about, I strongly recommend looking at the {ref}`complex-guide` chapter.
34|
35|## Why not Argparse?
36|
37|Click is internally based on `optparse` instead of `argparse`. This is an implementation detail that a user does not
38|have to be concerned with. Click is not based on `argparse` because it has some behaviors that make handling arbitrary
39|command line interfaces hard:
40|
41|- `argparse` has built-in behavior to guess if something is an argument or an option. This becomes a problem when
42|  dealing with incomplete command lines; the behaviour becomes unpredictable without full knowledge of a command line.
43|  This goes against Click's ambitions of dispatching to subparsers.
44|- `argparse` does not support disabling interspersed arguments. Without this feature, it's not possible to safely
45|  implement Click's nested parsing.
46|
47|## Why not Docopt etc.?
48|
49|Docopt, and many tools like it, are cool in how they work, but very few of these tools deal with nesting of commands and
50|composability in a way like Click. To the best of the developer's knowledge, Click is the first Python library that aims
51|to create a level of composability of applications that goes beyond what the system itself supports.
52|
53|Docopt, for instance, acts by parsing your help pages and then parsing according to those rules. The side effect of this
54|is that docopt is quite rigid in how it handles the command line interface. The upside of docopt is that it gives you
55|strong control over your help page; the downside is that due to this it cannot rewrap your output for the current
56|terminal width, and it makes translations hard. On top of that, docopt is restricted to basic parsing. It does not
57|handle argument dispatching and callback invocation or types. This means there is a lot of code that needs to be written
58|in addition to the basic help page to handle the parsing results.
59|
60|Most of all, however, it makes composability hard. While docopt does support dispatching to subcommands, it, for
61|instance, does not directly support any kind of automatic subcommand enumeration based on what's available or it does
62|not enforce subcommands to work in a consistent way.
63|
64|This is fine, but it's different from how Click wants to work. Click aims to support fully composable command line user
65|interfaces by doing the following:
66|
67|- Click does not just parse, it also dispatches to the appropriate code.
68|- Click has a strong concept of an invocation context that allows subcommands to respond to data from the parent
69|  command.
70|- Click has strong information available for all parameters and commands, so it can generate unified help pages for the
71|  full CLI and assist the user in converting the input data as necessary.
72|- Click has a strong understanding of what types are, and it can give the user consistent error messages if something
73|  goes wrong. A subcommand written by a different developer will not suddenly die with a different error message because
74|  it's manually handled.
75|- Click has enough meta information available for its whole program to evolve over time and improve the user experience
76|  without forcing developers to adjust their programs. For instance, if Click decides to change how help pages are
77|  formatted, all Click programs will automatically benefit from this.
78|
79|The aim of Click is to make composable systems. Whereas, the aim of docopt is to build the most beautiful and
80|hand-crafted command line interfaces. These two goals conflict with one another in subtle ways. Click actively prevents
81|people from implementing certain patterns in order to achieve unified command line interfaces. For instance, as a
82|developer, you are given very little choice in formatting your help pages.
83|
84|## Why Hardcoded Behaviors?
85|
86|The other question is why Click goes away from optparse and hardcodes certain behaviors instead of staying configurable.
87|There are multiple reasons for this. The biggest one is that too much configurability makes it hard to achieve a
88|consistent command line experience.
89|
90|The best example for this is optparse's `callback` functionality for accepting an arbitrary number of arguments. Due to
91|syntactical ambiguities on the command line, there is no way to implement fully variadic arguments. There are always
92|tradeoffs that need to be made and in case of `argparse` these tradeoffs have been critical enough, that a system like
93|Click cannot even be implemented on top of it.
94|
95|In this particular case, Click attempts to stay with a handful of accepted paradigms for building command line
96|interfaces that can be well documented and tested.
97|
98|## Why No Auto Correction?
99|
100|The question came up why Click does not auto correct parameters given that even optparse and `argparse` support
101|automatic expansion of long arguments. The reason for this is that it's a liability for backwards compatibility. If
102|people start relying on automatically modified parameters and someone adds a new parameter in the future, the script
103|might stop working. These kinds of problems are hard to find, so Click does not attempt to be magical about this.
104|
105|This sort of behavior however can be implemented on a higher level to support things such as explicit aliases. For more
106|information see {ref}`aliases`.
--- END FILE: docs/why.md ---
--- FILE: docs/quickstart.md ---
1|# Quickstart
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|## Install
7|
8|Install from PyPI:
9|
10|```console
11|pip install click
12|```
13|
14|Installing into a virtual environment is highly recommended. We suggest {ref}`virtualenv-heading`.
15|
16|## Examples
17|
18|Some standalone examples of Click applications are packaged with Click. They are available in the
19|[examples folder](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples) of the repo.
20|
21|- [inout](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/inout) : A very simple example of an application that can
22|  read from files and write to files and also accept input from stdin or write to stdout.
23|- [validation](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/validation) : A simple example of an application that
24|  performs custom validation of parameters in different ways.
25|- [naval](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/naval) : Port of the [docopt](http://docopt.org/) naval
26|  example.
27|- [colors](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/colors) : A simple example that colorizes text.
28|- [aliases](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/aliases) : An advanced example that implements
29|  {ref}`aliases`.
30|- [imagepipe](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/imagepipe) : A complex example that implements some
31|  {ref}`command-pipelines` . It chains together image processing instructions. Requires pillow.
32|- [repo](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/repo) : An advanced example that implements a
33|  Git-/Mercurial-like command line interface.
34|- [complex](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/complex) : A very advanced example that implements
35|  loading subcommands dynamically from a plugin folder.
36|- [termui](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/termui) : A simple example that showcases terminal UI
37|  helpers provided by click.
38|
39|## Basic Concepts - Creating a Command
40|
41|Click is based on declaring commands through decorators. Internally, there is a non-decorator interface for advanced use
42|cases, but it's discouraged for high-level usage.
43|
44|A function becomes a Click command line tool by decorating it through {func}`command`. At its simplest, just
45|decorating a function with this decorator will make it into a callable script:
46|
47|
48|```{eval-rst}
49|.. click:example::
50|    import click
51|
52|    @click.command()
53|    def hello():
54|        click.echo('Hello World!')
55|
56|What's happening is that the decorator converts the function into a :class:`Command` which then can be invoked:
57|
58|.. click:example::
59|    if __name__ == '__main__':
60|        hello()
61|
62|And what it looks like:
63|
64|.. click:run::
65|    invoke(hello, args=[], prog_name='python hello.py')
66|
67|And the corresponding help page:
68|
69|.. click:run::
70|    invoke(hello, args=['--help'], prog_name='python hello.py')
71|```
72|
73|## Echoing
74|
75|Why does this example use {func}`echo` instead of the regular {func}`print` function? The answer to this question is
76|that Click attempts to support different environments consistently and to be very robust even when the environment is
77|misconfigured. Click wants to be functional at least on a basic level even if everything is completely broken.
78|
79|What this means is that the {func}`echo` function applies some error correction in case the terminal is misconfigured
80|instead of dying with a {exc}`UnicodeError`.
81|
82|The echo function also supports color and other styles in output. It will automatically remove styles if the output
83|stream is a file. See {ref}`ansi-colors`.
84|
85|If you don't need this, you can also use the `print()` construct / function.
86|
87|## Nesting Commands
88|
89|Commands can be attached to other commands of type {class}`Group`. This allows arbitrary nesting of scripts. As an
90|example here is a script that implements two commands for managing databases:
91|
92|```{eval-rst}
93|.. click:example::
94|    @click.group()
95|    def cli():
96|        pass
97|
98|    @click.command()
99|    def initdb():
100|        click.echo('Initialized the database')
101|
102|    @click.command()
103|    def dropdb():
104|        click.echo('Dropped the database')
105|
106|    cli.add_command(initdb)
107|    cli.add_command(dropdb)
108|```
109|
110|As you can see, the {func}`group` decorator works like the {func}`command` decorator, but creates a {class}`Group`
111|object instead which can be given multiple subcommands that can be attached with {meth}`Group.add_command`.
112|
113|For simple scripts, it's also possible to automatically attach and create a command by using the {meth}`Group.command`
114|decorator instead. The above script can instead be written like this:
115|
116|```{eval-rst}
117|.. click:example::
118|    @click.group()
119|    def cli():
120|        pass
121|
122|    @cli.command()
123|    def initdb():
124|        click.echo('Initialized the database')
125|
126|    @cli.command()
127|    def dropdb():
128|        click.echo('Dropped the database')
129|
130|You would then invoke the :class:`Group` in your entry points or other invocations:
131|
132|.. click:example::
133|    if __name__ == '__main__':
134|        cli()
135|```
136|
137|## Registering Commands Later
138|
139|Instead of using the `@group.command()` decorator, commands can be decorated with the plain `@command()` decorator
140|and registered with a group later with `group.add_command()`. This could be used to split commands into multiple Python
141|modules.
142|
143|```{code-block} python
144|@click.command()
145|def greet():
146|    click.echo("Hello, World!")
147|```
148|
149|```{code-block} python
150|@click.group()
151|def group():
152|    pass
153|
154|group.add_command(greet)
155|```
156|
157|## Adding Parameters
158|
159|To add parameters, use the {func}`option` and {func}`argument` decorators:
160|
161|```{eval-rst}
162|.. click:example::
163|    @click.command()
164|    @click.option('--count', default=1, help='number of greetings')
165|    @click.argument('name')
166|    def hello(count, name):
167|        for x in range(count):
168|            click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
169|
170|What it looks like:
171|
172|.. click:run::
173|    invoke(hello, args=['--help'], prog_name='python hello.py')
174|```
175|
176|## Switching to Entry Points
177|
178|In the code you wrote so far there is a block at the end of the file which looks like this:
179|`if __name__ == '__main__':`. This is traditionally how a standalone Python file looks like. With Click you can continue
180|doing that, but a better way is to package your app with an entry point.
181|
182|There are two main (and many more) reasons for this:
183|
184|The first one is that installers automatically generate executable wrappers for Windows so your command line utilities
185|work on Windows too.
186|
187|The second reason is that entry point scripts work with virtualenv on Unix without the virtualenv having to be
188|activated. This is a very useful concept which allows you to bundle your scripts with all requirements into a
189|virtualenv.
190|
191|Click is perfectly equipped to work with that and in fact the rest of the documentation will assume that you are writing
192|applications as distributed packages.
193|
194|Look at the {doc}`entry-points` chapter before reading the rest as the examples assume that you will be using entry
195|points.

2|
3|# click-contrib
4|
5|As the user number of Click grows, more and more major feature requests are
6|made. To users, it may seem reasonable to include those features with Click;
7|however, many of them are experimental or aren't practical to support
8|generically. Maintainers have to choose what is reasonable to maintain in Click
9|core.
10|
11|The [click-contrib](https://github.com/click-contrib/) GitHub organization exists as a place to collect third-party
12|packages that extend Click's features. It is also meant to ease the effort of
13|searching for such extensions.
14|
15|Please note that the quality and stability of those packages may be different
16|from Click itself. While published under a common organization, they are still
17|separate from Click and the Pallets maintainers.
18|
19|## Third-party projects
20|
21|Other projects that extend Click's features are available outside the
22|[click-contrib](https://github.com/click-contrib/) organization.
23|

35|## Interactive input libraries
36|
37|Click reads a prompt with the built-in {func}`input` and embeds no line editor of its own. If you need fancy features like completion of arbitrary values, selection menus or fuzzy search you need to replace {func}`click.prompt` with a third-party library. The projects below are popular and actively maintained:

1|(exception-handling-exit-codes)=
2|
3|# Exception Handling and Exit Codes
4|
5|```{eval-rst}
6|.. currentmodule:: click
7|```
8|
9|Click internally uses exceptions to signal various error conditions that
10|the user of the application might have caused. Primarily this is things
11|like incorrect usage.
12|
13|```{contents}
14|:depth: 1
15|:local:
16|```
17|
18|## Where are Errors Handled?
19|
20|Click's main error handling is happening in {meth}`Command.main`. In
21|there it handles all subclasses of {exc}`ClickException` as well as the
22|standard {exc}`EOFError` and {exc}`KeyboardInterrupt` exceptions.
23|
24|The table below lists every way a command can end, and what Click does
25|for each. The middle column is the default. The last column applies when
26|{meth}`Command.main` runs with ``standalone_mode=False``, which the next
27|section describes.
28|
29|| How the command ends | Standalone mode | ``standalone_mode=False`` |
30|| --- | --- | --- |
31|| It returns | Exit with code ``0`` | Return the value of {meth}`Command.invoke` |
32|| It called {meth}`Context.exit` | Exit with the given code | Return the given code |
33|| It raised a {exc}`ClickException` | Call {meth}`ClickException.show`, then exit with {attr}`ClickException.exit_code` | Propagate it |
34|| The user pressed {kbd}`Ctrl+C`, which raises a {exc}`KeyboardInterrupt` | Print a blank line, then ``Aborted!`` to standard error, and exit with code ``1`` | Print a blank line, then raise {exc}`Abort` with the original exception as its ``__cause__`` |
35|| The user pressed {kbd}`Ctrl+D`, or {kbd}`Ctrl+Z` on Windows, which raises an {exc}`EOFError` | The same as {kbd}`Ctrl+C` | The same as {kbd}`Ctrl+C` |
36|| It raised an {exc}`Abort` | Print ``Aborted!`` to standard error, and exit with code ``1`` | Propagate it |
37|| The output pipe closed early, which raises an {exc}`OSError` with ``EPIPE`` | Silence the flush errors, and exit with code ``1`` | The same |
38|| It raised any other exception | Propagate it | Propagate it |
39|
40|Click writes the message and exits once that handling is done. An
41|interrupt arriving during this last step cannot change the exit code the
42|table gave. It can only cost the message.
43|
44|## What if I Don't Want That?
45|
46|Generally you always have the option to invoke the {meth}`Command.invoke`
47|method yourself. For instance if you have a {class}`Command` you can
48|invoke it manually like this:
49|
50|```python
51|ctx = command.make_context("command-name", ["args", "go", "here"])
52|with ctx:
53|    result = command.invoke(ctx)
54|```
55|
56|In this case exceptions will not be handled at all and bubbled up as you
57|would expect.
58|
59|Starting with Click 3.0 you can also use the {meth}`Command.main` method
60|but disable the standalone mode which will do two things: disable
61|exception handling and disable the implicit {func}`sys.exit` at the end.
62|
63|So you can do something like this:
64|
65|```python
66|command.main(
67|    ["command-name", "args", "go", "here"],
68|    standalone_mode=False,
69|)
70|```
71|
72|This is also how you replace the ``Aborted!`` message. Standalone mode
73|turns off every row of the table above, so catch the cases you want to
74|keep and write your own message for the rest:
75|
76|```python
77|try:
78|    command.main(
79|        ["command-name", "args", "go", "here"],
80|        standalone_mode=False,
81|    )
82|except click.Abort:
83|    click.echo("Bye!", err=True)
84|    raise SystemExit(1)
85|except click.ClickException as e:
86|    e.show()
87|    raise SystemExit(e.exit_code)
88|```
89|
90|## Which Exceptions Exist?
91|
92|Click has two exception bases: {exc}`ClickException` which is raised for
93|all exceptions that Click wants to signal to the user and {exc}`Abort`
94|which is used to instruct Click to abort the execution.
95|
96|A {exc}`ClickException` has a {meth}`ClickException.show` method which
97|can render an error message to stderr or the given file object. If you
98|want to use the exception yourself for doing something check the API docs
99|about what else they provide.
100|
101|The following common subclasses exist:
102|
103|- {exc}`UsageError` to inform the user that something went wrong.
104|- {exc}`BadParameter` to inform the user that something went wrong with
105|  a specific parameter. These are often handled internally in Click and
106|  augmented with extra information if possible. For instance if those
107|  are raised from a callback Click will automatically augment it with
108|  the parameter name if possible.
109|- {exc}`FileError` this is an error that is raised by the
110|  {class}`FileType` if Click encounters issues opening the file.
111|
112|(help-page-exit-codes)=
113|
114|## Help Pages and Exit Codes
115|
116|Triggering the a help page intentionally (by passing in ``--help``)
117|returns exit code 0. If a help page is displayed due to incorrect user
118|input, the program returns exit code 2. See {ref}`exit-codes` for more
119|general information.
120|
121|For clarity, here is an example.
122|
123|```{eval-rst}
124|.. click:example::
125|
126|    @click.group('printer_group')
127|    def printer_group():
128|        pass
129|
130|    @printer_group.command('printer')
131|    @click.option('--this')
132|    def printer(this):
133|        if this:
134|            click.echo(this)
135|
136|.. click:run::
137|    invoke(printer_group, args=['--help'])
138|
139|The above invocation returns exit code 0.
140|
141|.. click:run::
142|    invoke(printer_group, args=[])
143|```
144|
145|The above invocation returns exit code 2 since the user invoked the command incorrectly. However, since this is such a common error when first using a command, Click invokes the help page for the user. To see that `printer-group` is an invalid invocation, turn `no_args_is_help` off.
146|
147|```{eval-rst}
148|.. click:example::
149|
150|    @click.group('printer_group', no_args_is_help=False)
151|    def printer_group():
152|        pass
153|
154|    @printer_group.command('printer')
155|    @click.option('--this')
156|    def printer(this):
157|        if this:
158|            click.echo(this)
159|
160|.. click:run::
161|    invoke(printer_group, args=[])
162|```

1|(arguments)=
2|
3|# Arguments
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click
6|```
7|
8|Arguments are:
9|
10|* Are positional in nature.
11|* Similar to a limited version of {ref}`options <options>` that
12|  can take an arbitrary number of inputs
13|* Can take an optional `help` string shown in the `Positional arguments`
14|  section of the help page, or be {ref}`documented in the command docstring
15|  <documenting-arguments>`. One argument with a `help` makes the section list
16|  all the arguments of the command.
17|
18|Useful and often used kwargs are:
19|
20|* `help`: Help text for the argument.
21|* `default`: Passes a default.
22|* `nargs`: Sets the number of arguments. Set to -1 to take an arbitrary number.
23|
24|## Basic Arguments
25|
26|A minimal {class}`click.Argument` solely takes one string argument:
27|the name of the argument. This will assume the argument is required,
28|has no default, and is of the type `str`.
29|
30|Example:
31|
32|```{eval-rst}
33|.. click:example::
34|
35|    @click.command()
36|    @click.argument('filename')
37|    def touch(filename: str):
38|        """Print FILENAME."""
39|        click.echo(filename)
40|
41|And from the command line:
42|
43|.. click:run::
44|
45|    invoke(touch, args=['foo.txt'])
46|```
47|
48|An argument may be assigned a {ref}`parameter type <parameter-types>`.
49|If no type is provided, the type of the default value is used if it is
50|recognized, otherwise {data}`STRING` is used. If no default value is
51|provided, the type is assumed to be {data}`STRING`. See
52|{ref}`type-inference` for the types that are recognized.
53|
54|```{admonition} Note on Required Arguments
55|:class: note
56|
57|   It is possible to make an argument required by setting
58|   `required=True`. It is not recommended since we think command line
59|   tools should gracefully degrade into becoming no ops. We think this
60|   because command line tools are often invoked with wildcard inputs
61|   and they should not error out if the wildcard is empty.
62|```
63|
64|## Multiple Arguments
65|
66|To set the number of argument use the `nargs` kwarg. It can be set to
67|any positive integer and -1. Setting it to -1, makes the number of
68|arguments arbitrary (which is called variadic) and can only be used
69|once. The arguments are then packed as a tuple and passed to the
70|function.
71|
72|```{eval-rst}
73|.. click:example::
74|
75|    @click.command()
76|    @click.argument('src', nargs=1)
77|    @click.argument('dsts', nargs=-1)
78|    def copy(src: str, dsts: tuple[str, ...]):
79|        """Move file SRC to DST."""
80|        for destination in dsts:
81|            click.echo(f"Copy {src} to folder {destination}")
82|
83|And from the command line:
84|
85|.. click:run::
86|
87|    invoke(copy, args=['foo.txt', 'usr/david/foo.txt', 'usr/mitsuko/foo.txt'])
88|```
89|
90|```{admonition} Note on Handling Files
91|:class: note
92|
93|   This is not how you should handle files and files paths. This
94|   merely used as a simple example. See {ref}`handling-files` to learn
95|   more about how to handle files in parameters.
96|```
97|
98|## Argument Escape Sequences
99|
100|If you want to process arguments that look like options, like a file
101|named `-foo.txt` or `--foo.txt`, you must pass the `--` separator
102|first. After you pass the `--`, you may only pass arguments. This is a
103|common feature for POSIX command line tools.
104|
105|Example usage:
106|
107|```{eval-rst}
108|.. click:example::
109|
110|    @click.command()
111|    @click.argument('files', nargs=-1, type=click.Path())
112|    def touch(files):
113|        """Print all FILES file names."""
114|        for filename in files:
115|            click.echo(filename)
116|
117|And from the command line:
118|
119|.. click:run::
120|
121|    invoke(touch, ['--', '-foo.txt', 'bar.txt'])
122|```
123|
124|If you don't like the `--` marker, you can set
125|`ignore_unknown_options` to `True` to avoid checking unknown options:
126|
127|```{eval-rst}
128|.. click:example::
129|
130|    @click.command(context_settings={"ignore_unknown_options": True})
131|    @click.argument('files', nargs=-1, type=click.Path())
132|    def touch(files):
133|        """Print all FILES file names."""
134|        for filename in files:
135|            click.echo(filename)
136|
137|And from the command line:
138|
139|.. click:run::
140|
141|    invoke(touch, ['-foo.txt', 'bar.txt'])
142|```
143|
144|(environment-variables)=
145|
146|## Environment Variables
147|
148|Arguments can use environment variables. To do so, pass the name(s) of
149|the environment variable(s) via `envvar` in `click.argument`.
150|
151|Checking one environment variable:
152|
153|```{eval-rst}
154|.. click:example::
155|
156|    @click.command()
157|    @click.argument('src', envvar='SRC', type=click.File('r'))
158|    def echo(src):
159|        """Print value of SRC environment variable."""
160|        click.echo(src.read())
161|
162|And from the command line:
163|
164|.. click:run::
165|
166|    with isolated_filesystem():
167|        # Writing the file in the filesystem.
168|        with open('hello.txt', 'w') as f:
169|            f.write('Hello World!')
170|        invoke(echo, env={'SRC': 'hello.txt'})
171|
172|
173|Checking multiple environment variables:
174|
175|.. click:example::
176|
177|    @click.command()
178|    @click.argument('src', envvar=['SRC', 'SRC_2'], type=click.File('r'))
179|    def echo(src):
180|        """Print value of SRC environment variable."""
181|        click.echo(src.read())
182|
183|And from the command line:
184|
185|.. click:run::
186|
187|    with isolated_filesystem():
188|        # Writing the file in the filesystem.
189|        with open('hello.txt', 'w') as f:
190|            f.write('Hello World from second variable!')
191|        invoke(echo, env={'SRC_2': 'hello.txt'})
192|```

1|# User Input Prompts
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|Click supports prompts in two different places. The first is automated prompts when the parameter handling happens, and
7|the second is to ask for prompts at a later point independently.
8|
9|This can be accomplished with the {func}`prompt` function, which asks for valid input according to a type, or the
10|{func}`confirm` function, which asks for confirmation (yes/no).
11|
12|```{contents}
13|---
14|depth: 2
15|local: true
16|---
17|```
18|
19|(option-prompting)=
20|
21|## Option Prompts
22|
23|Option prompts are integrated into the option interface. Internally, it automatically calls either {func}`prompt` or
24|{func}`confirm` as necessary.
25|
26|In some cases, you want parameters that can be provided from the command line, but if not provided, ask for user input
27|instead. This can be implemented with Click by defining a prompt string.
28|
29|Example:
30|
31|```{eval-rst}
32|.. click:example::
33|
34|    @click.command()
35|    @click.option('--name', prompt=True)
36|    def hello(name):
37|        click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
38|
39|And what it looks like:
40|
41|.. click:run::
42|
43|    invoke(hello, args=['--name=John'])
44|    invoke(hello, input=['John'])
45|```
46|
47|If you are not happy with the default prompt string, you can ask for
48|a different one:
49|
50|```{eval-rst}
51|.. click:example::
52|
53|    @click.command()
54|    @click.option('--name', prompt='Your name please')
55|    def hello(name):
56|        click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
57|
58|What it looks like:
59|
60|.. click:run::
61|
62|    invoke(hello, input=['John'])
63|```
64|
65|It is advised that prompt not be used in conjunction with the multiple flag set to True. Instead, prompt in the function
66|interactively.
67|
68|By default, the user will be prompted for an input if one was not passed through the command line. To turn this behavior
69|off, see {ref}`optional-value`.
70|
71|## Input Prompts
72|
73|To manually ask for user input, you can use the {func}`prompt` function. By default, it accepts any Unicode string, but
74|you can ask for any other type. For instance, you can ask for a valid integer:
75|
76|```python
77|value = click.prompt('Please enter a valid integer', type=int)
78|```
79|
80|Additionally, the type will be determined automatically if a default value is provided. For instance, the following will
81|only accept floats:
82|
83|```python
84|value = click.prompt('Please enter a number', default=42.0)
85|```
86|
87|## Optional Prompts
88|
89|If the option has `prompt` enabled, then setting `prompt_required=False` tells Click to only show the prompt if the
90|option's flag is given, instead of if the option is not provided at all.
91|
92|```{eval-rst}
93|.. click:example::
94|
95|    @click.command()
96|    @click.option('--name', prompt=True, prompt_required=False, default="Default")
97|    def hello(name):
98|        click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
99|
100|.. click:run::
101|
102|    invoke(hello)
103|    invoke(hello, args=["--name", "Value"])
104|    invoke(hello, args=["--name"], input="Prompt")
105|```
106|
107|If `required=True`, then the option will still prompt if it is not given, but it will also prompt if only the flag is
108|given.
109|
110|## Confirmation Prompts
111|
112|To ask if a user wants to continue with an action, the {func}`confirm` function comes in handy. By default, it returns
113|the result of the prompt as a boolean value:
114|
115|```python
116|if click.confirm('Do you want to continue?'):
117|    click.echo('Well done!')
118|```
119|
120|There is also the option to make the function automatically abort the execution of the program if it does not return
121|`True`:
122|
123|```python
124|click.confirm('Do you want to continue?', abort=True)
125|```
126|
127|## Dynamic Defaults for Prompts
128|
129|The `auto_envvar_prefix` and `default_map` options for the context allow the program to read option values from the
130|environment or a configuration file. However, this overrides the prompting mechanism, so that the user does not get the
131|option to change the value interactively.
132|
133|If you want to let the user configure the default value, but still be prompted if the option isn't specified on the
134|command line, you can do so by supplying a callable as the default value. For example, to get a default from the
135|environment:
136|
137|```python
138|import os
139|
140|@click.command()
141|@click.option(
142|    "--username", prompt=True,
143|    default=lambda: os.environ.get("USER", "")
144|)
145|def hello(username):
146|    click.echo(f"Hello, {username}!")
147|```
148|
149|To describe what the default value will be, set it in ``show_default``.
150|
151|```{eval-rst}
152|.. click:example::
153|
154|    import os
155|
156|    @click.command()
157|    @click.option(
158|        "--username", prompt=True,
159|        default=lambda: os.environ.get("USER", ""),
160|        show_default="current user"
161|    )
162|    def hello(username):
163|        click.echo(f"Hello, {username}!")
164|
165|.. click:run::
166|
167|   invoke(hello, args=["--help"])
168|```

1|# Unicode Support
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|Click has to take extra care to support Unicode text in different environments.
7|
8|- The command line in Unix is traditionally bytes, not Unicode. While there are encoding hints, there are some
9|  situations where this can break. The most common one is SSH connections to machines with different locales.
10|
11|  Misconfigured environments can cause a wide range of Unicode problems due to the lack of support for roundtripping
12|  surrogate escapes. This will not be fixed in Click itself!
13|
14|- Standard input and output is opened in text mode by default. Click has to reopen the stream in binary mode in certain
15|  situations. Because there is no standard way to do this, it might not always work. Primarily this can become a problem
16|  when testing command-line applications.
17|
18|  This is not supported:
19|
20|  ```python
21|  sys.stdin = io.StringIO('Input here')
22|  sys.stdout = io.StringIO()
23|  ```
24|
25|  Instead you need to do this:
26|
27|  ```python
28|  input = 'Input here'
29|  in_stream = io.BytesIO(input.encode('utf-8'))
30|  sys.stdin = io.TextIOWrapper(in_stream, encoding='utf-8')
31|  out_stream = io.BytesIO()
32|  sys.stdout = io.TextIOWrapper(out_stream, encoding='utf-8')
33|  ```
34|
35|  Remember in that case, you need to use `out_stream.getvalue()` and not `sys.stdout.getvalue()` if you want to access
36|  the buffer contents as the wrapper will not forward that method.
37|
38|- `sys.stdin`, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` are by default text-based. When Click needs a binary stream, it attempts to
39|  discover the underlying binary stream.
40|
41|- `sys.argv` is always text. This means that the native type for input values to the types in Click is Unicode, not
42|  bytes.
43|
44|  This causes problems if the terminal is incorrectly set and Python does not figure out the encoding. In that case, the
45|  Unicode string will contain error bytes encoded as surrogate escapes.
46|
47|- When dealing with files, Click will always use the Unicode file system API by using the operating system's reported or
48|  guessed filesystem encoding. Surrogates are supported for filenames, so it should be possible to open files through
49|  the {func}`File` type even if the environment is misconfigured.
50|
51|## Surrogate Handling
52|
53|Click does all the Unicode handling in the standard library and is subject to its behavior. Unicode requires extra care.
54|The reason for this is that the encoding detection is done in the interpreter, and on Linux and certain other operating
55|systems, its encoding handling is problematic.
56|
57|The biggest source of frustration is that Click scripts invoked by init systems, deployment tools, or cron jobs will
58|refuse to work unless a Unicode locale is exported.
59|
60|If Click encounters such an environment it will prevent further execution to force you to set a locale. This is done
61|because Click cannot know about the state of the system once it's invoked and restore the values before Python's Unicode
62|handling kicked in.
63|
64|If you see something like this error:
65|
66|```console
67|Traceback (most recent call last):
68|  ...
69|RuntimeError: Click will abort further execution because Python was
70|  configured to use ASCII as encoding for the environment. Consult
71|  https://click.palletsprojects.com/unicode-support/ for mitigation
72|  steps.
73|```
74|
75|You are dealing with an environment where Python thinks you are restricted to ASCII data. The solution to these problems
76|is different depending on which locale your computer is running in.
77|
78|For instance, if you have a German Linux machine, you can fix the problem by exporting the locale to `de_DE.utf-8`:
79|
80|```console
81|export LC_ALL=de_DE.utf-8
82|export LANG=de_DE.utf-8
83|```
84|
85|If you are on a US machine, `en_US.utf-8` is the encoding of choice. On some newer Linux systems, you could also try
86|`C.UTF-8` as the locale:
87|
88|```console
89|export LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
90|export LANG=C.UTF-8
91|```
92|
93|On some systems it was reported that `UTF-8` has to be written as `UTF8` and vice versa. To see which locales are
94|supported you can invoke `locale -a`.
95|
96|You need to export the values before you invoke your Python script.
97|
98|In Python 3.7 and later you will no longer get a `RuntimeError` in many cases thanks to {pep}`538` and {pep}`540`, which
99|changed the default assumption in unconfigured environments. This doesn't change the general issue that your locale may
100|be misconfigured.
--- END FILE: docs/unicode-support.md ---
--- FILE: docs/parameters.md ---
1|(parameters)=
2|
3|# Parameters
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click
6|```
7|
8|Click supports only two principle types of parameters for scripts (by design): options and arguments.
9|
10|## Options
11|
12|- Are optional.
13|- Recommended to use for everything except subcommands, urls, or files.
14|- Can take a fixed number of arguments. The default is 1. They may be specified multiple times using {ref}`multiple-options`.
15|- Are fully documented by the help page.
16|- Have automatic prompting for missing input.
17|- Can act as flags (boolean or otherwise).
18|- Can be pulled from environment variables.
19|
20|## Arguments
21|
22|- Are optional within reason, but not entirely so.
23|- Recommended to use for subcommands, urls, or files.
24|- Can take an arbitrary number of arguments.
25|- Are not fully documented by the help page since they may be too specific to be automatically documented. For more see {ref}`documenting-arguments`.
26|- Can be pulled from environment variables but only explicitly named ones. For more see {ref}`environment-variables`.
27|
28|On each principle type you can specify {ref}`parameter-types`. Specifying these types helps Click add details to your help pages and help with the handling of those types.
29|
30|(parameter-names)=
31|
32|## Parameter Names
33|
34|Three distinct strings designate a parameter, and each one has its own audience:
35|
36|- `decls` are the declarations you pass to the decorator. Click parses them to derive every other string in this section.
37|- `spec` is what the user reads in `--help` and types on the command line. Read it from {attr}`Parameter.spec`, or from {meth}`Parameter.get_help_spec` for the longer form the help page lays out in its left column.
38|- `name` is what Click uses internally to identify the parameter. It is used as a Python argument and is passed to the decorated function. Read it from {attr}`Parameter.name`.
39|
40|Click also keeps the parsed declarations on the parameter. {attr}`Parameter.opts` holds every spelling an option answers to, and {attr}`Parameter.secondary_opts` the ones that set a boolean flag to false.
41|
42|```{eval-rst}
43|.. click:example::
44|
45|    @click.command()
46|    @click.argument('recipe')
47|    @click.option('-g', '--gluten-free/--no-gluten-free', default=False)
48|    def bake(recipe, gluten_free):
49|        """Bake the RECIPE, with or without gluten."""
50|        note = 'no gluten' if gluten_free else 'with gluten'
51|        click.echo(f'{recipe}: {note}')
52|
53|.. click:run::
54|
55|    invoke(bake, ['--gluten-free', 'brioche'], prog_name='bake')
56|
57|
58|.. click:run::
59|
60|    invoke(bake, ['--help'], prog_name='bake')
61|```
62|
63|The example holds one argument and one option. The table lists all five strings for each of them:
64|
65|| | `@click.argument('recipe')` | `@click.option('-g', '--gluten-free/--no-gluten-free')` |
66||---|---|---|
67|| `decls` | `('recipe',)` | `('-g', '--gluten-free/--no-gluten-free')` |
68|| `spec` | `RECIPE` | `--gluten-free` |
69|| `name` | `recipe` | `gluten_free` |
70|| `opts` | `['recipe']` | `['-g', '--gluten-free']` |
71|| `secondary_opts` | `[]` | `['--no-gluten-free']` |
72|
73|Click derives an option's `name` from the declaration with the longest prefix, so it picks `--gluten-free` over `-g`. It then lowercases that declaration and replaces its dashes with underscores, which gives `gluten_free`. The name must match the Python argument name of the decorated function. More declarations are available for options and are covered in {ref}`options`.
74|
75|An argument has a single declaration. It becomes the only entry in `opts`, and `name` is that declaration lowercased, with dashes replaced by underscores. The `spec` is the name in upper case. `secondary_opts` stays empty, since the parser binds an argument by name and never matches a spelling. To choose the spec an argument shows in help text, see {ref}`doc-meta-variables`.
76|
77|The help page above shows each `spec` where the user reads it: `RECIPE` in the usage line, and `-g, --gluten-free / --no-gluten-free` in the left column of the options list, which is the longer form {meth}`Parameter.get_help_spec` returns.
--- END FILE: docs/parameters.md ---

1|# Upgrade Guides
2|
3|```{contents}
4|:depth: 1
5|:local: true
6|```
7|
8|## Upgrading 8.3.X to 9.0
9|**This is under active construction and will not be finalized until 9.0.0 is released.**
10|
11|This guide assumes the user is on version 8.3.X.
12|
13|### Deprecations
14|
15|For each deprecation, provide a brief explanation, and direct users to new function / class if available.
16|- A parameter name that is not a valid Python identifier, or that is a [Python keyword](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#keywords), is deprecated and raises `TypeError` in 9.0. [`str.isidentifier()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.isidentifier) decides the first case, so `click.argument("0foo")` fails it. It accepts a keyword, so `click.option("--from")` names a parameter `from`, which no callback can declare. [Soft keywords](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/lexical_analysis.html#soft-keywords) such as `match` and `type` are contextual and unaffected, and `--True` and `--None` lower case out of the keyword set. To migrate, pass an explicit name (`click.option("--from", "source")`, `click.option("--0-file", "zero_file")`). An argument takes one declaration and has no explicit-name channel, so rename it and pass `metavar` to keep its old display (`click.argument("zero_file", metavar="0-FILE")`). See [#3827](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3827) and [#3866](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3866).
17|- An option name written as a Python identifier is deprecated when it is not already lower cased: `click.option("--x", "Foo_Bar")` names `foo_bar` rather than `Foo_Bar`. To migrate, spell the name the way the callback declares it. See [#3827](https://github.com/pallets/click/pull/3827).
18|- `CliRunner.isolated_filesystem()` is deprecated and will be removed in Click 9.0. The helper predates Python 3 and modern pytest, and it relies on `os.chdir`, which mutates process-global state and is therefore not thread-safe. Replace it with a temporary directory (`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory`, or pytest's `tmp_path` fixture) and pass absolute paths to the command instead of relying on the current working directory. To run commands in parallel, use process-based isolation (such as `pytest-xdist`) rather than threads, since `CliRunner.invoke()` also redirects the process-global standard streams and other interpreter-wide state. See [#3700](https://github.com/pallets/click/issues/3700), [#3501](https://github.com/pallets/click/issues/3501) and the [testing guide](testing.md#running-tests-in-parallel).
19|- `Parameter.human_readable_name` is deprecated and will be removed in Click 9.0. Use `Parameter.spec` instead, which returns how the user spells the parameter on the command line. For an argument the two agree, since both return the metavar. For an option the old property returned the internal `name`, so the value changes from `my_option` to `--my-option`. Click no longer reads the property, so an override in a subclass has no effect: override `Parameter.spec` instead. Defining a subclass that still overrides `human_readable_name` emits a `DeprecationWarning`. See the [parameter names](parameters.md#parameter-names) section for the three strings that designate a parameter.
20|
21|### Removals with prior deprecation
22|
23|For each removal, provide a brief explanation, and direct users to new function / class if available. If possible, deprecate and remove in 10.0.0, rather than removing outright.
24|- TBD
25|
26|### Removals with no prior deprecation
27|
28|The changes were not able to be deprecated prior to removal. Explain clearly why then were not able to be deprecated first.
29|- TBD
30|
31|### Changes
32|
33|- Error messages and deprecation warnings name an option by its spec rather than its internal name, so `The option 'my_option' is deprecated.` now reads `The option '--my-option' is deprecated.` Tests asserting on the old wording need updating.
34|
35|### Fixes
36|
37|- TBD
