1|# Standalone Application with Briefcase
2|
3|[Briefcase](https://briefcase.beeware.org/) is a tool for packaging Python
4|projects as standalone native applications. It can produce installers and
5|executables for macOS, Windows, and Linux that do not require the user to
6|install Python or any dependencies.
7|
8|- Produces platform-native installers (``.pkg`` on macOS, ``.msi`` on
9|    Windows, ``.deb``/``.rpm`` on Linux).
10|- Bundles a Python interpreter and all dependencies.
11|- Supports passing command line arguments to the app.
12|
13|This page outlines the basics of packaging a Click application with
14|Briefcase. Be sure to read its
15|[documentation](https://briefcase.beeware.org/en/stable/how-to/building/cli-apps/)
16|and use ``briefcase --help`` to understand what features are available.
17|
18|## Installation
19|
20|Install Briefcase in the virtual environment:
21|
22|```console
23|pip install briefcase
24|```
25|
26|## Configuration
27|
28|Add a ``[tool.briefcase]`` section and a
29|``[tool.briefcase.app.<app-name>]`` section to ``pyproject.toml``.
30|Set ``console_app = true`` so Briefcase treats the project as a command
31|line application rather than a GUI application.
32|
33|Given a Click application with the following project structure:
34|
35|```text
36|hello-cli/
37|    src/
38|        hello_cli/
39|            __init__.py
40|            app.py
41|    LICENSE
42|    pyproject.toml
43|```
44|
45|Where ``app.py`` contains a Click command:
46|
47|```python
48|import click
49|
50|@click.command()
51|@click.argument("name", default="World")
52|@click.option("--count", default=1, help="Number of times to greet.")
53|def main(name, count):
54|    """Greet someone by NAME (default: World)."""
55|    for _ in range(count):
56|        click.echo(f"Hello, {name}!")
57|```
58|
59|Add the following Briefcase configuration to ``pyproject.toml``:
60|
61|```toml
62|[tool.briefcase]
63|project_name = "Hello CLI"
64|bundle = "com.example"
65|version = "0.0.1"
66|url = "https://example.com/hello-cli"
67|license.file = "LICENSE"
68|author = "Your Name"
69|author_email = "you@example.com"
70|
71|[tool.briefcase.app.hello-cli]
72|formal_name = "Hello CLI"
73|description = "My first application"
74|long_description = """More details about the app should go here.
75|"""
76|sources = [
77|    "src/hello_cli",
78|]
79|console_app = true
80|requires = [
81|    "click",
82|]
83|```
84|
85|The key settings are:
86|
87|- ``console_app = true`` -- tells Briefcase this is a terminal
88|    application, not a GUI.
89|- ``sources`` -- the list of source packages to include.
90|- ``requires`` -- the Python dependencies to bundle (Click and any other
91|    libraries the project needs).
92|
93|## Entry Point
94|
95|Briefcase launches the application by running the package with
96|``python -m <package>``, so a ``__main__.py`` file **must** exist in the
97|package. Without it, Briefcase will not be able to start the application.
98|
99|Create ``__main__.py`` in the package directory and call the Click
100|command:
101|
102|```python
103|from hello_cli.app import main
104|
105|if __name__ == "__main__":
106|    main()
107|```
108|
109|## Running
110|
111|Use ``briefcase dev`` to run the application directly from the source
112|tree. Pass command line arguments after ``--``:
113|
114|```console
115|$ briefcase dev -- World
116|Hello, World!
117|$ briefcase dev -- World --count 2
118|Hello, World!
119|Hello, World!
120|```
121|
122|## Building and Packaging
123|
124|To create a distributable executable, run the following commands:
125|
126|```console
127|briefcase create
128|briefcase build
129|briefcase package
130|```
131|
132|``briefcase create`` downloads a Python interpreter and installs
133|dependencies into an isolated app bundle. ``briefcase build`` compiles
134|the app, and ``briefcase package`` produces the final platform installer.
135|
136|On macOS, this produces a ``.pkg`` installer. On Windows, it produces a
137|``.msi`` installer. On Linux, it produces a system package (``.deb``,
138|``.rpm``, etc.) for the current distribution.
139|
140|Once installed, users can run the application directly from the terminal:
141|
142|```console
143|$ hello-cli World
144|Hello, World!
145|$ hello-cli World --count 2
146|Hello, World!
147|Hello, World!
148|```
--- END FILE: docs/standalone-apps.md ---
--- FILE: docs/extending-click.md ---
1|# Extending Click
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|In addition to common functionality that is implemented in the library itself, there are countless patterns that can be
7|implemented by extending Click. This page should give some insight into what can be accomplished.
8|
9|```{contents}
10|:depth: 2
11|:local: true
12|```
13|
14|(custom-groups)=
15|
16|## Custom Groups
17|
18|You can customize the behavior of a group beyond the arguments it accepts by subclassing {class}`click.Group`.
19|
20|The most common methods to override are {meth}`~click.Group.get_command` and {meth}`~click.Group.list_commands`.
21|
22|The following example implements a basic plugin system that loads commands from Python files in a folder. The command is
23|lazily loaded to avoid slow startup.
24|
25|```python
26|import importlib.util
27|import os
28|import click
29|
30|class PluginGroup(click.Group):
31|    def __init__(self, name=None, plugin_folder="commands", **kwargs):
32|        super().__init__(name=name, **kwargs)
33|        self.plugin_folder = plugin_folder
34|
35|    def list_commands(self, ctx):
36|        rv = []
37|
38|        for filename in os.listdir(self.plugin_folder):
39|            if filename.endswith(".py"):
40|                rv.append(filename[:-3])
41|
42|        rv.sort()
43|        return rv
44|
45|    def get_command(self, ctx, name):
46|        path = os.path.join(self.plugin_folder, f"{name}.py")
47|        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
48|        module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
49|        spec.loader.exec_module(module)
50|        return module.cli
51|
52|cli = PluginGroup(
53|    plugin_folder=os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "commands")
54|)
55|
56|if __name__ == "__main__":
57|    cli()
58|```
59|
60|Custom classes can also be used with decorators:
61|
62|```python
63|@click.group(
64|    cls=PluginGroup,
65|    plugin_folder=os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "commands")
66|)
67|def cli():
68|    pass
69|```
70|
71|(aliases)=
72|
73|## Command Aliases
74|
75|Many tools support aliases for commands. For example, you can configure `git` to accept `git ci` as alias for
76|`git commit`. Other tools also support auto-discovery for aliases by automatically shortening them.
77|
78|It's possible to customize {class}`Group` to provide this functionality. As explained in {ref}`custom-groups`, a group
79|provides two methods: {meth}`~Group.list_commands` and {meth}`~Group.get_command`. In this particular case, you only
80|need to override the latter as you generally don't want to enumerate the aliases on the help page in order to avoid
81|confusion.
82|
83|The following example implements a subclass of {class}`Group` that accepts a prefix for a command. If there was a
84|command called `push`, it would accept `pus` as an alias (so long as it was unique):
85|
86|```{eval-rst}
87|.. click:example::
88|
89|    class AliasedGroup(click.Group):
90|        def get_command(self, ctx, cmd_name):
91|            rv = super().get_command(ctx, cmd_name)
92|
93|            if rv is not None:
94|                return rv
95|
96|            matches = [
97|                x for x in self.list_commands(ctx)
98|                if x.startswith(cmd_name)
99|            ]
100|
101|            if not matches:
102|                return None
103|
104|            if len(matches) == 1:
105|                return click.Group.get_command(self, ctx, matches[0])
106|
107|            ctx.fail(f"Too many matches: {', '.join(sorted(matches))}")
108|
109|        def resolve_command(self, ctx, args):
110|            # always return the full command name
111|            _, cmd, args = super().resolve_command(ctx, args)
112|            return cmd.name, cmd, args
113|```
114|
115|It can be used like this:
116|
117|```python
118|
119|    @click.group(cls=AliasedGroup)
120|    def cli():
121|        pass
122|
123|    @cli.command
124|    def push():
125|        pass
126|
127|    @cli.command
128|    def pop():
129|        pass
130|```
131|
132|See the [alias example](https://github.com/pallets/click/tree/main/examples/aliases) in Click's repository for another example.
--- END FILE: docs/extending-click.md ---
--- FILE: docs/handling-files.md ---
1|(handling-files)=
2|
3|# Handling Files
4|
5|```{currentmodule} click
6|```
7|
8|Click has built in features to support file and file path handling. The examples use arguments but the same principle
9|applies to options as well.
10|
11|(file-args)=
12|
13|## File Arguments
14|
15|Click supports working with files with the {class}`File` type. Some notable features are:
16|
17|- Support for `-` to mean a special file that refers to stdin when used for reading, and stdout when used for writing.
18|  This is a common pattern for POSIX command line utilities.
19|- Deals with `str` and `bytes` correctly for all versions of Python.
20|
21|Example:
22|
23|```{eval-rst}
24|.. click:example::
25|
26|    @click.command()
27|    @click.argument('input', type=click.File('rb'))
28|    @click.argument('output', type=click.File('wb'))
29|    def inout(input, output):
30|        """Copy contents of INPUT to OUTPUT."""
31|        while True:
32|            chunk = input.read(1024)
33|            if not chunk:
34|                break
35|            output.write(chunk)
36|
37|And from the command line:
38|
39|.. click:run::
40|
41|    with isolated_filesystem():
42|        invoke(inout, args=['-', 'hello.txt'], input=['hello'],
43|               terminate_input=True)
44|        invoke(inout, args=['hello.txt', '-'])
45|```
46|
47|## File Path Arguments
48|
49|For handling paths, the {class}`Path` type is better than a `str`. Some notable features are:
50|
51|- The `exists` argument will verify whether the path exists.
52|- `readable`, `writable`, and `executable` can perform permission checks.
53|- `file_okay` and `dir_okay` allow specifying whether files/directories are accepted.
54|- Error messages are nicely formatted using {func}`format_filename` so any undecodable bytes will be printed nicely.
55|
56|See {class}`Path` for all features.
57|
58|Example:
59|
60|```{eval-rst}
61|.. click:example::
62|
63|    @click.command()
64|    @click.argument('filename', type=click.Path(exists=True))
65|    def touch(filename):
66|        """Print FILENAME if the file exists."""
67|        click.echo(click.format_filename(filename))
68|
69|And from the command line:
70|
71|.. click:run::
72|
73|    with isolated_filesystem():
74|        with open('hello.txt', 'w') as f:
75|            f.write('Hello World!\n')
76|        invoke(touch, args=['hello.txt'])
77|        println()
78|        invoke(touch, args=['missing.txt'])
79|```
80|
81|## File Opening Behaviors
82|
83|The {class}`File` type attempts to be "intelligent" about when to open a file. Stdin/stdout and files opened for reading
84|will be opened immediately. This will give the user direct feedback when a file cannot be opened. Files opened for
85|writing will only be open on the first IO operation. This is done by automatically wrapping the file in a special
86|wrapper.
87|
88|File open behavior can be controlled by the boolean kwarg `lazy`. If a file is opened lazily:
89|
90|- A failure at first IO operation will happen by raising an {exc}`FileError`.
91|- It can help minimize resource handling confusion by lazily closing it. This is not needed for
92|  parameters, but is necessary for manually prompting. For manual prompts with the {func}`prompt` function you do not
93|  know if a stream like stdout was opened (which was already open before) or a real file was opened (that needs
94|  closing).
95|
96|Since files opened for writing will typically empty the file, the lazy mode should only be disabled if the developer is
97|absolutely sure that this is intended behavior.
98|
99|It is also possible to open files in atomic mode by passing `atomic=True`. In atomic mode, all writes go into a separate
100|file in the same folder, and upon completion, the file will be moved over to the original location. This is useful if a
101|file regularly read by other users is modified.
--- END FILE: docs/handling-files.md ---
--- FILE: docs/wincmd.md ---
1|# Windows Console Notes
2|
3|```{versionadded} 6.0
4|```
5|
6|Click emulates output streams on Windows to support unicode to the Windows console through separate APIs and we perform
7|different decoding of parameters.
8|
9|Here is a brief overview of how this works and what it means to you.
10|
11|## Unicode Arguments
12|
13|Click internally is generally based on the concept that any argument can come in as either byte string or unicode string
14|and conversion is performed to the type expected value as late as possible. This has some advantages as it allows us to
15|accept the data in the most appropriate form for the operating system and Python version.
16|
17|This caused some problems on Windows where initially the wrong encoding was used and garbage ended up in your input
18|data. We not only fixed the encoding part, but we also now extract unicode parameters from `sys.argv`.
19|
20|There is also another limitation with this: if `sys.argv` was modified prior to invoking a click handler, we have to
21|fall back to the regular byte input in which case not all unicode values are available but only a subset of the codepage
22|used for parameters.
23|
24|## Unicode Output and Input
25|
26|Unicode output and input on Windows is implemented through the concept of a
27|dispatching text stream. This means that when click first needs a text output
28|(or input) stream on windows it goes through a few checks to figure out if a
29|windows console is connected or not. If no Windows console is present then the
30|text output stream is returned as such and the encoding for that stream is set
31|to `utf-8` like on all platforms.
32|
33|However if a console is connected the stream will instead be emulated and use the cmd.exe unicode APIs to output text
34|information. In this case the stream will also use `utf-16-le` as internal encoding. However there is some hackery going
35|on that the underlying raw IO buffer is still bypassing the unicode APIs and byte output through an indirection is still
36|possible.
37|
38|- This unicode support is limited to `click.echo`, `click.prompt` as well as `click.get_text_stream`.
39|- Depending on if unicode values or byte strings are passed the control flow goes completely different places internally
40|  which can have some odd artifacts if data partially ends up being buffered. Click attempts to protect against that by
41|  manually always flushing but if you are mixing and matching different string types to `stdout` or `stderr` you will
42|  need to manually flush.
43|- The raw output stream is set to binary mode, which is a global operation on Windows, so `print` calls will be
44|  affected. Prefer `click.echo` over `print`.
45|- On Windows 7 and below, there is a limitation where at most 64k characters can be written in one call in binary mode.
46|  In this situation, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr` are replaced with wrappers that work around the limitation.
47|
48|Another important thing to note is that the Windows console's default fonts do not support a lot of characters which
49|means that you are mostly limited to international letters but no emojis or special characters.
--- END FILE: docs/wincmd.md ---
--- FILE: docs/click-concepts.md ---
1|# Click Concepts
2|
3|This section covers concepts about Click's design.
4|
5|```{contents}
6|---
7|depth: 1
8|local: true
9|---
10|```
11|
12|(callback-evaluation-order)=
13|
14|## Callback Evaluation Order
15|
16|Click works a bit differently than some other command line parsers in that
17|it attempts to reconcile the order of arguments as defined by the
18|programmer with the order of arguments as defined by the user before
19|invoking any callbacks.
20|
21|This is an important concept to understand when porting complex
22|patterns to Click from optparse or other systems.  A parameter
23|callback invocation in optparse happens as part of the parsing step,
24|whereas a callback invocation in Click happens after the parsing.
25|
26|The main difference is that in optparse, callbacks are invoked with the raw
27|value as it happens, whereas a callback in Click is invoked after the
28|value has been fully converted.
29|
30|Generally, the order of invocation is driven by the order in which the user
31|provides the arguments to the script; if there is an option called `--foo`
32|and an option called `--bar` and the user calls it as `--bar --foo`, then
33|the callback for `bar` will fire before the one for `foo`.
34|
35|There are three exceptions to this rule which are important to know:
36|
37|Eagerness:
38|>    An option can be set to be "eager".  All eager parameters are
39|>    evaluated before all non-eager parameters, but again in the order as
40|>    they were provided on the command line by the user.
41|
42|>    This is important for parameters that execute and exit like `--help`
43|>    and `--version`.  Both are eager parameters, but whatever parameter
44|>    comes first on the command line will win and exit the program.
45|
46|Repeated parameters:
47|>    If an option or argument is split up on the command line into multiple
48|>    places because it is repeated -- for instance, `--exclude foo --include
49|>    baz --exclude bar` -- the callback will fire based on the position of
50|>    the first option.  In this case, the callback will fire for
51|>    `exclude` and it will be passed both options (`foo` and
52|>    `bar`), then the callback for `include` will fire with `baz`
53|>    only.
54|
55|>    Note that even if a parameter does not allow multiple versions, Click
56|>    will still accept the position of the first, but it will ignore every
57|>    value except the last.  The reason for this is to allow composability
58|>    through shell aliases that set defaults.
59|
60|Missing parameters:
61|>    If a parameter is not defined on the command line, the callback will
62|>    still fire.  This is different from how it works in optparse where
63|>    undefined values do not fire the callback.  Missing parameters fire
64|>    their callbacks at the very end which makes it possible for them to
65|>    default to values from a parameter that came before.
66|
67|Most of the time you do not need to be concerned about any of this,
68|but it is important to know how it works for some advanced cases.
--- END FILE: docs/click-concepts.md ---

1|{.hide-header}
2|# Welcome to Click
3|
4|```{image} _static/click-name.svg
5|:align: center
6|:height: 200px
7|```
8|
9|Click is a Python package for creating beautiful command line interfaces
10|in a composable way with as little code as necessary. It's the "Command
11|Line Interface Creation Kit". It's highly configurable but comes with
12|sensible defaults out of the box.
13|
14|It aims to make the process of writing command line tools quick and fun
15|while also preventing any frustration caused by the inability to implement
16|an intended CLI API.
17|
18|Click in three points:
19|
20|- arbitrary nesting of commands
21|- automatic help page generation
22|- supports lazy loading of subcommands at runtime
23|
24|What does it look like? Here is an example of a simple Click program:
25|
26|```{eval-rst}
27|.. click:example::
28|
29|    import click
30|
31|    @click.command()
32|    @click.option('--count', default=1, help='Number of greetings.')
33|    @click.option('--name', prompt='Your name',
34|                  help='The person to greet.')
35|    def hello(count, name):
36|        """Simple program that greets NAME for a total of COUNT times."""
37|        for x in range(count):
38|            click.echo(f"Hello {name}!")
39|
40|    if __name__ == '__main__':
41|        hello()
42|
43|
44|And what it looks like when run:
45|
46|
47|.. click:run::
48|
49|    invoke(hello, ['--count=3'], prog_name='python hello.py', input='John\n')
50|
51|
52|It automatically generates nicely formatted help pages:
53|
54|
55|.. click:run::
56|
57|    invoke(hello, ['--help'], prog_name='python hello.py')
58|```
59|
60|You can get the library directly from PyPI:
61|
62|```
63|pip install click
64|```

--- FILE: docs/option-decorators.md ---
1|# Options Shortcut Decorators
2|
3|```{currentmodule} click
4|```
5|
6|For convenience commonly used combinations of options arguments are available as their own decorators.
7|
8|```{contents}
9|---
10|depth: 2
11|local: true
12|---
13|```
14|
15|## Password Option
16|
17|Click supports hidden prompts and asking for confirmation. This is useful for password input:
18|
19|```{eval-rst}
20|.. click:example::
21|
22|    import codecs
23|
24|    @click.command()
25|    @click.option(
26|        "--password", prompt=True, hide_input=True,
27|        confirmation_prompt=True
28|    )
29|    def encode(password):
30|        click.echo(f"encoded: {codecs.encode(password, 'rot13')}")
31|
32|.. click:run::
33|
34|    invoke(encode, input=['secret', 'secret'])
35|```
36|
37|Because this combination of parameters is quite common, this can also be
38|replaced with the {func}`password_option` decorator:
39|
40|```python
41|    @click.command()
42|    @click.password_option()
43|    def encrypt(password):
44|        click.echo(f"encoded: to {codecs.encode(password, 'rot13')}")
45|```
46|
47|## Confirmation Option
48|
49|For dangerous operations, it's very useful to be able to ask a user for confirmation. This can be done by adding a
50|boolean `--yes` flag and asking for confirmation if the user did not provide it and to fail in a callback:
51|
52|```{eval-rst}
53|.. click:example::
54|
55|    def abort_if_false(ctx, param, value):
56|        if not value:
57|            ctx.abort()
58|
59|    @click.command()
60|    @click.option('--yes', is_flag=True, callback=abort_if_false,
61|                  expose_value=False,
62|                  prompt='Are you sure you want to drop the db?')
63|    def dropdb():
64|        click.echo('Dropped all tables!')
65|
66|And what it looks like on the command line:
67|
68|.. click:run::
69|
70|    invoke(dropdb, input=['n'])
71|    invoke(dropdb, args=['--yes'])
72|
73|Because this combination of parameters is quite common, this can also be
74|replaced with the :func:`confirmation_option` decorator:
75|
76|.. click:example::
77|
78|    @click.command()
79|    @click.confirmation_option(prompt='Are you sure you want to drop the db?')
80|    def dropdb():
81|        click.echo('Dropped all tables!')
82|```
83|
84|## Version Option
85|
86|{func}`version_option` adds a `--version` option which immediately prints the version number and exits the program.
87|
88|The message and values it can show are intentionally limited, and its feature set is frozen. If you need values it does not expose, such as the Python version or git metadata, use {func}`custom_version_option` and produce the output yourself in a callback.
--- END FILE: docs/option-decorators.md ---
--- FILE: docs/entry-points.md ---
1|# Packaging Entry Points
2|
3|```{eval-rst}
4|.. currentmodule:: click
5|```
6|
7|It's recommended to write command line utilities as installable packages with
8|entry points instead of telling users to run ``python hello.py``.
9|
10|A distribution package is a ``.whl`` file you install with pip or another Python
11|installer. You use a ``pyproject.toml`` file to describe the project and how it
12|is built into a package. You might upload this package to PyPI, or distribute it
13|to your users in another way.
14|
15|Python installers create executable scripts that will run a specified Python
16|function. These are known as "entry points". The installer knows how to create
17|an executable regardless of the operating system, so it will work on Linux,
18|Windows, MacOS, etc.
19|
20|## Project Files
21|
22|To install your app with an entry point, all you need is the script and a
23|``pyproject.toml`` file. Here's an example project directory:
24|
25|```text
26|hello-project/
27|    src/
28|        hello/
29|            __init__.py
30|            hello.py
31|    pyproject.toml
32|```
33|
34|Contents of ``hello.py``:
35|
36|```{eval-rst}
37|.. click:example::
38|    import click
39|
40|    @click.command()
41|    def cli():
42|        """Prints a greeting."""
43|        click.echo("Hello, World!")
44|```
45|
46|Contents of ``pyproject.toml``:
47|
48|```toml
49|[project]
50|name = "hello"
51|version = "1.0.0"
52|description = "Hello CLI"
53|requires-python = ">=3.11"
54|dependencies = [
55|    "click>=8.1",
56|]
57|
58|[project.scripts]
59|hello = "hello.hello:cli"
60|
61|[build-system]
62|requires = ["flit_core<4"]
63|build-backend = "flit_core.buildapi"
64|```
65|
66|The magic is in the ``project.scripts`` section. Each line identifies one executable
67|script. The first part before the equals sign (``=``) is the name of the script that
68|should be generated, the second part is the import path followed by a colon
69|(``:``) with the function to call (the Click command).
70|
71|## Installation
72|
73|When your package is installed, the installer will create an executable script
74|based on the configuration. During development, you can install in editable
75|mode using the ``-e`` option. Remember to use a virtual environment!
76|
77|```console
78|$ python -m venv .venv
79|$ . .venv/bin/activate
80|$ pip install -e .
81|```
82|
83|Afterwards, your command should be available:
84|
85|```console
86|$ hello
87|Hello, World!
88|```
--- END FILE: docs/entry-points.md ---
--- FILE: docs/support-multiple-versions.md ---
1|# Supporting Multiple Versions
2|
3|If you are a library maintainer, you may want to support multiple versions of
4|Click. See the Pallets [version policy] for information about our version
5|numbers and support policy.
6|
7|[version policy]: https://palletsprojects.com/versions
8|
9|Most features of Click are stable across releases, and don't require special
10|handling. However, feature releases may deprecate and change APIs. Occasionally,
11|a change will require special handling.
12|
13|## Use Feature Detection
14|
15|Prefer using feature detection. Looking at the version can be tempting, but is
16|often more brittle or results in more complicated code. Try to use `if` or `try`
17|blocks to decide whether to use a new or old pattern.
18|
19|If you do need to look at the version, use {func}`importlib.metadata.version`,
20|the standardized way to get versions for any installed Python package.
21|
22|## Changes in 8.2
23|
24|### `ParamType` methods require `ctx`
25|
26|In 8.2, several methods of `ParamType` now have a `ctx: click.Context`
27|argument. Because this changes the signature of the methods from 8.1, it's not
28|obvious how to support both when subclassing or calling.
29|
30|This example uses `ParamType.get_metavar`, and the same technique should be
31|applicable to other methods such as `get_missing_message`.
32|
33|Update your methods overrides to take the new `ctx` argument. Use the
34|following decorator to wrap each method. In 8.1, it will get the context where
35|possible and pass it using the 8.2 signature.
36|
37|```python
38|import functools
39|import typing as t
40|import click
41|
42|F = t.TypeVar("F", bound=t.Callable[..., t.Any])
43|
44|def add_ctx_arg(f: F) -> F:
45|    @functools.wraps(f)
46|    def wrapper(*args: t.Any, **kwargs: t.Any) -> t.Any:
47|        if "ctx" not in kwargs:
48|            kwargs["ctx"] = click.get_current_context(silent=True)
49|
50|        return f(*args, **kwargs)
51|
52|    return wrapper  # type: ignore[return-value]
53|```
54|
55|Here's an example ``ParamType`` subclass which uses this:
56|
57|```python
58|class CommaDelimitedString(click.ParamType[str]):
59|    @add_ctx_arg
60|    def get_metavar(self, param: click.Parameter, ctx: click.Context | None) -> str:
61|        return "TEXT,TEXT,..."
62|```
--- END FILE: docs/support-multiple-versions.md ---

3|# Virtualenv
4|
5|## Why Use Virtualenv?
6|
7|You should use [Virtualenv](https://virtualenv.pypa.io/en/latest/) because:
8|
9|- It allows you to install multiple versions of the same dependency.
10|- If you have an operating system version of Python, it prevents you from changing its dependencies and potentially
11|  messing up your os.
12|
13|## How to Use Virtualenv
14|
15|Create your project folder, then a virtualenv within it:
16|
17|```console
18|$ mkdir myproject
19|$ cd myproject
20|$ python3 -m venv .venv
21|```
22|
23|Now, whenever you want to work on a project, you only have to activate the corresponding environment.
24|
25|

30|
31|        .. code-block:: text
32|
33|            $ . .venv/bin/activate

45|

53|

56|```

1|# Contributing
2|
3|This is a quick reference for Click-specific development
4|tasks. For setting up the development environment and the
5|general contribution workflow, see the Pallets [quick
6|reference](https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/quick/)
7|and the [detailed contributing
8|guide](https://palletsprojects.com/contributing/).
9|
10|## Extra Test Environments
11|
12|Click includes some extra test environments:
13|
14|-   `tox r -e stress` runs stress tests for race conditions
15|    in Click's test runner.
16|
17|    ```shell-session
18|    $ tox r -e stress
19|    ```
20|
21|-   `tox r -e random` runs tests in parallel in a random
22|    order to detect test pollution.
23|
24|    ```shell-session
25|    $ tox r -e random
26|    ```
27|
28|-   The nightly workflow
29|    (`.github/workflows/nightly.yaml`) runs Flask's test
30|    suite against `main` and `stable` to catch downstream
31|    regressions.
32|
33|## Code Style
34|
35|Avoid ternary expressions (`x if cond else y`): coverage
36|cannot measure both branches. Use an explicit `if`/`else`
37|block instead.
38|
39|Do not add unnecessary dependencies. If a feature can be
40|implemented with the standard library, do not pull in an
41|external package for it.
42|
43|## Formatting
44|
45|Wrap lines in Markdown files at 80 characters.

14|## Exit Codes
15|
16|When a command is executed from the command line, then an exit code is return. The exit code, also called exit status or exit status code, is a positive integer that tells you whether the command executed with or without errors.
17|
18|| Exit Code | Meaning                                         |
19||-----------|-------------------------------------------------|
20|| 0         | Success — the command completed without errors. |
21|| > 0       | Executed with errors                            |
22|
23|Exit codes greater than zero mean are specific to the Operating System, Shell, and/or command.
24|
25|To access the exit code, execute the command, then do the following depending:
26|
27|```{eval-rst}
28|.. tabs::
29|
30|    .. group-tab:: Powershell
31|
32|        .. code-block:: powershell
33|
34|           > echo $LASTEXITCODE
35|
36|    .. group-tab:: Bash
37|
38|        .. code-block:: bash
39|
40|            $ echo $?
41|
42|    .. group-tab:: Command Prompt
43|
44|
45|        .. code-block:: text
46|
47|            > echo %ERRORLEVEL%
48|```
49|
50|For Click specific behavior on exit codes, see {ref}`exception-handling-exit-codes`.

12|## Options over arguments
13|{ref}`Positional arguments <arguments>` should be used sparingly, and if used should be required:
14|- The more positional arguments there are, the more confusing the CLI invocation becomes to read. (This is true of Python too.)
15|- Making some arguments optional, or arbitrary length, can make it harder to reason about. The parser handles this consistently by filling left to right, with an error if there is a non-optional unfilled after that. But that's not obvious to a user just looking at a command line.
16|- A command should be doing one thing, and the arguments should be related directly to that.
17|    - A group, where the argument is the sub-command name.
18|    - A command acts on some files.
19|    - A command looks at a source and acts on a destination.

930|    incrementally instead of buffering until the end (issues #3242, #2542).

481|def test_tempdir_isolation_is_thread_safe():
482|    """The recommended replacement is thread-safe, unlike ``isolated_filesystem()``.
483|
484|    Each thread owns a ``tempfile.TemporaryDirectory`` and works through
485|    absolute paths, so there is no ``os.chdir`` and no process-global CWD race
486|    (the reason ``isolated_filesystem()`` is not thread-safe, issue #3501).
487|
488|    ``invoke()`` is deliberately not called concurrently here: it redirects the
489|    process-global standard streams, so parallel invocations in one process
490|    corrupt each other regardless of the filesystem. To run commands in
491|    parallel, use separate processes (like pytest-xdist), not threads.
492|    """
493|    import tempfile
494|    import threading
495|
496|    workers = 8
497|    cwd_before = os.path.realpath(os.getcwd())
498|    results: list[tuple[str, str, str]] = []
499|    barrier = threading.Barrier(workers)
500|    lock = threading.Lock()
501|
502|    def worker(index):
503|        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
504|            target = os.path.join(d, "data.txt")
505|            # Release every thread at once to maximize contention.
506|            barrier.wait(timeout=10)
507|            with open(target, "w") as f:
508|                f.write(f"payload-{index}")
509|            with open(target) as f:
510|                content = f.read()
511|            with lock:
512|                results.append(
513|                    (
514|                        os.path.realpath(d),
515|                        os.path.realpath(os.getcwd()),
516|                        content,
517|                    )
518|                )
519|
520|    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(i,)) for i in range(workers)]
521|    for t in threads:
522|        t.start()
523|    for t in threads:
524|        t.join(timeout=10)
525|
526|    assert len(results) == workers
527|    # Every thread had its own distinct directory.
528|    assert len({d for d, _, _ in results}) == workers
529|    # No thread mutated the process-global working directory.
530|    assert {cwd for _, cwd, _ in results} == {cwd_before}
531|    # Each thread read back exactly the payload it wrote, with no cross-talk.
532|    assert sorted(content for _, _, content in results) == sorted(
533|        f"payload-{i}" for i in range(workers)
534|    )

14|def test_path_dash_no_byteswarning():
15|    """Detecting the ``-`` dash sentinel must not compare ``bytes`` against
16|    ``str``, which raises a ``BytesWarning`` under ``python -bb``.
17|
18|    The warning is only emitted when the interpreter runs with ``-b``, so this
19|    has to be checked in a subprocess. ``-bb`` turns the warning into an error,
20|    so a clean exit means no mismatched comparison happened.
21|    """
22|    program = (
23|        "import click\n"
24|        "convert = click.Path(allow_dash=True).convert\n"
25|        "for value in ('-', '', b'-', b''):\n"
26|        "    convert(value, None, None)\n"
27|    )
28|    result = subprocess.run(
29|        [sys.executable, "-bb", "-c", program],
30|        capture_output=True,
31|        text=True,
32|    )
33|    assert result.returncode == 0, result.stderr
34|    assert "BytesWarning" not in result.stderr
